t: Performance on MySQL, v1: microservice databases, per-user queries
x: Customers are drawn from 600,000, uniformly by default. The skew block draws them from a Zipf distribution (s = 1.0), so that a few customers are very busy. Ranks map through a fixed shuffle, so the hot customers are spread across warehouses. Requests come from files of 200,000 URLs, through oha's --urls-from-file. Because the files are generated rather than taken from a URL regex, the user ids really are uniform. Closed loop for throughput: 30 s runs after a 5 s warm-up. Open loop for latency under load, latency corrected, at 25-110% of capacity measured in the same block. MySQL directly: sysbench sends each query's SQL, with the same random parameters, in autocommit: one statement per call, as a service with its own connection would. sysbench's standard oltp_read_only runs on its own tables for reference. What every run records: throughput, latency percentiles, every status code; CPU for the gateway, MySQL and the load generator; MySQL's Questions counter, for statements per request (exact and immediate); and the clock and temperature.

Each run starts a fresh process, so the cache starts empty: | Customers | Query | Calls/s | p50 | Cache hits | MySQL statements per call | | uniform | order_status | 582 (578-583) | 54.7 ms | - | 2.00 | | uniform | order_status_cached | 537 (535-541) | 59.3 ms | 5% | 1.90 | | Zipf | order_status | 581 (580-582) | 54.7 ms | - | 2.00 | | Zipf | order_status_cached | 717 (714-719) | 44.3 ms | 59% | 0.83 | Skewed traffic is where a response cache pays. With a few users making most of the calls, 59% were answered from the cache: +23% throughput, and 58% fewer statements reached MySQL. Uniform traffic doesn't benefit. With 600,000 equally likely users, only 5% of calls repeat within 30 s, and storing the 95% that never get reused costs 8%. Skew alone changes nothing without the cache: 581 against 582. MySQL's buffer pool already holds everything. The response cache here is per process, with no Redis: one worker, one cache. Several workers or instances without Redis each fill their own, so the hit rate falls; with QUERYAPIGATE_REDIS_URL they share one.

t: Performance on MySQL, v1: microservice databases, per-user queries
x: Six services in one MySQL server raise a question PostgreSQL's case didn't: can a key for one service be kept out of another's tables? This is the result of checking, not a performance number. A key with "allowed_tables": ["customer"], ad-hoc SQL, and a decoy billing.customer table: | SQL | Result | | SELECT COUNT() FROM crm.customer | 200: allowed, as intended | | SELECT COUNT() FROM billing.customer | 200: allowed, though it's another service's table | | SELECT COUNT(*) FROM billing.history | 403 table_not_allowed, as intended | On MySQL, the table allow-list matched bare table names (0.42 and earlier), so customer meant customer in any database the connection's user could reach. Only Trino connections matched catalog.schema.table. Fixed in 0.43: grants are schema-qualified on every SQL connection, so customer means the connection's own database's customer, and billing.customer is refused unless granted (the CHANGELOG's Security entry). Keeping services apart with MySQL's own grants is still the stronger boundary: one MySQL user per service, granted only its databases, each as its own QueryAPIGate connection, with keys granted only their service's connection. The integration tests check both. Saved queries aren't affected. A key granted named queries can only run those queries' SQL, and that SQL is written by whoever publishes it.

t: Performance on MySQL, v1: microservice databases, per-user queries
x: Every call is recorded in the store's event log (ADR 0020), which keeps events for 24 hours by default. In this run, the single-instance SQLite store took in 10.6 million events in five hours: 6 GB, about 570 bytes a call. That's more events than the 9.65 million requests in this report's totals, because the totals leave out the warm-ups before each run and the calls the round-trip block (m9) made to count statements. Run history, by contrast, stays small, because it keeps only the newest 50 runs per saved query version. This is the store's event log, in queryapigate.db. The server's own log on stdout is separate, and grew to 6.6 GB in the same run (see What to do with this). So plan the store's disk for the traffic you serve: | Sustained calls a second | Event log after 24 hours | | 50 | about 2.5 GB | | 500 | about 25 GB | | 2,000 | about 100 GB | QUERYAPIGATE_EVENTS_RETENTION_HOURS shortens how long events are kept, and the disk needed shrinks with it. On a PostgreSQL store, rows are larger, so expect more.

x: The rule from Performance, v3, with MySQL's figures: CPU: plan on about 440 calls a second per worker for order_status-class queries, or 490 with the metadata cache. That's 75% of measured capacity, where p99 is around 5 ms. Single-table lookups go about 15% higher. Waiting: a worker serves at most threads ÷ (query time + 3 round trips × network round-trip time) calls a second. Workers needed = the larger of the two figures divided into your calls a second, plus one spare. Two examples, with a 0.5 ms network round trip: | Calls | CPU figure | Waiting figure | Threads to use | | A per-user lookup, 0.1 ms in MySQL | 440 a second | 8 ÷ (0.1 + 3 × 0.5 ms) = 5,000 a second | CPU-bound: 1-2 threads beat 8 | | A 20 ms report query | 440 a second, or fewer | 8 ÷ (20 + 1.5 ms) = 370 a second | Waiting-bound: more threads help | MySQL won't be what you size first. On two cores it ran these queries 8-110 times faster than one gateway worker could ask for them. Its limit shows only with many workers on the heavier queries: 2.5 cores at 8 workers on stock_level.

x: For running QueryAPIGate in front of MySQL: One connection with a read-only user covering the services' databases works, and joins across them cost no more than joins within one. Use one connection per service if the services must be kept apart (see Isolating services). Turn on the metadata cache: +12-15% on one instance, even with the store on local SQLite. With several instances on a shared PostgreSQL store, it removes 2.5 ms of store round trips from every call. Its trade-off - a change made on another instance takes up to the TTL to arrive - is explained in PERFORMANCE.md. For per-user lookups on a database on the same host, run 1-2 threads per worker, not 8: up to 28% more throughput. Keep more for slow queries, and - from 0.43 - for a database across a network. Set them with QUERYAPIGATE_THREADS (from 0.43; see Tune a deployment for throughput). Put cache_ttl on queries whose callers repeat themselves - a dashboard a user keeps refreshing, popular accounts. Don't put it on queries every user calls once: there it costs 8%. Turn off the per-request log lines if a proxy already logs requests: QUERYAPIGATE_LOG_REQUESTS=off, and from 0.43 QUERYAPIGATE_ACCESS_LOG=off for gunicorn's access log. t: Performance on MySQL, v1: microservice databases, per-user queries
x: One machine, on separate cores. The scale-out is workers sharing four physical cores, not separate hosts. Every query is cheap, because the 1.9 GB of data sits in MySQL's buffer pool. Real per-user queries that touch disk, or take tens of milliseconds, move the limit from the gateway's CPU to waiting. The sizing rule covers that, but this run didn't measure it. The network is simulated: one-way delay, no jitter or loss. No TLS termination, load balancer or Redis in front of the gateway. One query shape per run. Real services mix them. Mixing reads and writes was measured on PostgreSQL (v3), not here. Writes weren't measured on MySQL at all. MySQL's general log counts statements, not packets. The third round trip was found by timing, and explained by reading mysql-connector's code. p99.99 wasn't measured: there were no 150 s runs in this session.

t: Performance, v2: an OLTP benchmark on PostgreSQL
x: Closed loop, for throughput: oha -c N keeps N callers, each sending its next request when the last one answers. Each run is 30 s, after a 5 s warm-up at 8 callers that also fills the pool and the governance caches. Open loop, for latency against load: oha -q R --latency-correction sends R requests a second whatever happens, and measures each from when it should have been sent. That avoids coordinated omission, where a closed loop under-reports latency at saturation because a slow answer delays the next request. Rates of 25%, 50%, 75%, 90%, 100% and 110% of the build's closed-loop capacity, 20 s each, 128 connections available. Interleaved. Within a block, every round runs every build (or setting) once, in an order rotated each round - A B C, then B C A, then C A B - so none always runs first, warmest or coolest.

x: For running QueryAPIGate: Plan on about 550 requests a second per worker for fast OLTP queries, or 650 with the metadata cache. That's 75% of capacity, where p99 stays under 4 ms. Then measure your own queries, which will usually cost more than these. Turn on QUERYAPIGATE_METADATA_CACHE_TTL if a few seconds' delay is acceptable for a change made on another instance to reach this one. In return, a worker serves 16-24% more, PostgreSQL does half the work, and across a network a single call takes 40% less time. Its trade-off is in PERFORMANCE.md. For fast queries, try --threads 2 to 4. Keep 8 if calls wait on slow queries, exports or /events. Turn off gunicorn's access log if a proxy in front already logs requests: +7%. Scale with processes on their own cores. Hyperthreads gave about half a core each here. For QueryAPIGate itself - findings worth an issue each, in the order I'd take them: Fewer round trips per query. Set default_transaction_read_only and statement_timeout once per pooled session, or send BEGIN and SET LOCAL in one round trip with the query. That's 4 round trips down to 1 or 2, and over a network, the largest remaining part of a call. Skip refuse_store_access's path checks for server databases. Only SQLite, DuckDB and H2 open a file. That would save 7-10% of CPU on every PostgreSQL, MySQL, ClickHouse and Trino call. Cache the masking hash key. It's read on every go

x: One machine. The gateway, the database and the load generator share it, on separate cores but one memory bus and one cooling system. This page is what we measured, where the time goes, and how to measure it on your own hardware. Every number comes from one laptop, so read them as a guide to proportions, not a promise. t: Performance
x: Column masking has to know which source column each result column comes from, so it traces the query through its aliases, joins, subqueries and unions - a few milliseconds of SQL analysis. The table check parses the query to find the tables it reads. Before the caches, both ran on every call, and a governed key was 4-8 times slower than a plain one. Caching doesn't change what is masked or what is refused. A query that can't be traced or checked is refused every time, the same as before. Both caches have a fixed size, so a key sending many different ad-hoc queries can't make them grow without bound.

t: Performance
x: QUERYAPIGATE_METADATA_CACHE_TTL (seconds, off by default) keeps the rows a call reads from the store - the API key, the saved query, the connection - in memory for that long, instead of reading them again on every call. In the tests above, it took the store out of a call's path: 10-20% more throughput for a container, and a third off the latency of a single call (1.8 ms to 1.2 ms). What it caches is the rows, never a decision: whether a key is active, expired, used from an allowed address or still inside a rotation's grace period is checked on every call, against the cached row. What it can delay is a change: A change made through the same server - the Console, the Management API - is seen at once: every change to the store clears this server's cache. A change made anywhere else - another instance, another gunicorn worker, the queryapigate CLI, an edit straight to the database - is seen up to one TTL later. A key revoked on one instance keeps working on the others for that long. So it is a trade: a few seconds of delay for a revocation that reaches other instances, for fewer reads on the store. Leave it off if a revoked key must stop working everywhere at once; with one instance, a TTL of a few seconds changes nothing anyone would notice. Where it is set: | Setup | QUERYAPIGATE_METADATA_CACHE_TTL | Why | | The server and the Docker image | 0, off | The image runs anywhere, ofte

t: Performance
x: More containers, not more threads. Each container is one Python process. Run several behind a load balancer on a shared PostgreSQL store and Redis, and throughput grows with the number of containers - see Scaling out and Run several instances behind a load balancer. Why one worker per container. /metrics is counted per process (and, without Redis, so are rate limits), so with several workers in one container a scraper would read one worker's numbers at random. One worker per container keeps every count complete. The eight threads are for waiting. They let one container keep serving while some calls wait on a slow database or a long-lived /events connection. They don't add CPU: in an earlier, slower run on the same laptop, one worker served 119, 169 and 164 requests a second with 1, 2 and 8 threads. The database can take it. In that earlier run, at 8 processes and 1,700 requests a second, PostgreSQL used about four cores - mostly for QueryAPIGate's own store, not the queries. The metadata cache takes most of that away.

t: Performance
x: Cache what you can. A saved query with a cache_ttl is answered without the database for repeat calls. Turn on the metadata cache if a few seconds' delay for a change made on another instance is acceptable. Tune the connection pool for the number of callers - Diagnose and tune the connection pool. The default of 8 idle connections matches the Docker image's 8 threads. Below that, a busy server closes connections only to open new ones for the next calls. Stream large results with ?stream=true instead of paging through them - see Streaming exports. Look at the database first. On anything bigger than a primary-key lookup, the query plan and indexes usually matter more than anything in the gateway.

t: Threat model
x: SECURITY.md tells you what to do - a checklist to run through before a deployment goes live. This page explains why: what QueryAPIGate is actually defending against, how each defense works under the hood, and - just as importantly - where the defenses stop and become the operator's job instead. Read it before deciding QueryAPIGate is (or isn't) an appropriate way to expose a database to something you don't fully trust.

t: Threat model
x: QueryAPIGate sits between a caller and one or more real databases. Four things are worth protecting, in roughly descending order of damage if lost: The ability to execute arbitrary SQL/Mongo operations against a connected database - the whole point of the service, and therefore its biggest liability if it reaches the wrong caller. Database credentials - held in the store (queryapigate.db, or a PostgreSQL schema), needed to reach the databases at all. Query results and SQL text - a saved query's SQL, and the rows it returns, can themselves be sensitive (customer data, schema details, business logic) independent of write access. API key secrets and the audit trail - if either is compromised, every other control built on top of them (scoping, accountability) stops meaning anything.

t: Threat model
h: Who might attack it, and from where
x: An unauthenticated network attacker - anyone who can reach the HTTP port at all. The only thing standing between them and everything above is whether QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY is set (see Open-access mode below) and whether TLS is actually terminated somewhere in front of the service. A caller holding a scoped (non-admin) API key, acting maliciously or - more realistically - a legitimate integration whose key has leaked. The threat here isn't "can they authenticate," it's "how far can that one key's specific grants actually reach." An administrator - the holder of the shared QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY or of a named administrator's admin token - or anyone who steals one. What they can change depends on the role (below); but every role except auditor can run any SQL on every connection, so for the data each is equivalent to a database superuser scoped to whatever connections exist. This tier is not defended against by QueryAPIGate itself - see Non-goals. Someone with filesystem or volume access to QUERYAPIGATE_HOME - a compromised host, a misconfigured backup, a leaked volume snapshot. queryapigate.db is a single SQLite file holding connections, saved-query SQL, API key hashes, roles, execution history and the audit log - see Data at rest.

t: Threat model
Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › Authentication: one shared secret, or many scoped ones
x: Every request carries (or omits) an X-API-Key header, checked once per request in app.py's before_request hook, before anything else runs. Two kinds of key exist: The admin key (QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY) is a single value living in the server's environment, compared with hmac.compare_digest (constant-time, so response timing can't be used to guess it character by character). It is never stored anywhere on disk - only in the process environment - and grants everything: every connection, every saved query, admin-only routes (managing connections, keys, roles). Admin tokens (qagadm_...) belong to named administrators (admins.py, ADR 0003): generated by the server, shown once, stored only as a SHA-256 hash and looked up by it, like scoped keys - but in their own table, and they authorize management by role rather than data access by grant. Each can carry an expiry; deactivating an administrator stops all of theirs at once. Scoped keys (POST /api/v1/api-keys, owners and admins to create) are generated by the server and shown exactly once - their secret is never stored, only a SHA-256 hash, in queryapigate.db's api_keys table. A lost scoped key cannot be recovered, only revoked and replaced, the same property a password reset flow gives you and a plaintext-stored secret never could. A key's secret can be reissued (ADR 0009, POST /api/v1/api-keys/{name}/rotate, access.write): the new one

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › Authorization: what a scoped key can actually do
x: Three grant fields say what a key reaches, and they add up - a saved query is reachable if connections, collections or queries reaches it. The rest narrow what that reach may do, and none of them widens what another restricts: | Grant | Narrows | | connections | Which database connections ad-hoc SQL can target ("*" = all). | | collections | Which saved queries are reachable, by current collection membership - re-evaluated live, no wildcard. | | queries | Specific saved-query names reachable regardless of connection grants - the only way to give an external client curated access with no ad-hoc SQL capability at all. | | allow_writes | Whether write statements are permitted at all, on top of the server-wide QUERYAPIGATE_ALLOW_WRITES ceiling (a key can never grant itself more than the server allows). | | allowed_write_ops | Which specific write verbs (insert/update/delete/...) if writes are allowed. | | allowed_tables | Which tables a statement may touch - enforced via a real SQL parser (sqlglot), not a regex; unsupported for H2/JDBC connections, which are refused outright for a table-restricted key rather than silently under-checked. | | rate_limit | A per-key request budget, additive with the server-wide IP-based limit, never a way around it. | | expires_at | A day after which the key stops authenticating at all, checked live on every request. | | allowed_ips | Which source IPs/

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › Administration: named administrators and roles
x: The Management API (/api/v1) is for administrators only. Every operation needs one capability, and each of four fixed roles holds a fixed set (adminroles.py), checked before any route runs; a test fails if an operation has no entry, so a new route can't ship unguarded. A scoped key or signed-in app user gets 403 admin_only; an administrator whose role lacks the capability, 403 role_forbidden. | Role | Can change | Data plane | | owner | everything, including administrators | any SQL, every connection | | admin | connections, API keys and roles, queries, cache - not administrators | any SQL, every connection | | developer | saved queries and collections | any SQL, every connection | | auditor | nothing - reads configuration, the audit log and history | none | What this buys, and what it doesn't: A stolen developer token can't mint keys, change connections or create administrators - but it can read every row on every connection. Roles bound management blast radius; for data, the database account behind each connection is still the backstop. Give someone a scoped API key instead when they need less data reach. Who can call what is an owner's or admin's decision. Moving a query into a collection, or merging collections, in a way that gives an API key or role new reach needs access.write, even for a role that may otherwise organise queries. A developer still decides what saved queri

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › Workspaces: one team's reach, not another's (ADR 0023, experimental)
x: Workspaces (ADR 0023) let several teams administer one server: each owns its connections, saved queries, keys, roles, destinations and exports. The boundary they draw is between teams who share a server, not between a hosted service's tenants. What it holds against, and how: Every lookup is in one workspace. A request's workspace is settled once (app.settle_workspace(), kept on the request, never on a thread a later request reuses) and every statement on a workspace's table filters on it - names are unique per workspace in the store's own keys, so there is nothing for a forgotten filter to match by name alone across workspaces. Work that outlives the request - a stream's rows, queued history, events and usage counts carries the workspace it was started in. tests/test_workspace_isolation.py builds two workspaces with the same names for everything and checks each route reaches only its own: a lookup that forgot its workspace shows up there as the other workspace's data. A key can't leave its workspace, prefix or not: its secret says which workspace it is in. Naming another, or one that doesn't exist, is the same 404 - a caller can't use the error to list workspaces. A signed-in user can't leave their workspace either. A federated (JWT) user's workspace comes from the token - the QUERYAPIGATE_JWT_WORKSPACE_CLAIM claim, or the default workspace when that isn't configured - never fr

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › Column masking: which values leave
x: A mask grant on a key, role or export (ADR 0005) hashes, masks, nulls or drops the values of named source columns in everything that caller receives. The design choice that matters: result columns are traced to their sources through the SQL (sqlglot lineage, by position, with the connection's schema for SELECT ), not matched by name - so SELECT email AS e, lower(email), a CTE or a UNION is still masked - and anything that can't be traced is refused before it runs, never served unmasked. Probing during the build found, and the tests now hold against, the ways tracing could be led astray: DuckDB's COLUMNS('regex') (columns picked by pattern), a table alias that renames columns (customer AS c(a, e)), SELECT over a NATURAL/USING join (fewer columns than parsed, which would shift every mask), whole-row references (row_to_json(c)), and a VALUES row holding a subquery. The database's error text, which can quote a value, is never returned to a caller with rules. The cache is keyed per set of rules, and run history records what was masked. What remains: Inference. A caller that writes SQL can filter and group on a masked column (WHERE email LIKE 'a%', GROUP BY email) - masking hides values in results, not answers about them. For callers near sensitive data, especially AI agents, grant saved queries only, or allowed_tables on a view that leaves the column out. Hashes show equality. hash

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › Query execution: what actually stops a bad statement
x: This is the part worth being the most precise about, because it's also the part with the sharpest edges. Bound :name parameters are real parameterization. sqltools.bind_parameters() rewrites :name into the target driver's native paramstyle and hands values to the driver separately from the SQL text - the same mechanism that makes parameterized queries safe in any language. Values never become part of the SQL string, so this path has no SQL-injection surface by construction. The read-only / single-statement guard is a regex-based classifier, not a SQL parser. It strips string literals and comments (dialect-aware - MySQL/ClickHouse honor backslash escapes inside string literals by default, PostgreSQL/SQLite/H2 do not, and the guard accounts for the difference), checks for a bare ; outside what's left to block multi-statement smuggling, and classifies the leading keyword against an allow-list when writes aren't permitted - then looks behind a read-only one for writes it can hide: a writable CTE (WITH d AS (DELETE ... RETURNING *) SELECT ...), the statement EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs, and SELECT ... INTO. The same rule covers a key's allowed_write_ops. PostgreSQL, MySQL, ClickHouse and SQLite connections also run read-only queries read-only in the database (a read-only transaction on PostgreSQL and MySQL, a read-only setting or file mode on ClickHouse and SQLite), so the database refuses

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › MongoDB: a find() and nothing else
x: A mongo connection has no SQL guard to rely on; what keeps it read-only and inside its grants is that only one operation exists. Reviewed for its graduation to tier 1 in 0.37 (ADR 0022): Only find() is ever sent - no aggregation pipeline, no write, no command a caller can name. There is no allow_writes to get wrong. No server-side JavaScript. $where, $function and $accumulator are refused in the filter, the projection and the sort (mongotools.py), on every request and when a saved query is saved. Until 0.34.2 only the filter was checked, and MongoDB 4.4+ evaluates $function in a projection: any key with a MongoDB connection could run JavaScript on the database server. A parameter is a value, never operators. A :name placeholder takes a string, number, boolean, null or a list of those - {"$ne": null} is refused (param_invalid), not run as a filter matching the whole collection. Until 0.34.2 an untyped placeholder took any JSON. allowed_tables is the collections a key may read, checked before the server is asked anything - in paged runs, streams and exports. Until 0.34.1 it wasn't checked on MongoDB at all. Collection names are compared case-insensitively, as table names are, so orders in a grant also reads a collection named Orders: a limit, documented with the type. The time limit is the cursor's maxTimeMS, over the whole cursor - a stream included - and the caller's concurrenc

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › Trino: a federation engine behind one grant (ADR 0026, experimental)
x: A trino connection reaches every catalog the Trino cluster federates - Hive, Iceberg, Kafka, other databases - through one QueryAPIGate connection. That reach is the point, and the risk: the controls other SQL connections have within one database must hold across catalogs. Reviewed for its introduction (experimental, ADR 0026): allowed_tables is matched fully qualified (catalog.schema.table), not by bare name. A reference's missing parts are filled from the connection's default catalog (its database field) and schema, and a grant is filled the same way (tableguard.qualify_grant). So a grant of orders reaches only the default catalog+schema's orders - never orders in another catalog or schema - and hive.sales.orders reaches exactly that table. This is the federation-specific fix: bare-name matching would have let one grant read the same table name in every catalog the connection can see. The schema browser applies the same qualified grants (schema._only_allowed). A data-reading table function is refused. tableguard passes only pure value generators; a Trino TABLE(...) polymorphic function that reads data - system.query(...) (a pass-through that would run arbitrary SQL on a backend), table_changes(...) - names no base table the allow-list can account for, so a table-restricted key is refused (table_not_allowed), as read_parquet()/url() are on other dialects. Read-only rests on th

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › The Rust data plane (ADR 0028, a prototype)
x: A second process, dataplane/, can listen on the public port in front of the Python server. It serves /q/ reads itself from plans Python gives it, and forwards everything else unchanged (ADR 0028). It's in the Docker image, and the Helm chart's dataplane block runs it as a second container in each API server pod (ADR 0030), but it runs only when started: nothing changes for a deployment that doesn't. It isn't in the PyPI package. Where it does run: It makes no security decision of its own. The SQL guard, the table allow-list, masking and every refusal stay in Python. A plan is Python's verdict for one key, one saved query version and one connection, made only on a call that succeeded, and only for a scoped API key in the default workspace with no rate limit, quota, concurrency, time or row limit of its own. Administrators, signed-in users (JWT, SSO, MCP OAuth), other workspaces, writes, streams, other formats and every dialect but PostgreSQL and MySQL are always forwarded. With a server-wide rate limit or OpenTelemetry tracing configured, it forwards every call. Behind trusted proxies, it finds the client as Python does. With QUERYAPIGATE_TRUST_PROXY set, the address a key's allowed_ips is checked against comes from X-Forwarded-For, as ProxyFix takes it, so this is an access decision made in two places. The data plane serves only a call whose forwarding headers read one way: one

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › The ClickHouse run store (ADR 0029, a prototype)
x: With QUERYAPIGATE_RUN_STORE_URL set, run history, the event log and usage rollups are kept in ClickHouse rather than the metadata store (ADR 0029). Keys, queries, connections and the audit log stay in the metadata store, so the run store never decides who may do what. Where it is used: What its credentials reach. The run store holds every run's history entry - who called, which query, when, how many rows, the error message, an ad-hoc statement as QUERYAPIGATE_HISTORY_ADHOC_SQL keeps it - but never a result row. A stolen credential reads those entries, and one that can insert can forge runs and events: history and live events would show calls that didn't happen. It can't change a key, a query or a grant. Give the data plane a user that can only insert into events (guide 65); its rows reach history and the rollups through views that run as the user who made them. What such a writer puts in a row stays inside its own event: a frame's data is always one line (a line break can't start a frame of the writer's own), and ids above 2^53 are refused by the table. In transit: https:// is required except to a loopback host, since the URL carries a password and every run. It is a secret setting: it can be read from a file (QUERYAPIGATE_RUN_STORE_URL_FILE), is masked in Settings, and only its host, port and database are written to the metadata store or the log. Queries are parameterised. Eve

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › Secrets at rest
x: Connection passwords in the store can be a literal string, an "${ENV_VAR}" reference resolved from the process environment at load time (never written back to disk), or - with QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY set - Fernet-encrypted at rest. Encryption is opt-in, not the default; without a secret key, a connection password is only as protected as the file/volume it sits in. The key itself must be kept outside QUERYAPIGATE_HOME and out of version control - there is no recovery path for an encrypted password without it, by design, the same property that makes it real encryption rather than obfuscation. API responses always mask stored passwords regardless of how they're stored. The key can be rotated without taking a connection down (ADR 0009): QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY lists the new key first and the old one after it, queryapigate rekey re-encrypts every stored password under the new one in a single transaction (all or nothing), and the old key is then removed. A key suspected leaked is replaced the same way; backups taken before the rekey still open with the old key, so they need retiring with it.

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › The audit trail
x: The audit log is a hash chain (ADR 0012): each entry's hash covers the previous entry's, so changing, removing, inserting or reordering one breaks every hash after it, and queryapigate audit verify (and a check every 5 minutes) names the first. Against someone who can write to the store, a plain hash is only consistency - they can recompute it - so with QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_KEY set the chain is HMAC-signed with a key kept outside the store, and a key once set means every newer entry must carry it. What the chain can't show alone: the newest entries deleted (its end can't know what came after it), and a rewrite by someone holding both the store and the key. Both are why a copy outside - the SIEM stream, or the export file shipped elsewhere - matters. The stream sends each entry with its seq and hash over TLS - the server's certificate verified, the client's optional - so a later rewrite of the store contradicts what the SIEM already has; its delivery is at least once, and syslog over TCP can lose the batch sent to a SIEM that dies without closing the connection (OTLP, acknowledged per batch, doesn't). queryapigate audit verify --file checks the SIEM's copy on its own - repeats from at-least-once delivery dropped only when exact. Reviewed for 0.32 (ADR 0019). Looked at, against rsyslog, syslog-ng and the OpenTelemetry Collector rather than a receiver of our own: the server's certif

t: Threat model
x: QueryAPIGate does not terminate TLS itself - that is explicitly the reverse proxy's job (Caddy, nginx, Traefik; see DEPLOYMENT.md). An API key travels in a request header, so serving over plain HTTP means the key is recoverable by anyone who can observe the traffic - TLS termination in front of QueryAPIGate is not optional once a key exists. Response headers don't depend on that proxy (ADR 0010): every response sets nosniff, Cache-Control: no-store (a cached saved query private, never shareable: callers authenticate with X-API-Key, which HTTP's shared-cache rule doesn't cover - the 0.22.1 fix) and, on API responses, a CSP that runs nothing and a no-referrer policy. HSTS is the deployer's choice (QUERYAPIGATE_HSTS_MAX_AGE), sent only over HTTPS. /docs, where people type an API key, loads one exact Swagger UI release with Subresource Integrity hashes and a CSP allowing only those files: a compromised CDN, or a bad release of the library, can't run script there. The Console bundles everything it runs. Tracing (ADR 0010, experimental, off unless an OTLP endpoint is set) sends spans to a collector the deployer runs. Its readers are treated like the audit log's: no data access. So spans carry the route, the saved query's name and the row count - never a parameter value, row, statement, header or credential, and not exception messages, which can carry values; a test enforces it on eve

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › On Kubernetes (the Helm chart, ADR 0013)
x: The chart's pods run as UID 1000, with a read-only root filesystem, every capability dropped, the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile, and no service account token: QueryAPIGate never calls the Kubernetes API, so a compromised pod has no credential for it. The server writes only to /data (the store's volume, or an empty directory on PostgreSQL) and /tmp. What stays the deployer's: Secrets in a Kubernetes Secret are only as safe as the cluster. Anyone who can get secrets in the namespace, or read etcd unencrypted, reads the API key, the Fernet key and the database URL. Keep that RBAC narrow, and encrypt Secrets at rest. With secret.create, the values are also in your values file and in Helm's release record (itself a Secret in the namespace). existingSecret keeps them out of both. The chart refuses a secret setting in config: the keys, the database and Redis URLs, the SSO client secret and OTLP headers. config is plain text in the Deployment, where get deployments reads it. NetworkPolicy is off by default, because the right rules depend on the cluster. Without it, any pod in the cluster can reach the API and the MCP server. networkPolicy.enabled limits who can connect in, and narrows what a pod can reach out to, to egress - so a stolen admin key can't point a new connection at an internal address it doesn't list. The chart and image are signed by this repository's release workflow (f

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › Configuration as code (ADR 0014)
x: A configuration file can change anything an owner can - connections, grants, keys - so applying one is an owner's capability (config.apply), and so is reading what applying one would do. What keeps a file safe to put in git, and what's still the deployer's: A file never holds a secret. A password must be a ${VAR} reference - a literal is refused - and a reference to the server's own settings or credentials, or to a variable QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_ENV_VARS doesn't list, is refused, as through the API (a connection pointed at a host of the author's would otherwise send it there). Export turns stored values into references. Not checked: a secret inside another field - a JDBC URL with password= in it - which is in the file as it is in the store. A key is in a file by its secret's hash. That's safe to publish only because the secret is 32 random bytes: config new-key makes one. A key someone gave a guessable secret could be found from its hash, offline. Two keys can't share a secret. Who can change the file can change the server. With QUERYAPIGATE_CONFIG_FILE (the chart's configAsCode), anyone who can edit the file - the repository's main branch, the ConfigMap - has an owner's reach at the next start. Protect the branch and require review; that is the control this feature exists to give. Applying is all or nothing, and audited - each change via: config, under one config_applied entry w

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › Secrets from secrets managers (ADR 0015)
x: A reference - ${file:...}, ${vault:...}, ${aws-sm:...} - or a connection's credentials lets an administrator make the server fetch a secret and use it as a password. The server's identity (its files, Vault token, IAM role) reaches far more than any one connection should, and an administrator could point a connection at a host of theirs to be sent whatever it fetches. So: Nothing is reachable until the deployer says so: QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_FILE_DIRS, QUERYAPIGATE_VAULT_PATHS, QUERYAPIGATE_VAULT_DATABASE_ROLES, QUERYAPIGATE_AWS_SECRET_PREFIXES and QUERYAPIGATE_AWS_RDS_HOSTS, checked when a reference is saved and again when it's used. The store's own folder is never readable, and the server's own QUERYAPIGATE_*/OTEL_* settings never reachable, by any reference - nor, through ${file:...}, a file one of them or the server's own credentials name, the Kubernetes and EKS service account tokens, or /proc. A file is opened at the real path that was checked, so a symbolic link changed in between can't point it elsewhere. A Vault database role can be bound to the host its credentials may go to (reporting-ro@warehouse.internal), and an RDS IAM token is made only for the listed hosts. h: Security architecture, by control › What is kept, and the cryptography it rests on (ADR 0016)
x: Where data goes is the inventory; what bears on threats: Values stay out of what's kept by default. Run history keeps parameter names, never values; traces never hold one; the access log has paths without query strings and no referrer (QUERYAPIGATE_ACCESS_LOG_QUERY puts the query string back - then the log platform holds whatever callers put in URLs). What can still carry a value: an ad-hoc statement's text in history and the log (QUERYAPIGATE_HISTORY_ADHOC_SQL=hash keeps both to its SHA-256), a database's own error message in the log, an agent's write arguments for 30 days, an export's watermark, and the response cache's rows. Treat the log platform and the store as holding personal data. Erasure is an owner's, and it isn't silent. history forget deletes a caller's runs and usage counts - any caller, a key's too, so an owner could clear the record of what a key ran. The audit log records each erasure, its counts and the caller's SHA-256 (key names are few: the hash names the key to anyone who has the list), so it can be seen, not undone. The audit log itself can't be erased from without breaking its chain (ADR 0012). The cryptography is FIPS-approved algorithms only, enforced by a test over the code; whether it runs in a validated module is the platform's (a FIPS-mode OpenSSL, the distribution's cryptography). h: Security architecture, by control › Live events (ADR 0020)
x: GET /events - on the main server, and queryapigate events for many clients - streams each run as it happens: which query, on which connection, by which key, how it went, and an ad-hoc run's SQL as history keeps it. So: Never public. A real key or a signed-in user's token, in a header - never the URL, where it would reach access logs - unless the server runs with no keys at all. A stream is checked again every minute, so a revoked key or an expired token loses it within about a minute and a quarter. The admin key and data administrators see every run; anyone else only their own - the runs made with that key, or by that user, since the key was created. Filters only narrow that, and their values are bound, never SQL. Key names can't hold the : of jwt:, and an administrator's name can't be a key's. Resource use is bounded: QUERYAPIGATE_EVENTS_MAX_CONNECTIONS streams a process, QUERYAPIGATE_EVENTS_MAX_STREAMS on the main server (each a request thread), QUERYAPIGATE_RATE_LIMIT before a key is even checked, 10 seconds and 100 headers for a request, and a client that stops reading cut off once 1,000 events wait for it. Not bounded: how many of those streams one key holds. Kept for a while, and forgettable: the event log keeps QUERYAPIGATE_EVENTS_RETENTION_HOURS (24 by default), and history forget erases a caller's events with their runs. Reviewed for 0.34 (ADR 0021). t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › Rate limiting and abuse prevention
x: The rate limiter throttles both by source IP (server-wide) and, additively, by API key (rate_limit grant). Without QUERYAPIGATE_REDIS_URL its state is in each process's memory, so running more than one process silently multiplies the effective limit. With it, every instance and process counts against one budget in Redis (an atomic token bucket, on Redis's own clock); if Redis becomes unreachable, each process falls back to its own counting - limits stay enforced, per process, never lifted - and the rate_limits_not_shared alert and a metric say so. QUERYAPIGATE_TRUST_PROXY tells the server how many reverse-proxy hops to trust when resolving the real client IP from X-Forwarded-For - left at its default of 0 with a direct-connecting client, or set to the actual hop count behind a proxy; getting this wrong in either direction lets a client forge its apparent IP and evade both the rate limiter and allowed_ips checks. A rate limit counts calls, not what they cost, so a key under its rate can still hold every pooled connection with slow queries and starve everyone sharing them. A key's or role's own max_concurrent, query_timeout and max_rows (ADR 0011) bound that: queries running at once (a stream counts until its last row), how long each may run, how many rows a call returns - each only ever narrowing the server's limits. Counted in Redis across instances, with leases so a crashed pr

t: Security policy
x: Releases meet SLSA Build Level 2: each artifact is built on a GitHub-hosted runner by a workflow in this repository, and comes with provenance - which workflow, at which commit, from which tag - that the build platform signs (GitHub artifact attestations, through Sigstore), so it can't be forged without that workflow. That holds for: the images and the Helm chart, from 0.31 (docker.yml); the sdist and wheel on PyPI, from 0.35.1 (release.yml). Earlier ones carry only PyPI's own attestations (PEP 740), which say who uploaded them, not how they were built. To check one: bash pip download queryapigate==0.35.1 --no-deps -d . gh attestation verify queryapigate-0.35.1-py3-none-any.whl --owner AnanthaRajuC Not Level 3. Level 3 asks that the steps doing the build can't influence the provenance. Here the attestation is made in the same job as the build, so a compromised build step - a poisoned dependency of the build, say - could in principle shape what gets attested. Building and attesting in a reusable workflow, isolated from the caller, is the documented way to Level 3; it isn't done yet.

t: Security policy
x: Set QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY, and put the service behind TLS (a reverse proxy) - the key is sent in a header. It is the shared, full-access admin key; give anyone or anything that only needs to run queries a scoped key instead (POST /api/v1/api-keys), limited to specific connections and, separately, to read-only access. Give the people (and pipelines) who manage the server their own admin tokens, with the narrowest role that fits - queryapigate admins create NAME --role owner for the first - and then keep the shared key sealed as a break-glass key, or remove it (guide 43). Leave QUERYAPIGATE_ALLOW_WRITES unset unless you really need writes, and connect with a database account that only has the privileges the API should have. The read-only guard - including the single-statement check it relies on - is defence in depth, not a substitute for grants; it is dialect-aware (MySQL/ClickHouse honour backslash escapes in string literals by default, PostgreSQL/SQLite/H2 do not) and is exercised by a fuzz test suite (tests/test_sql_guard_fuzz.py), but a regex-based guard can never be a full SQL parser for every server mode. Keep database passwords out of the store: use "password": "${ENV_VAR}" references, or set QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY to encrypt them at rest (guide 22). t: Architecture overview
h: 1. What it is, and the trust boundary
x: QueryAPIGate is a self-hosted gateway, open source under Apache-2.0. It turns saved SQL queries into REST endpoints, MCP tools for AI agents, live server-sent events and exports. A saved query is versioned, and its parameters are typed and bound to the driver rather than written into the SQL. Every call goes through one governed path: authentication, limits, grants, a SQL guard, masking and a run-history record. It is a Python (Flask) application. The admin UI, the Console, is a React single-page app that ships inside the same package. Trust boundary. QueryAPIGate runs inside the customer's network, on infrastructure the customer operates. No part of it is a hosted service. It connects outward only to systems the deployer configures: the databases and file locations that connections name; its own metadata store (SQLite or PostgreSQL) and, optionally, Redis; an identity provider, for Console sign-in, signed-in app users and MCP clients; secret providers: files, HashiCorp Vault, and AWS (experimental); export destinations (object-storage buckets or allowed local folders); a SIEM, an OpenTelemetry collector and a Prometheus scraper. QueryAPIGate does not terminate TLS. A reverse proxy or ingress in front of it does that, and is required once any key exists. QueryAPIGate is not a network perimeter or a web application firewall: network policy, a VPN or a proxy still decides who can

x: From 0.31, every image (both variants, multi-arch) and the Helm chart is signed keyless with cosign, by digest, by the repository's docker.yml release workflow on the release tag. The signature is recorded in Sigstore's public log. Each release is signed in two forms: the Sigstore bundle and the classic .sig tag, which admission controllers need. Releases before 0.31 are not signed. Provenance and SBOM: images carry SLSA provenance, an SPDX SBOM and a GitHub artifact attestation naming the commit; the chart has a GitHub attestation; PyPI releases use trusted publishing, with PEP 740 attestations. Pinned builds: base images are pinned by digest; every GitHub Action is pinned by commit SHA, and a test refuses a uses: without one; downloaded tools are checked against their published checksums; Dependabot proposes updates as reviewed commits. Verifying: cosign verify with the workflow identity and the GitHub OIDC issuer, gh attestation verify, the SBOM, and an admission policy that admits only signed images. Sigstore policy-controller and Kyverno are covered. Guide 59 walks through each one. SECURITY.md has the summary. A signature shows which workflow and tag built a release. It does not show that the code is correct, and builds are not reproducible byte for byte (ADR 0018).

x: Are administrative actions logged? Answer: Yes. Every configuration change is appended to the audit log, recording: the actor; how they authenticated (via: their own token, break-glass key, SSO, CLI, configuration file); the action and target; a diff of what changed. Passwords appear only as or "changed", and secrets and hashes never appear. Every SSO sign-in, refusal and sign-out is recorded. Source: THREAT_MODEL.md#audit-logging-and-data-at-rest, API.md, Audit log Is the audit log tamper-evident? Answer: Yes. It is a hash chain, HMAC-signed when QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_KEY is set. Changing, removing, inserting or reordering an entry breaks the chain, which queryapigate audit verify detects; a check runs every 5 minutes and raises the critical audit_chain_broken alert. The chain alone can't show that its newest entries were deleted, or that someone holding both the store and the key rewrote it. A copy kept outside the store is what proves those. Source: THREAT_MODEL.md#the-audit-trail Can audit logs be sent to a SIEM? Answer: Yes. The audit log can be sent as syslog over TLS (RFC 5425), with optional mutual TLS, or as OTLP logs. Each entry carries its seq and hash, and audit verify --file checks the SIEM's copy. Delivery is at least once and survives the SIEM being down. Syslog over TCP can lose a batch if the receiver dies without closing the connection; OTLP acknowledges each bat

t: Why QueryAPIGate
x: Organizations often have valuable SQL sitting inside reports, BI dashboards, ETL pipelines, ad-hoc analysis and application code, with no path to a REST endpoint except writing a backend service around it. SQL Query | v +------------------+ | QueryAPIGate | | | | Parameters | | SQL Guard | | Permissions | | Rate Limiting | | Caching | | Connection Pool | | Streaming | | Observability | +--------+---------+ | v REST API | +--------+--------+ v v v JSON CSV XLSX If you already know SQL, you can produce a governed API without building an API application around it.

t: Why QueryAPIGate
x: Internal data APIs. Expose internal data to web apps, mobile apps, internal tools and other engineering teams without building a service per query: GET /q/film_by_id?id=7 GET /q/example_top_films?top_n=5&category=Comedy Reporting APIs. Turn an existing analytical SQL report into a reusable endpoint that dashboards or scheduled jobs can call directly, in JSON or as a CSV/XLSX export. Partner and external-client integrations. Give a partner an API key scoped to a curated list of saved queries, with its own rate limit and expiry, instead of database credentials: Partner --API Key--> QueryAPIGate --queries grant--> Database Data engineering to application engineering. Data teams write and version the SQL; application teams consume it as a normal REST endpoint, without either side depending on the other's deploy cycle. Data export. Stream large results as CSV, TSV, XLSX, JSON or NDJSON without loading the whole result into memory first. Rapid prototyping. Get a working, parameterized API around an existing query for a proof of concept or internal tool without standing up a backend application for it.

t: Why QueryAPIGate
x: | Approach | Primary model | | QueryAPIGate | SQL query -> governed REST API | | PostgREST | PostgreSQL schema -> REST API | | Hasura | Database -> GraphQL/API platform | | DreamFactory | Data source -> generated APIs | | SQLPad | SQL -> interactive query environment | QueryAPIGate's primary abstraction is the SQL query as an API resource, not the schema as a whole - so it fits well when an API should expose one specific, curated query rather than automatically surface an entire database.

t: Why QueryAPIGate
x: Your database already contains the data logic. The goal isn't to replace application backends; it's to remove repetitive boilerplate when the actual requirement is "expose this query safely as an API" - existing SQL, plus governance, is the API.

t: Technology stack
h: Technology Stack › The frontend: the Console
x: The admin UI (/console) is the QueryAPIGate Console, in frontend/: React 19 and TypeScript, built with Vite, with TanStack Query for server state, React Router, CodeMirror 6 for the SQL editor, and a client generated from the backend's own OpenAPI description (openapi-typescript and openapi-fetch). No component library: the stylesheet is the hand-written one the earlier admin page had (src/styles/classic.css). Tests: Vitest with Testing Library, and Playwright end to end. See ADR 0001. The build is committed to nothing: release builds (the wheel and the Docker image) run npm run build and ship the result in queryapigate/console_dist/, so pip install queryapigate still needs no Node.js. A source checkout without a build serves a short "not built" page at /console. It replaced a single hand-written HTML/CSS/JavaScript page in a Python string (queryapigate/ui.py), which was removed once every screen had moved over; /ui redirects to /console.

x: The queryapigate package is a Flask application, split into focused modules rather than one large file: | Module | Responsibility | | app.py | Flask app factory, request hooks, and the runtime routes (/q/, /execute_sql, /catalog, /events, ...). | | v1.py, v1_spec.py | The Management API (/api/v1) routes, and their OpenAPI description. | | services/ | What each Management API operation means - queries, connections, access (keys and roles), administrators, collections, audit, MCP - kept apart from HTTP. | | governance.py | What every front door (REST, MCP, the events server) applies: authentication, rate limits, metrics. | | admins.py, adminroles.py | Named administrators and their admin tokens; the four admin roles and the capability each /api/v1 operation needs (ADR 0003). | | jwtauth.py | Signed-in users' tokens: verification, roles from claims, from_claim parameters. | | engine.py | Looks up the connection, validates the SQL, runs it, wraps the page of results. | | runners.py | One driver class per database type: connect, bind parameters in that driver's own style, run, reset. | | pool.py | A thread-safe pool of idle connections (reset on return, health-checked, discarded after errors). | | sqltools.py | SQL validation (single statement, read-only unless permitted - including writes hidden behind a read-only keyword), pagination, :name bound-parameter and {name} text-substitu

t: Turn your first SQL query into a REST API
x: Time: about 10 minutes. You'll end up with: a real HTTP endpoint, backed by your own SQL, with typed/validated parameters - callable with curl, from a browser, or from any HTTP client - and no controller, router or serialization code written by hand. This guide uses the built-in example database (zero setup - no external database needed) so you can see the whole flow end to end first. Once you've done this once, connect your own database and repeat exactly the same steps against it.

t: Turn your first SQL query into a REST API
x: QueryAPIGate installed: pip install "queryapigate[server]" (or use the Docker image - see README.md). A terminal, and a browser.

t: Turn your first SQL query into a REST API
h: Step 1: Start a server with real data to query
x: QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY=demo-key queryapigate examples load # also prints one scoped API key per example scenario - ignore those for now, you're using the admin key QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY=demo-key queryapigate serve # Serving on http://127.0.0.1:5000 examples load installs a small generated database (examples - films, customers, rentals) and some worked saved queries you can look at later. Setting QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY gives you an admin key (demo-key) to use through this guide - as soon as any API key exists, the server requires one for every request, so set it before you load anything. Leave that terminal running. Open a second terminal (or your browser) for everything below.

t: Turn your first SQL query into a REST API
h: Step 2: Open the admin UI and go to API Designer
x: Open . The first time, it asks for an API key - enter demo-key. In the left sidebar, under API, click API Designer. This is the "write and run SQL, then save it as an endpoint" screen - distinct from API Repository, which lists endpoints you've already saved.

t: Turn your first SQL query into a REST API
h: Step 3: Pick a connection and look at what's there
x: At the top of API Designer, the Connection dropdown lists every database connection this server knows about. Select examples. Click the Schema tab on the right side of the screen. It lists every table (film, customer, rental, payment, category, ...) - click one to see its columns. This is the same schema QueryAPIGate itself queries when it validates your SQL; no separate documentation to keep in sync.

t: Turn your first SQL query into a REST API
h: Step 4: Write and run a query
x: In the SQL editor, replace whatever's there with: SELECT film_id, title, rating, rental_rate FROM film WHERE rating = :rating ORDER BY title Click Run. You should see a real result grid - films with a G rating won't show yet, because :rating has no value bound to it. That's expected: :rating is a bound parameter, resolved at request time - the same mechanism documentation/API.md uses everywhere, never string-substituted into the SQL. (If you want to see it actually run with a real value first: temporarily replace :rating with 'PG', click Run, see real rows come back, then put :rating back before continuing - this step isn't required, just reassuring the first time.)

t: Turn your first SQL query into a REST API
h: Step 5: Save it as a new API
x: Click Save as New API, right below the editor. A form opens on the same screen - no navigation, your query stays exactly as you wrote it. Fill in: | Field | Value for this guide | | Filename | films_by_rating | | Author | your name | | Description | Films with a given rating | | Collection | leave blank | | Tags | leave blank | | query_parameters | {"rating": {"type": "str", "enum": ["G", "PG", "PG-13", "R", "NC-17"], "description": "MPAA rating"}} | That last field is what turns :rating from "any text someone sends" into a validated, documented parameter - a request with a rating outside that list gets rejected with a clear error before your SQL ever runs. See How to use bound parameters safely for every available rule (min/max, pattern, default, required, and more). Click Save. A toast confirms it, and API Repository's query count in the sidebar increments - your query is now a real, versioned, saved endpoint.

t: Turn your first SQL query into a REST API
x: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/films_by_rating?rating=PG' -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' You should get back a real JSON array of films. Try an invalid value to see the validation you just configured actually enforced: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/films_by_rating?rating=NOT-A-RATING' -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' # {"error": "Invalid parameters: rating must be one of: G, PG, PG-13, R, NC-17", # "errors": {"rating": "must be one of: G, PG, PG-13, R, NC-17"}} Other formats work the same way, no extra code: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/films_by_rating?rating=PG&format=csv' -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/films_by_rating?rating=PG&format=yaml' -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key'

t: Turn your first SQL query into a REST API
x: You wrote one SELECT statement and ended up with an endpoint that has: typed/validated parameters, pagination (?page/?page_size), eight output formats (json/ndjson/csv/tsv/xml/yaml/xlsx/parquet), a version history (save it again under the same name and this becomes version 2, with version 1 still callable), and a run history visible in API Repository's History tab for this query - all without writing a controller, a repository layer, or a serializer. Nothing here required the admin key specifically except saving the query - once it's saved, you'd normally hand out a narrower, purpose-built key to whoever actually calls it. t: Connect to PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, DuckDB, ClickHouse or H2
x: Time: 5-15 minutes depending on the database. You'll end up with: a real, active connection you can query through QueryAPIGate - the admin UI's schema browser will list its tables, and the API Designer will run real SQL against it. Every connection - regardless of database type - is one JSON object with the same handful of fields: db, host, port, database, user, password, active. This guide shows the exact shape for each of the six built-in SQL dialects, and both ways to add one: the admin UI, or the API directly. What each type supports - read-only enforcement, time limits, allowed_tables, schema browsing, streaming - is in the support matrix. PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, DuckDB and ClickHouse are tier 1: every feature, tested against a real server in CI. H2 is experimental. For anything not listed here - Oracle, SQL Server, Snowflake, DB2, or any other JDBC-compliant database - see Connect to anything else via generic JDBC (experimental); the mechanics below (test, activate, query) are identical once a jdbc connection exists. For Trino - one connection federating many catalogs - there's a native, governed type with allowed_tables, masking and a schema browser: Connect to Trino (experimental).

h: Two ways to add a connection
x: Admin UI: open , go to Connections (under Data in the sidebar), click New connection, fill in the form, Test it, then Save. API directly (what this guide's examples use, since it's copy-pasteable and identical for every dialect): curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name": "", "db": "...", ... }' POST /api/v1/connections creates one (a name already taken is a 409); PATCH /api/v1/connections/ changes some of an existing one's fields and keeps the rest. Test any connection's fields (saved or not) before committing to them: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections/test -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"db": "...", ...}' # {"elapsed_ms": 12.4} A faster starting point: queryapigate init (run once, in an empty QUERYAPIGATE_HOME) seeds an inactive template connection for every supported type - example-sqlite, example-postgres, example-mysql, example-clickhouse, example-h2, example-duckdb. Edit one's real values and flip "active": true instead of writing the JSON from scratch.

ClickHouse also honors backslash escapes inside quoted string literals (like MySQL, unlike Postgres/SQLite/H2) - QueryAPIGate's SQL guard already accounts for this per-dialect, nothing you need to configure.

t: Connect to PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, DuckDB, ClickHouse or H2
x: An embedded analytical database: database is its own .duckdb file, which must already exist - like SQLite, QueryAPIGate never creates one, so a mistyped path fails rather than opening an empty database. Create it with python -c "import duckdb; duckdb.connect('analytics.duckdb')" (or the DuckDB CLI). It can also read CSV, Parquet and JSON files - local, in a bucket or on the web - straight from SQL, but only the ones its allowed_paths lists (guide 41); see DuckDB connections. curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name": "analytics", "db": "duckdb", "database": "analytics.duckdb", "active": true}' Needs pip install "queryapigate[duckdb]". One difference from SQLite worth knowing: DuckDB has no read-only session to fall back on, so the read-only default rests on QueryAPIGate's SQL check alone.

t: Connect to PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, DuckDB, ClickHouse or H2
x: Experimental - may change in any minor release, always noted in the changelog (what that means). H2 is different from the others: QueryAPIGate connects to a running H2 TCP server, not an embedded file directly - and needs a JVM (either the -h2 Docker image variant, or a local Java install plus pip install "queryapigate[h2]"). curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "shop-h2", "db": "h2", "host": "localhost", "database": "test", "user": "SA", "password": "${H2_PASSWORD}", "active": true }' This connects to jdbc:h2:tcp://localhost/~/test under the hood (add "port": if your H2 server isn't on H2's default TCP port, 9092). Two things worth knowing before you rely on this connection: the read-only guarantee rests entirely on the SQL guard, not the database connection itself (Connection.setReadOnly() is advisory in JDBC, not enforced), and allowed_tables isn't supported - a key restricted to tables is refused on an H2 connection rather than let through. QUERYAPIGATE_QUERY_TIMEOUT does apply.

t: Connect to anything else via generic JDBC
x: Time: 15 minutes. You'll end up with: a working connection to a database QueryAPIGate has no native driver for - Oracle, SQL Server, DB2, Snowflake, or anything else with a JDBC driver - running saved queries and ad-hoc SQL, with a clear list of what doesn't work on it. Experimental - may change in any minor release, always noted in the changelog (what that means). Generic JDBC loads your database vendor's own driver .jar into an embedded Java virtual machine. It was verified for this guide with H2's driver standing in for a vendor - the same way the CI tests it - so every command and response below is real. The vendor examples at the end come from each vendor's documentation and weren't run here.

t: Connect to anything else via generic JDBC
x: Java. Either the -h2 Docker image (ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate:-h2), which includes it, or a Java runtime on the host plus pip install "queryapigate[h2]" (JayDeBeApi and JPype). Your vendor's JDBC driver - a .jar file from the vendor, readable by QueryAPIGate. In Docker, mount it: -v /opt/jdbc:/opt/jdbc:ro. From the vendor's documentation: the driver's class name and its JDBC URL format.

t: Connect to anything else via generic JDBC

t: Connect to anything else via generic JDBC
x: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "inventory", "db": "jdbc", "jar": "/opt/jdbc/h2-2.2.224.jar", "driver_class": "org.h2.Driver", "jdbc_url": "jdbc:h2:tcp://localhost:9093/inventory", "user": "sa", "password": "${INVENTORY_PASSWORD}", "active": true }' curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/execute_sql -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"sql": "SELECT id, name, qty FROM parts WHERE qty > :min ORDER BY id", "connection_name": "inventory", "params": {"min": 0}}' # [{"ID": 1, "NAME": "bolt", "QTY": 120}, {"ID": 2, "NAME": "nut", "QTY": 300}] Note the column names: they come back as the driver reports them - upper case here, because that's H2's habit. Write AS name in the SQL if callers should see a particular spelling. Saved queries work as on any connection - parameters, validation, versions, ?format=, and streamed exports: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/parts_in_stock?stream=true&format=csv' -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' # ID,NAME,QTY # 1,bolt,120 # 2,nut,300

t: Connect to anything else via generic JDBC
x: | Feature | On a jdbc connection | | Query time limit | not enforced. With QUERYAPIGATE_QUERY_TIMEOUT=1, a 2.1-second query ran to the end. JDBC has no portable way to cancel a statement - set a statement timeout in the database itself, or in the JDBC URL if your driver supports one. | | Schema browser, list_tables | refused: Schema introspection isn't supported for 'jdbc' connections yet (unsupported_operation). Every vendor's catalogue differs. | | allowed_tables | a table-restricted key is refused on every query: Table access restrictions aren't supported for 'jdbc' connections yet (table_check_unsupported) - never left unrestricted. | | Read-only, enforced by the database | no - only QueryAPIGate's own SQL check stands between a caller and a write. DELETE FROM parts was refused with read_only, but give the connection a database user that can't write, as the real safeguard. | | Table DDL, the tables-and-joins diagram | not available. | The full comparison is in the support matrix.

A server with a jdbc connection logs at startup that it's experimental: Experimental: H2 and JDBC connections (connection inventory) ...

t: Connect to MongoDB
x: Time: 10 minutes. You'll end up with: a find()-based saved query - with bound parameters, projection and sort - callable as a versioned, validated REST endpoint, exactly like a SQL one. Stable since 0.37, under the compatibility promise - what that covers, what may still be added and its limits: MongoDB connections. MongoDB support in QueryAPIGate is find()-only, read-only, full stop - no aggregation pipelines, no writes, no response caching (yet). Everything below is what's actually built; nothing here is a partial feature with hidden gaps.

t: Connect to MongoDB
x: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "shop-mongo", "db": "mongo", "host": "localhost", "port": 27017, "database": "shop", "user": "${MONGO_USER}", "password": "${MONGO_PASSWORD}", "active": true }' Needs pip install "queryapigate[mongo]". user/password are optional - omit both for an unauthenticated local instance, as this guide's own examples do. database selects which database find() runs against per call; unlike the SQL dialects, it isn't part of the driver's own connection string. Test and browse it the same way as any other connection: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections/test -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"db": "mongo", "host": "localhost", "port": 27017, "database": "shop"}' # {"elapsed_ms": 12.6} curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/connections/shop-mongo/schema -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' # {"tables": [{"name": "orders", "type": "collection", "columns": []}], "truncated": false} Schema introspection lists collection names only - Mongo documents are schemaless, so there are no columns to list the way a SQL table has.

t: Connect to MongoDB
x: POST /execute_mongo is the Mongo sibling of /execute_sql - same idea (run something ad hoc against a connection before deciding to save it), different shape: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/execute_mongo -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "collection": "orders", "connection_name": "shop-mongo", "filter": {"status": ":status"}, "params": {"status": "paid"}, "projection": {"customer": 1, "total": 1, "_id": 0}, "sort": {"total": -1} }' [{"customer": "Carol", "total": 87.25}, {"customer": "Alice", "total": 42.5}] :status here is the exact same idea as a SQL query's bound :name parameter - a placeholder that only ever becomes a real value through params, never text spliced into the filter. It works as a whole string leaf anywhere in the filter document, including nested inside an operator: {"filter": {"total": {"$gte": ":min_total"}}, "params": {"min_total": 50}} Two operators are rejected outright, on any request: $where and $function/$accumulator run arbitrary server-side JavaScript - the Mongo equivalent of SQL injection into a WHERE clause, and the one thing a find-only path must never allow through, so there's no configuration to get right here, they're simply never permitted - in the filter, the projection or the sort. And a parameter's value is a value - a string, number, boolean, null, or a list of those - never a document: {"name": ":u"} g

t: Connect to MongoDB
h: Step 3: Save it as a REST endpoint
x: Same idea as a SQL saved query - POST /api/v1/queries, just with query_type: "mongo" and mongo_*-prefixed fields instead of sql: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/queries -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "orders_by_status", "query_type": "mongo", "mongo_collection": "orders", "mongo_filter": {"status": ":status"}, "mongo_projection": {"customer": 1, "total": 1, "_id": 0}, "mongo_sort": {"total": -1}, "parameters": {"status": {"type": "str", "enum": ["paid", "pending"], "description": "Order status"}}, "connection_name": "shop-mongo", "author": "you", "description": "Orders filtered by status", "publish": true }' parameters works exactly the same as for a SQL saved query - see Use bound parameters safely for every available rule. Call it: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/orders_by_status?status=paid' -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' # [{"customer": "Carol", "total": 87.25}, {"customer": "Alice", "total": 42.5}] curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/orders_by_status?status=refunded' -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' # {"error": "Invalid parameters: status must be one of: paid, pending", ...} In the admin UI, this is exactly the same API Designer -> Save as New API flow as a SQL query - pick shop-mongo as the connection, and the SQL editor becomes a filter/projection/sort JSON editor instead.

t: Connect to MongoDB
h: What's schemaless documents mean for the response shape
x: A collection's documents don't all have to share the same fields. QueryAPIGate builds each response's column list as the union of every key seen across the page, in first-seen order - so a query against a collection with inconsistent document shapes still produces one flat table (every existing output format - JSON, CSV, XLSX, XML, YAML - keeps working unmodified), but a document missing a field just shows that field as absent/null in its row, not an error.

t: Connect to MongoDB
x: A page is at most QUERYAPIGATE_MAX_PAGE_SIZE documents. ?stream=true sends all of them, read from the cursor as they come, in NDJSON, CSV, TSV or Parquet: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/orders_by_status?status=paid&stream=true&format=ndjson' -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -o paid.ndjson queryapigate export orders_by_status --param status=paid --format parquet --out 'paid-{date}.parquet' Each format handles documents that don't share fields in its own way: NDJSON writes each document whole - nested documents and arrays stay nested. Nothing is ever left out. Parquet makes every field of every document a column. CSV and TSV send their header line first, so the columns are decided before any document is written: the projection's fields, in its order - {"customer": 1, "total": 1, "_id": 0} above gives customer,total - or, without an inclusion projection, the fields of the first 1,000 documents. A field that first appears after those has no column and is left out; the run's history says how many (fields_dropped). Name your columns in the projection and that can't happen. The same works ad hoc (POST /execute_mongo?stream=true&format=csv) and in saved exports to a bucket or a folder - there, every field becomes a column whatever the format. Exports of a MongoDB query are full exports: incremental isn't supported for one yet.

t: Connect to MongoDB
x: Worth knowing up front so you don't go looking for it: No writes. insert/update/delete aren't reachable through QueryAPIGate at all for Mongo - only find(). There's no allow_writes equivalent to turn on. No incremental exports. A saved export of a Mongo query delivers the whole result each run. No column masking. A caller with mask rules is refused on a Mongo connection. No cache_ttl. Response caching (see Cache a saved query's response) isn't available for a Mongo saved query yet, only SQL ones. No aggregation pipeline. find() and its filter/projection/sort only - no $group, $lookup, or anything else from the aggregation framework.

t: Connect to MongoDB
