t: Diagnose and tune the connection pool
x: Time: 15 minutes. You'll end up with: an understanding of how many connections QueryAPIGate opens to your database, numbers to check that against, and the two settings that change it.

t: Diagnose and tune the connection pool
x: For PostgreSQL, MySQL, ClickHouse, DuckDB, H2 and JDBC connections, QueryAPIGate keeps database connections open after a request and reuses them for the next one, instead of connecting every time. (SQLite files are opened per request - there's nothing to pool.) | Setting | Default | Meaning | | QUERYAPIGATE_POOL_SIZE | 8 | idle connections kept per connection (per distinct set of connection details); 0 turns pooling off | | QUERYAPIGATE_POOL_IDLE_TIMEOUT | 300 | seconds an idle connection may wait for reuse before it's closed | The important detail: the pool limits idle connections, not concurrent ones. Each request in progress uses its own connection; how many run at once is limited by the server's threads - 8 in the Docker image's gunicorn.

t: Diagnose and tune the connection pool
x: QueryAPIGate under gunicorn as the Docker image runs it (1 worker, 8 threads), against a PostgreSQL 16 container. 20 queries of SELECT pg_sleep(0.5) sent at once; connections counted in PostgreSQL's pg_stat_activity: | | During the burst | Afterwards (idle) | SELECT 1, median | | QUERYAPIGATE_POOL_SIZE=5 | 8 | 5 | 1.8 ms | | QUERYAPIGATE_POOL_SIZE=0 | 8 | 0 | 6.6 ms | During the burst, 8 connections - one per thread; the other 12 requests waited for a thread, not a connection. Afterwards, the pool kept 5 and closed the other 3. With the default of 8 - one per thread - it keeps all 8, so a busy server never closes a connection only to open another for the next request. Without the pool, every request paid for a new connection: about 5 ms more here, on the same machine. Over a network, with TLS and authentication, it's typically tens of milliseconds. /metrics shows the idle count - queryapigate_pool_idle_connections 5 after the burst - and the Grafana dashboard has a panel for it (guide 35).

t: Diagnose and tune the connection pool
x: With QUERYAPIGATE_POOL_IDLE_TIMEOUT=4, five idle connections were still open 6 seconds later. The next request closed the expired ones and reused one: pg_stat_activity then showed 1. Expired connections are closed when the pool is next used, not by a background timer - so a server that goes completely quiet keeps its idle connections until traffic returns. If your database or a firewall drops idle connections sooner than that, it's handled: a connection idle for more than a few seconds is checked before reuse, and a dead one is replaced.

t: Diagnose and tune the connection pool
x: The most connections QueryAPIGate holds to one database is roughly: busy: threads × processes (8 × 1 in the Docker image), plus one per streamed export in progress; idle: QUERYAPIGATE_POOL_SIZE × processes, per connection that points at that database. Add queryapigate mcp and queryapigate events processes if they query the same database, and keep the total below the database's max_connections - leaving room for everything else that uses it. Symptoms and what to change: | You see | Likely cause | Change | | Latency rises with traffic, CPU is low, queryapigate_active_queries sits at the thread count | requests are queuing for threads | more threads, QUERYAPIGATE_THREADS (see Tune a deployment for throughput) | | "too many connections" errors from the database | threads (or several QueryAPIGate processes) exceed its limit | fewer threads, a higher max_connections, or a pooler such as PgBouncer in front of the database | | Every request pays connection setup; queryapigate_pool_idle_connections stays at 0 | pooling is off, or traffic is so sparse that connections expire | default QUERYAPIGATE_POOL_SIZE, longer QUERYAPIGATE_POOL_IDLE_TIMEOUT | | The DBA asks why connections sit idle all night | the lazy timeout above | QUERYAPIGATE_POOL_SIZE=1 or 2 on that server, or accept it - idle connections cost little | | Other queries slow down while large exports run | each ?stream=true expor

t: Diagnose and tune the connection pool
x: Changes to a connection drop its pool. Saving, editing or deleting a connection closes its idle pooled connections at once, so new details (a password, a host) take effect on the next request. A failed or timed-out query's connection is closed, not handed to the next request. Clean hand-over: each connection's transaction ends before reuse, so a request never sees a stale snapshot or another request's settings. Per process: each gunicorn worker and each QueryAPIGate process has its own pool.

t: Allow a browser-based frontend to call the API directly
x: Time: 10 minutes. You'll end up with: a web page on another origin - https://app.example.com calling https://api.example.com - that can call QueryAPIGate from the browser and read the responses, and an understanding of what that does and doesn't protect.

t: Allow a browser-based frontend to call the API directly
x: Browsers block a page's JavaScript from reading responses from a different origin unless the server allows that origin with CORS headers. Calls that send X-API-Key also get a "preflight" OPTIONS request first, which the server must answer. QueryAPIGate does neither until you turn it on - verified in Chromium: a page on http://localhost:8099 calling the API on http://127.0.0.1:5055 failed with TypeError: Failed to fetch.

t: Allow a browser-based frontend to call the API directly
x: QUERYAPIGATE_CORS_ORIGINS=https://app.example.com queryapigate serve Several origins are comma-separated: https://app.example.com, https://admin.example.com. An origin is scheme, host and port - https://app.example.com doesn't cover http://app.example.com or https://app.example.com:8443.

t: Allow a browser-based frontend to call the API directly
h: Step 2: Call it from the page
x: const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/q/orders_by_status?status=paid&page_size=2', { headers: { 'X-API-Key': key }, }); const rows = await res.json(); res.headers.get('X-Has-More'); // pagination res.headers.get('X-RateLimit-Key-Remaining'); // this key's own rate limit res.headers.get('X-Request-Id'); // for support requests Verified in Chromium, with the page's origin listed: {"status": 200, "rows": 2, "hasMore": "true", "keyRemaining": "99", "requestId": "b77f52110199"} and with a different origin listed instead (https://app.example.com), the same page got Failed to fetch again. What CORS lets through: Methods: GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE. Request headers: Content-Type, X-API-Key, Authorization, X-Request-Id. Response headers a page may read: X-Page, X-Page-Size, X-Has-More, X-RateLimit-* (server-wide and per-key), Retry-After, X-Request-Id, X-Cache, ETag, Deprecation, Link. No cookies - credentials are the header you send. The preflight answer is cached by the browser for 10 minutes.

t: Allow a browser-based frontend to call the API directly
x: CORS tells browsers which pages may read responses. It doesn't stop anything else - curl, a server, a script - from calling the API. The API key is what protects it. Two consequences: Any key in a page's JavaScript is public. Anyone who opens the page can read it in the developer tools. So the key a browser app uses must be one you'd accept anyone using: scoped to exactly the saved queries the page needs (guide 14) - connections: [], so no ad-hoc SQL; read-only, with a rate limit; or, better for an app with logins: no shared key at all - each user sends their own token as Authorization: Bearer ..., and a from_claim parameter limits each user to their own rows. See Signed-in users (JWT). * is for public data only. QUERYAPIGATE_CORS_ORIGINS=* allows every website. It worked in the test above, as expected - and it means any page anyone visits can call your API through their browser. The real trap is * on a server with no API key configured: then any website a person visits can query your databases through their browser - including a QueryAPIGate on their own laptop or office network, which the website itself could never reach. The Console's Alerts flag a server with no key (open_server) as critical. Don't combine the two.

t: Allow a browser-based frontend to call the API directly
x: If your reverse proxy also adds CORS headers, let only one of them do it - browsers reject a response with two Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers. Usually that means leaving it to QueryAPIGate and keeping the proxy out of it. The queryapigate events server reads the same QUERYAPIGATE_CORS_ORIGINS, so a page can open a live-events stream with fetch() too (guide 28).

t: Allow a browser-based frontend to call the API directly
x: Give an external partner access to exactly one query - the right shape for a browser key. Give each user of your app their own private activity feed - JWT for per-user access. Rate-limit a key.

t: Read the example APIs as a template for your own
x: Time: 20 minutes. You'll end up with: an understanding of why each of the 11 example queries, 4 collections and 5 roles is set up the way it is - and a recipe to copy for each kind of API you'll build. Load them first: Try it without any setup. What each scenario does is in EXAMPLES.md; this guide is about the choices behind them. Every definition below is read from a loaded server.

t: Read the example APIs as a template for your own
h: The shape: one collection and one role per audience
x: | Audience | Collection | Role | Rate limit | | Internal reporting | examples-reporting (3 queries) | example-reporting | 200/hour | | Wall dashboards | examples-dashboard (4 queries) | example-dashboard | 600/minute | | Bulk exports | examples-export (2 queries) | example-export | 20/hour | | An external partner | examples-partner (2 queries) | example-partner | 60/minute | | Executives (reporting + dashboards) | both of the first two | example-executive | 300/hour | Every role has connections: [] and no writes. That's the first thing to copy: no role gets a connection grant, so no key made from them can run ad-hoc SQL or browse a schema - only the saved queries in its collections. And because the grant is a collection, adding a query to examples-reporting later reaches every reporting key at once (guide 7). The rate limits follow the traffic each audience should produce: dashboards poll often (600/minute), an export should run a few times a day (20/hour). A limit is cheapest to set before the first caller depends on there being none (guide 17). example-executive shows that a role can span collections - two audiences' queries, one key - without copying any query.

t: Read the example APIs as a template for your own
x: SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', rental_date) AS month, COUNT(*) AS rentals, ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS revenue FROM rental WHERE rental_date >= date('now', '-' || :months || ' months') GROUP BY month ORDER BY month DESC Every parameter has a default and bounds. Called with no parameters, it answers something sensible; called with months=1000, it's refused before the database is touched. The bound is the cost control: nobody scans 80 years. A bound parameter inside an expression - '-' || :months || ' months' - is still a bound value, never SQL text. You don't need {months} text substitution for this (guide 6). SELECT * FROM (SELECT f.title, f.category, f.rating, COUNT() AS rentals, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT() DESC) AS rank FROM rental r JOIN film f ON f.film_id = r.film_id WHERE (:category IS NULL OR f.category = :category) GROUP BY f.film_id) WHERE rank <= :top_n ORDER BY rank, title An optional filter: (:category IS NULL OR f.category = :category). An optional parameter with no value binds as NULL, so one query serves "all categories" and "one category". enum for a closed set - the six categories. A typo gets a list of valid values back, not an empty result.

t: Read the example APIs as a template for your own
x: SELECT COUNT(*) AS active_rentals FROM rental WHERE return_date IS NULL All four dashboard queries carry cache_ttl: 30. Ten screens polling every five seconds cost one database query every 30 seconds, not 120 a minute. The trade - numbers up to 30 seconds old - is right for a wall display and wrong for anything a person just changed (guide 8). example_recent_rentals takes an hours window (1-168, default 24); each distinct value is cached separately.

t: Read the example APIs as a template for your own
h: Export: stream, and make it incremental
x: example_all_rentals - no parameters, about 20,000 rows over six joined tables. Meant to be called with ?stream=true&format=csv (guide 9) or queryapigate export (guide 30). example_rentals_since - the same idea, incremental: since (a YYYY-MM-DD string, checked by pattern, default 2000-01-01) and ORDER BY r.rental_id. A nightly job asks only for what's new; a stable order makes the files comparable from one run to the next. The low 20/hour limit says: this is a batch job, not something to poll.

t: Read the example APIs as a template for your own
x: example_film_lookup film_id: integer, required, >= 1 example_film_search text: string, required, 2-30 characters, pattern [A-Za-z ]+ Required, no defaults. A partner's call should say exactly what it wants. pattern closes a hole LIKE opens. example_film_search runs WHERE title LIKE '%' || :text || '%'. The value is bound, so it can't inject SQL - but % and _ are wildcards inside LIKE. The pattern allows only letters and spaces, so a partner can't turn a search into "give me everything". Verified: text=%% is refused - text must match the pattern [A-Za-z ]+ - and text=gar returns the films with "gar" in the title. Small results. A lookup returns one film's figures, not rows from the rentals behind them. For a real partner, add an expiry to the key itself - {"name": "acme-corp", "role": "example-partner", "expires_at": "2026-12-31"} - and consider allowed_ips (guides 18 and 19).

t: Read the example APIs as a template for your own
h: Copying a scenario for your own data
x: Create the collection by saving your first query into it - "collection": "sales-reporting". Create the role: {"name": "sales-reporting", "connections": [], "collections": ["sales-reporting"], "rate_limit": "200/hour"}. Create keys from the role, one per team or integration (guide 15). Check the result as the key would see it: GET /catalog with its secret (guide 21). Then remove the examples - queryapigate examples unload removes exactly what they installed, nothing of yours.

t: Use the threat model to decide how to expose QueryAPIGate
x: Time: 20 minutes. You'll end up with: a decision about how far to expose QueryAPIGate - your laptop, an internal network, partners on the internet, a browser app, an AI agent - and the settings each step needs, based on what QueryAPIGate does and doesn't defend against. The full reasoning is in the threat model, and the operational checklist in SECURITY.md. This guide turns them into decisions.

t: Use the threat model to decide how to expose QueryAPIGate
h: The four things to keep in mind
x: QueryAPIGate runs SQL against your databases. Anything that reaches it with the right key can do whatever that key's grants allow. Every administrator but an auditor can run any SQL on every connection, like a database superuser; their role only limits what they can change in QueryAPIGate. The SQL read-only check is a careful pattern-based classifier, not a SQL parser. It's tested by a fuzz suite and has had one real gap found and fixed. Treat it as a second lock. The first lock is the database user: connect with an account that has only the rights the API needs - read-only where it should be. It doesn't terminate TLS, and isn't a firewall. A proxy does TLS; your network decides who can reach it. Its own records aren't tamper-proof. The audit log and run history are ordinary tables; someone with direct access to the store could change them.

t: Use the threat model to decide how to expose QueryAPIGate
Use the threat model to decide how to expose QueryAPIGate
h: Decide by exposure › On your own machine
x: Fine with no API key - but know what that means: anyone who can reach the port can do anything. Verified: with no key configured, the server logs at startup - No API key is configured: every request is allowed, including changing connections and keys - and the Console's Alerts shows a critical Anyone can use this server. Keep the default bind address (127.0.0.1). Don't combine "no key" with QUERYAPIGATE_CORS_ORIGINS=*: any website you visit could then query your databases through your browser (guide 38).

t: Use the threat model to decide how to expose QueryAPIGate
h: Decide by exposure › On an internal network
x: Set QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY to a long random value - then give each administrator their own token and role, and keep the shared key as a break-glass key (guide 43). Give everything else a scoped key - an explicit connections list (omitting it means all), read-only (guide 13). HTTPS even internally - keys travel in a header on every request (guide 23). Least-privileged database users, one per connection. Encrypt connection passwords, and back up the store (guide 33).

t: Use the threat model to decide how to expose QueryAPIGate
h: Decide by exposure › Partners on the internet
x: Everything above, and for each partner: a key that reaches only named saved queries - connections: [], no ad-hoc SQL (guide 14); a rate limit, an expiry, and allowed_ips if their addresses are stable; strict parameter rules on those queries (guide 6); the proxy restricting /metrics and anything else you don't want public; QUERYAPIGATE_TRUST_PROXY set correctly - wrong in either direction, callers can choose their own apparent address. Check what a partner can reach with their key before handing it over: GET /catalog (guide 21).

t: Use the threat model to decide how to expose QueryAPIGate
h: Decide by exposure › A browser app
x: The key in a page is public - anyone can read it from the developer tools. So either a key you'd accept anyone using (named queries only, rate-limited, read-only), or better, signed-in users with from_claim parameters so each user only ever sees their own rows. List the app's origin in QUERYAPIGATE_CORS_ORIGINS (guide 38).

t: Use the threat model to decide how to expose QueryAPIGate
h: Decide by exposure › An AI agent
x: A scoped key, not the admin key. Prefer collections or queries grants - the agent gets saved-query tools only. Add a connections grant only if it should run its own SQL, and narrow that with allowed_tables (guide 25). Writes over MCP only through saved queries an author marked for agents, for a key whose grant allows the write - each approved by a person before it runs, unless it only inserts, and never more rows than the query allows (guide 49). Give agents their own keys: the credential that asked can't approve. execute_sql never writes. Results are capped (QUERYAPIGATE_MCP_MAX_ROWS), every call is in run history with "transport": "mcp". Remember that what the agent reads becomes part of its context - and whatever it does next. Give it data you'd be comfortable seeing in its output, and mask what it shouldn't see. A hosted assistant signing users in: OAuth through your identity provider. Tokens are bound to the MCP server - one issued for anything else is refused - but who gets one, and which role claim it carries, is your provider's configuration: check users can't set their own role claim. What it's told, and what it did: descriptions steer an agent's SQL, so only owners and admins write them - review imported database comments before relying on them. Observability → Agents shows each agent's calls, refusals and frequent statements, and agent_unusual_volume warns when one s

t: Use the threat model to decide how to expose QueryAPIGate
x: These are by design or not yet addressed - plan around them rather than discover them: Owners, admins and developers have no data limits inside QueryAPIGate - roles limit what they can change, not what they can read. Database grants are the backstop. Names can be probed. A saved query a key can't reach answers 403 naming its connection; a missing name answers 404. The MCP server ignores QUERYAPIGATE_TRUST_PROXY, so behind a proxy it can't tell MCP callers' addresses apart. Some connection types have gaps - no query time limit on generic JDBC, no database-enforced read-only on DuckDB, H2 and JDBC; see the support matrix. A JWT can't be revoked before it expires - keep token lifetimes short. Rate limits are per process unless Redis is configured (QUERYAPIGATE_REDIS_URL) - fine for protection, not for metering.

t: Use the threat model to decide how to expose QueryAPIGate
x: If callers must be able to run anything, give them a database account, not QueryAPIGate. If you can't give QueryAPIGate a database user with narrow rights, the read-only check alone shouldn't be what stands between the internet and your data.

t: Use the threat model to decide how to expose QueryAPIGate
x: The threat model - the reasoning behind all of this. SECURITY.md - the checklist, and how to report a vulnerability. Deploy with Docker for real.

t: Publish Parquet, CSV or JSON files in S3 as an API
x: Time: 15 minutes. You'll end up with: files in a bucket - or on a web server, or a local disk - served as governed REST endpoints and MCP tools, with no database to load them into: DuckDB reads them where they are. Every command and response below was run against an S3-compatible server (SeaweedFS) holding s3://sales/2026/orders.parquet - 5,000 orders - and a second bucket, hrdata, that the API must never reach.

t: Publish Parquet, CSV or JSON files in S3 as an API
h: Step 1: Decide what the connection may read
x: A DuckDB connection reads exactly the paths in its allowed_paths and nothing else - DuckDB itself refuses the rest, however a query asks. So start by naming the narrowest prefix that holds your files: here s3://sales/2026/. Give it credentials that can read only that prefix too (a bucket policy or IAM role). The allow-list is enforced by DuckDB; the credentials are enforced by the storage service - two locks, and the second is the one that holds even if the first were ever bypassed.

t: Publish Parquet, CSV or JSON files in S3 as an API
x: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "lake", "db": "duckdb", "database": ":memory:", "active": true, "allowed_paths": ["s3://sales/2026/"], "user": "AKIA...", "password": "${LAKE_SECRET_KEY}", "region": "eu-west-1", "views": {"orders": "SELECT * FROM read_parquet('"'"'s3://sales/2026/*.parquet'"'"')"} }' database: ":memory:" - the connection holds no tables of its own, only views over files. user and password are the access key ID and secret. The secret is handled like any connection password - here a ${LAKE_SECRET_KEY} reference to the server's environment; a typed one is masked and, with QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY, encrypted (guide 22). Leave both out for a public bucket. For an S3-compatible service (MinIO, SeaweedFS, Ceph), add "endpoint": "minio.internal:9000" and "url_style": "path" (and "use_ssl": false without TLS). For Google Cloud Storage use "storage": "gcs" with HMAC keys; for Cloudflare R2, "storage": "r2" and "account_id". views gives the files a name: orders. Or let the connection name them: "auto_views": true makes a view of each file and subfolder under each allowed prefix - s3://sales/2026/orders.parquet becomes orders, a subfolder returns/ becomes returns over every file in it (the rules). In the Console: Connections → New connection, type Files (Parquet, CSV, JSON) - no

t: Publish Parquet, CSV or JSON files in S3 as an API
x: Exactly as for any database (guide 1): curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/queries -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "daily_revenue", "connection_name": "lake", "publish": true, "description": "Revenue per day in a date range", "sql": "SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(total) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE day BETWEEN :from AND :to GROUP BY day ORDER BY day", "parameters": {"from": {"type": "str", "pattern": "\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}"}, "to": {"type": "str", "pattern": "\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}"}} }' curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/daily_revenue?from=2026-09-01&to=2026-09-03' -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' [{"day": "2026-09-01", "orders": 167, "revenue": 4158300.0}, {"day": "2026-09-02", "orders": 167, "revenue": 4159970.0}, {"day": "2026-09-03", "orders": 167, "revenue": 4161640.0}] Everything else works too - formats, ?stream=true exports, caching, run history, MCP tools. Each request reads the files, so for a dashboard polled often, add cache_ttl (guide 8): the files are read once per TTL, not once per poll.

t: Publish Parquet, CSV or JSON files in S3 as an API
x: A partner or an app gets the saved query only - no connections grant, so no SQL of its own (guide 14): curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/api-keys -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"name": "finance-dashboard", "connections": [], "queries": ["daily_revenue"], "rate_limit": "60/minute"}' An analyst who should write their own SQL - over the view, not the bucket - gets the connection with allowed_tables: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/api-keys -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"name": "analyst", "connections": ["lake"], "allowed_tables": ["orders"]}' Verified, for that key: | SQL | Result | | SELECT region, SUM(total) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY region | [{"region": "EU", "revenue": 124975000.0}] | | SELECT * FROM read_parquet('s3://sales/2026/orders.parquet') | 403 table_not_allowed - a table-restricted key can't call file-reading functions |

t: Publish Parquet, CSV or JSON files in S3 as an API
x: Even the admin key can't read outside allowed_paths: # SELECT * FROM read_parquet('s3://hrdata/salaries.parquet') # {"error": "This connection may not read 's3://hrdata/salaries.parquet' - it isn't under the connection's # allowed_paths", "code": "path_not_allowed", ...} The same goes for local files (/etc/passwd), other web addresses, ATTACH, COPY ... TO, installing or loading extensions, and attempts to change the settings back - each refused by DuckDB, which locks the connection's configuration as it opens. Web files work the same way, with one difference: a web address in allowed_paths must name a file (https://data.example.com/prices.parquet), never a folder - a web server resolves .. in a URL, so a prefix couldn't stop https://data.example.com/public/../private/....

t: Publish Parquet, CSV or JSON files in S3 as an API
x: Local files and folders work the same way, with absolute paths: "allowed_paths": ["/data/sales/"]. A DuckDB connection with no allowed_paths reads no files at all. Credentials are visible in part. Anyone who can run SQL on the connection can see its key ID and endpoint through DuckDB's duckdb_secrets() - never the secret. Another reason to give partners saved queries, not SQL. Costs: on a cloud bucket, each read is requests and egress you pay for. Cache, rate-limit, and prefer Parquet - DuckDB reads only the columns and row groups a query needs.

t: Publish Parquet, CSV or JSON files in S3 as an API
x: Cache a saved query's response. Let an AI agent call your saved queries via MCP - the bucket, as tools. DuckDB connections reference.

t: Run several instances behind a load balancer
x: Time: 30 minutes. You'll end up with: three QueryAPIGate instances serving as one - with Docker Compose or Kubernetes - that share keys, saved queries, rate limits and the cache, keep serving when one goes down, and can be upgraded one at a time. Both were run end to end before this guide was written: the Compose deployment on one machine, and the Kubernetes manifests on a local cluster (kind), each with a real PostgreSQL store, Redis and traffic.

t: Run several instances behind a load balancer
x: | | Why | | A PostgreSQL store (QUERYAPIGATE_DATABASE_URL) | connections, saved queries and versions, keys, roles, history and the audit log, shared - SQLite volumes per instance would make separate servers | | Redis (QUERYAPIGATE_REDIS_URL) | rate limits and the response cache, shared - without it each instance counts and caches on its own, and an alert says so | | queryapigate events for live events | it reads every instance's runs from the store; route /events to it | | The same secrets everywhere | QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY, QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY and any ${VAR} a connection uses | | One gunicorn worker per container | the image's default - scale with containers, not workers, so each /metrics is one process |

t: Run several instances behind a load balancer
x: The reference deployment is in the repository, under deploy/scale-out/: three instances, PostgreSQL, Redis, the events server and Caddy in front. cd deploy/scale-out cp .env.example .env && chmod 600 .env # pin QUERYAPIGATE_IMAGE; set the key, passwords and SITE_ADDRESS docker compose up -d docker compose ps # six services, healthy curl https://api.example.com/health Caddy round-robins requests across the three instances, checks each one's /health, takes a failing one out of the rotation, and retries a request on another instance if one can't be reached. /events goes to the events server, and /metrics is blocked at the proxy (scrape the instances directly).

t: Run several instances behind a load balancer
x: deploy/kubernetes/ has a Deployment of three replicas, the events server, Services, a PodDisruptionBudget and an Ingress (ingress-nginx; adapt the annotations for another controller): cp secret.example.yaml secret.yaml # fill in - or create the Secret from your secret manager kubectl apply -f secret.yaml -f queryapigate.yaml kubectl rollout status deploy/queryapigate Use a managed PostgreSQL and Redis in production; dev-dependencies.yaml starts throwaway ones for trying it. Settings in the manifest that matter, each found by running it: enableServiceLinks: false. Kubernetes puts _PORT=tcp://... into every pod for each Service, so a Service named queryapigate-events sets QUERYAPIGATE_EVENTS_PORT - one of QueryAPIGate's own settings. The first deployment of these manifests crashed on exactly that. QueryAPIGate now ignores such a value with a warning naming the cause, and the manifest switches service links off. A preStop pause and a 45-second grace period. Without them, a rolling update dropped requests that arrived while a pod was being removed - 2 of 1,633 in the test. With them: 1 of 1,805 in one run (a timeout) and 0 of 1,896 in another. maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1. Replace one pod at a time - the previous release keeps serving on the upgraded store meanwhile. Readiness and liveness probes on /health. A pod gets traffic only once it answers.

t: Run several instances behind a load balancer
h: Check that they act as one
x: curl https://api.example.com/api/v1/instances -H 'X-API-Key: ...' {"items": [{"role": "events", ...}, {"role": "serve", "host": "8e7a77dc4f96", "shared_limits": true, ...}, {"role": "serve", "host": "937cabe5b957", "shared_limits": true, ...}, {"role": "serve", "host": "db7a2881750c", "shared_limits": true, ...}], "problems": []} Three serve instances and the events server, all with shared_limits: true, and no problems - on both. What else was verified: | Check | Compose | Kubernetes | | Calls through the load balancer | answered by the three instances in turn | - | | A key with rate_limit: "4/minute", called across instances | 200 ×4, then 429 | 200 ×4, then 429 (one call per pod) | | A query against PostgreSQL | [{"n": 100, "total": 7575.0}] | the same | | /events | runs arrived through the proxy | the events server healthy | | One instance stopped, twelve calls | all twelve 200 | - | | A rolling update under steady traffic | - | 0 of 1,896 failed (1 of 1,805 in another run) | | /metrics through the proxy | 403 | - | An instance that stopped stays in GET /api/v1/instances for up to 90 seconds; a restarted one appears with a new id.

t: Run several instances behind a load balancer
x: Upgrades: one instance at a time - see Upgrade safely and DEPLOYMENT.md's Rolling upgrades. GET /api/v1/instances shows who is on which version meanwhile. Monitoring: scrape every instance's /metrics; the bundled Grafana dashboard sums them (guide 35). Backups: the store is PostgreSQL now - guide 33. Redis needs none. Database connections: each instance holds about nine connections to the store; see DEPLOYMENT.md's Shared metadata store. Alerts to know: instances_not_shared (some instances without Redis), instances_versions_differ (a rolling upgrade not finished), rate_limits_not_shared (Redis unreachable - limits fall back to per instance).

t: Give your team their own admin access
x: Time: 15 minutes. You'll end up with: everyone who manages QueryAPIGate signing in as themselves, with a role that fits what they do; CI on a token of its own; an audit log that says who changed what; and the shared QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY retired to a break-glass key - or removed. Until now, managing the server meant holding QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY: everyone could do everything, and the audit log said admin for every change. Named administrators change that (ADR 0003). Data callers - scoped API keys, signed-in app users - aren't affected. Every command and response below was run against a real server.

t: Give your team their own admin access
x: On the machine (or in the container) where the store is - no running server and no key needed: queryapigate admins create alice --role owner --email alice@corp.com --label laptop Created administrator alice (owner). Admin token tok_7c663440dc14 for alice (expires 2027-01-03) - store it now, it cannot be shown again: qagadm_9-2fLdbDffa6PaOdzKttS2U6j01oA9DiUoCawF3i8CE Use it as the X-API-Key header, or paste it into the Console's key box. In Docker: docker compose exec queryapigate queryapigate admins create alice --role owner. Tokens expire after 90 days unless you pass --expires YYYY-MM-DD (or never, for automation that rotates its own). Alice signs in by pasting the token into the Console's sign-in page, the first thing a tab without one sees - the sidebar then says Signed in as alice · Owner, and Sign out beside it ends that - or by sending it as X-API-Key: curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/me -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_9-2f...' # {"name": "alice", "role": "owner", "via": "token", "capabilities": ["access.read", ...], "data_access": true}

t: Give your team their own admin access
h: Step 2: Give each person a role
x: | Role | For | May | | owner | whoever runs the server | everything, including administrators | | admin | the platform team | connections, API keys and roles, queries, cache, settings - not administrators | | developer | people who write the APIs | saved queries and collections, SQL on every connection - no keys, no connection changes | | auditor | security, compliance | read everything that describes the server (audit log, history, keys, connections) - no SQL at all | In the Console: Access → Administrators → New administrator. Their first token, valid for 90 days, is shown once - hand it over the way you'd hand over a password. Or with the API: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/administrators -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_9-2f...' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name": "bob", "role": "developer", "email": "bob@corp.com"}' curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/administrators/bob/tokens -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_9-2f...' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"label": "laptop", "expires_at": "2027-01-03"}' # {"id": "tok_2cfa12f4a781", "admin": "bob", "label": "laptop", "expires_at": "2027-01-03", ..., # "secret": "qagadm_WfBE..."} What Bob's role allows is enforced by the server, whatever he uses to call it: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/api-keys -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_WfBE...' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name": "partner", "connections

t: Give your team their own admin access
h: Step 3: Move automation to its own token
x: A pipeline is an administrator too - give it the narrowest role that works, and a token with an expiry you'll notice: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/administrators -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_9-2f...' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name": "ci-deploy", "role": "developer"}' curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/administrators/ci-deploy/tokens -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_9-2f...' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"label": "github-actions", "expires_at": "2027-04-01"}' Store the secret in your CI's secret store and use it wherever the shared key was. A job that publishes saved queries (say, from a collection bundle) needs developer; one that also manages API keys needs admin.

t: Give your team their own admin access
x: Every change now names the person and how they signed in: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/audit' -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_9-2f...' {"actor": "bob", "via": "token", "action": "issue_admin_token", "target": "bob"} {"actor": "alice", "via": "token", "action": "issue_admin_token", "target": "ci-deploy"} {"actor": "alice", "via": "token", "action": "create_admin", "target": "ci-deploy"} via is token (their own), break-glass (the shared key), cli (a command on the server) or open.

t: Give your team their own admin access
x: QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY keeps working - as an owner - so nothing broke when you upgraded. Once an active owner exists, it is the break-glass key: each use is logged, WARNING queryapigate: The shared QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY (break-glass key) was used for GET /api/v1/connections although named administrators exist recorded in the audit log (break_glass_used), and raises an alert for 24 hours - The shared admin key was used on every instance's Alerts screen. When nothing uses it any more (the alert stays quiet), take it out of the environment and restart. Authentication stays on - administrators exist - so the server doesn't reopen: curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections # 401 {"error": "Unauthorized", "code": "unauthorized", ...} Or keep it, sealed somewhere safe, for emergencies: the alert tells you if it's ever used.

t: Give your team their own admin access
x: Someone lost their token - they issue themselves another from a token they still have, or an owner does it for them (Administrators → Tokens), or anyone on the server runs: bash queryapigate admins token alice --label recovery --expires 2026-10-12 Someone leaves - Administrators → Edit → Active off stops every token of theirs at once; or remove them (their name stays in the audit log). The last owner can't be lost by accident: without the shared key, demoting, deactivating or removing the only active owner is refused: 409 {"error": "This would leave no active owner, and QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY is not set - nobody could manage administrators any more. Make someone else an owner first.", "code": "last_owner", ...} Nobody can sign in at all - queryapigate admins list and queryapigate admins token NAME on the server always work, because they use the store directly; so does setting QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY again and restarting.

An administrator and an API key can't share a name (409 name_taken), and admin and cli are reserved - a name in the logs, /metrics and run history always means one caller. t: Deliver a daily file to a partner's bucket
x: Time: 20 minutes. You'll end up with: a saved query delivered every day as a Parquet file to a bucket your partner reads from - only the rows that are new since the last delivery, with every run on record, an alert when one fails, and nothing ever written outside the prefix you allowed. Every command and response below was run against a real server and an S3-compatible bucket (SeaweedFS), with the example APIs loaded. $TOKEN is an owner's or admin's admin token (the shared key works too).

t: Deliver a daily file to a partner's bucket
h: Step 1: A query that can say "only what's new"
x: An incremental export remembers the largest value of one column it has delivered - the watermark - and binds it to a parameter on the next run. So the query needs a column that only grows, and a parameter to compare it with: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/queries -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "rentals_after", "connection_name": "examples", "description": "Rentals after an id", "publish": true, "sql": "SELECT rental_id, rental_date, amount FROM rental WHERE rental_id > :after ORDER BY rental_id", "parameters": {"after": {"type": "int", "min": 0}} }' Pick the column with care. An id that only grows (rental_id) is the safest: nothing is missed and nothing is sent twice. A timestamp (updated_at > :since) works too, but > can miss a row written later with the same timestamp as the last one delivered, and >= re-sends the rows on the boundary. And the parameter must accept what the column holds: a date-only parameter can't take a timestamp watermark - the run says so, and writes nothing.

t: Deliver a daily file to a partner's bucket
h: Step 2: The destination - where it may write, and nowhere else
x: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/destinations -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "acme", "url": "s3://acme-exchange/from-us/", "user": "AKIA...", "password": "${ACME_SECRET_KEY}", "region": "eu-west-1" }' url is the prefix exports may write under: s3://, gs:// (with "storage": "gcs" HMAC keys), r2:// (with account_id), or a local folder - which must sit inside one the operator set in QUERYAPIGATE_EXPORT_DIRS, never the server's own home. For an S3-compatible service, add endpoint, "url_style": "path" and "use_ssl": false without TLS. The secret is stored like a connection password: here a ${ACME_SECRET_KEY} reference to the server's environment; a typed one is masked in every response and encrypted with QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY. Nothing can be written outside the prefix. Every write goes through a DuckDB connection locked to it - no path, parameter or file name can reach s3://acme-exchange/other-partner/; DuckDB refuses. Still give the credentials write access to that prefix only: two locks. Test it before anything depends on it - it writes one small file, _queryapigate_probe.csv, overwritten each time: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/destinations/acme/test -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" # {"object": "s3://acme-exchange/from-us/_queryapigate_probe.csv", "elapsed_ms": 251.0} In the Console: Delivery → Destinations → New destination

t: Deliver a daily file to a partner's bucket
x: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/exports -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "acme-rentals", "query": "rentals_after", "destination": "acme", "path": "rentals/{date}/rentals_{run}.parquet", "incremental": {"column": "rental_id", "parameter": "after", "start": 0} }' path is under the destination. {date} (YYYY-MM-DD), {time}, {run} (the run's id - every file unique), {name} and the query's parameters ({region}, plain values only) are filled in. format: parquet (default), csv or ndjson, written by DuckDB with the rows in the query's order. A Parquet file keeps the column types - decimals exact, dates as dates. It's checked now, not at 3 a.m.: the destination and the published query must exist, the query must use :after, every placeholder must fill in.

t: Deliver a daily file to a partner's bucket
x: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/exports/acme-rentals/runs -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" {"id": "ec7e7e7e8cb5", "export": "acme-rentals", "rows": 20000, "object": "s3://acme-exchange/from-us/rentals/2026-10-09/rentals_ec7e7e7e8cb5.parquet", "watermark": {"from": null, "to": 20000}, "duration_ms": 100.7} Run again straight away, and there is nothing new - so no file (skip_empty, on by default): {"id": "3ef429ef0f03", "rows": 0, "object": null, "watermark": {"from": 20000, "to": 20000}} Three new rentals later, the next run delivers exactly those: {"id": "622ec9e44786", "rows": 3, "object": "s3://acme-exchange/from-us/rentals/2026-10-09/rentals_622ec9e44786.parquet", "watermark": {"from": 20000, "to": 20003}} In the Console: Delivery → Exports → Run now, and Runs for its history.

t: Deliver a daily file to a partner's bucket
h: Step 5: Put it on a schedule
x: QueryAPIGate doesn't keep a clock; your scheduler calls it. From the server's own host - no server needed, it reads the store directly: # crontab: every day at 06:00 0 6 * * * QUERYAPIGATE_HOME=/srv/queryapigate ACME_SECRET_KEY=... queryapigate exports run acme-rentals # Wrote 3 rows to s3://acme-exchange/from-us/rentals/2026-10-09/rentals_622ec9e44786.parquet (run 622ec9e44786). # Watermark: 20000 -> 20003 Or over HTTP, from a Kubernetes CronJob or Airflow, with a token of its own - a developer may run exports, but not define or change them: apiVersion: batch/v1 kind: CronJob metadata: name: acme-rentals spec: schedule: "0 6 * * *" concurrencyPolicy: Forbid jobTemplate: spec: backoffLimit: 2 template: spec: restartPolicy: Never containers: name: run image: curlimages/curl:8.10.1 args: ["-fsS", "-X", "POST", "-H", "X-API-Key: $(QUERYAPIGATE_TOKEN)", "http://queryapigate:5000/api/v1/exports/acme-rentals/runs"] env: name: QUERYAPIGATE_TOKEN valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: queryapigate-ci, key: token}} -f makes a failed run fail the job, so Kubernetes retries it and reports it. Two runs of one export never overlap, whoever starts them: the second answers 409 export_running (with Retry-After) until the first finishes - and a run that crashed holds the export only until its lease expires.

t: Deliver a daily file to a partner's bucket
x: With the bucket unreachable: {"error": "Couldn't write s3://acme-exchange/from-us/rentals/2026-10-09/rentals_a55563feae35.parquet: IO Error: Could not connect to server ...", "code": "destination_unreachable"} Nothing is lost. The watermark moves only after a file is written, so it stayed at 20003. When the bucket was back, the next run delivered the one waiting row - {"rows": 1, "watermark": {"from": 20003, "to": 20004}}. An object store upload is all or nothing: a failed run leaves no partial file. You're told. The export_failing alert - Export 'acme-rentals' is failing - is on the Alerts screen and GET /api/v1/alerts until a run succeeds, and every run, failed or not, is in GET /api/v1/exports/acme-rentals/runs and run history, with who ran it. Re-send on purpose by moving the watermark back - audited: PATCH /api/v1/exports/acme-rentals with {"watermark": 19000}, or {"watermark": null} to start again from start.

t: Deliver a daily file to a partner's bucket
x: Memory. A run streams the rows through the server once, into a temporary file, and DuckDB writes from it: about 150 MB for a local file whatever the size, and 180-300 MB to S3 for 2-6 million rows (measured; the S3 upload's parts grow a little with the file). Who may do what. Owners and admins define destinations and exports - that decides who receives data. Developers may run them; auditors may read them. Scoped API keys can't touch them. What's in the files is what the query returns. To hide columns from a partner - email addresses, say - give the export masking rules. One-off files, without saving an export: queryapigate export rentals_after --param after=0 --to acme --format csv --out 'adhoc/{date}.csv'.

t: Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent
x: Time: 15 minutes. You'll end up with: one saved query - or a connection a partner or an AI agent may write SQL against - where the email addresses come back as stable codes and names as I*, whatever the SQL calls the columns; queries that masking can't follow refused rather than served; and a record of what was masked, for whom. Every command and response below was run against a real server with the example APIs loaded (demo-key is an admin).

t: Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent
h: Step 1: Give the caller its rules
x: Masking rules most often belong to the caller - an API key, a role (and so the keys made from it and the signed-in users mapped to it), or an export - so one saved query serves your own team as it is and a partner masked. A rule can also belong to the query itself, when a column should be masked for everyone who runs it, admins included - see Step 6. curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/api-keys -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "acme-partner", "connections": ["examples"], "mask": [{"column": "customer.email", "action": "hash"}, {"column": "customer.last_name", "action": "mask"}] }' A rule names a source column - table.column, or schema.table.column, with * as a wildcard (*.email, customer._name) - and what to do with its values: | Action | Turns isla.ito1@example.com into | When | | hash | eafbbd68098fdc3c | the same value always gives the same code, so counting, grouping and joining still work | | mask | i@example.com (text: Ito -> I*) | people should see there is a value, not what it is | | null | null | the column should stay, empty | | drop | (column removed) | it shouldn't appear at all | | keep | (unchanged) | to say a column is fine as it is - see views, below | The strictest rule that applies wins (drop > null > mask > hash). In the Console: API keys → New API key → Column masking; keys and roles with rules carry a masked t

t: Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent
x: The same saved query, for the admin and for the partner: curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/customer_contacts -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' # [{"customer_id": 1, "first_name": "Isla", "last_name": "Ito", "contact": "isla.ito1@example.com"}, ...] curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/customer_contacts -H 'X-API-Key: ' # [{"customer_id": 1, "first_name": "Isla", "last_name": "I*", "contact": "eafbbd68098fdc3c"}, # {"customer_id": 2, "first_name": "Ava", "last_name": "I*", "contact": "4b3ca6ce45e20366"}, ...] The query calls the column contact, not email - it's still hashed, because rules follow the data, not the name. The same goes for every format (?format=csv, Parquet), ?stream=true exports, MCP tools and the cache: a partner is never served a response cached for someone else. The caller can see what it gets masked, in GET /catalog: {"name": "customer_contacts", "masking": {"masked": [{"column": "last_name", "action": "mask"}, {"column": "contact", "action": "hash"}], "refused": null}}

t: Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent
h: Step 3: Let them write SQL - masking holds
x: A partner, or an AI agent over MCP, with the connection in its grant can write its own SQL. Each result column is traced through the SQL to the table columns it's computed from, so renaming, wrapping or nesting doesn't get the value out: # SELECT email FROM customer LIMIT 2 [{"email": "eafbbd68098fdc3c"}, {"email": "4b3ca6ce45e20366"}] # SELECT upper(email) AS e FROM customer LIMIT 2 - computed from email: hashed as a whole [{"e": "f94742444fd906a6"}, {"e": "b313c006e2be7cad"}] # WITH x AS (SELECT email AS e FROM customer) SELECT e AS anything FROM x LIMIT 2 [{"anything": "eafbbd68098fdc3c"}, {"anything": "4b3ca6ce45e20366"}] A query masking can't follow is refused - before it runs - rather than served unmasked: # SELECT c FROM customer c - the whole row as one value {"error": "This query's result columns can't be traced to their sources for masking: Column '\"c\"' could not be resolved", "code": "mask_unresolvable"} Refused the same way: table functions (read_parquet(...)), a table alias that renames columns (customer AS c(a, e)), SELECT * over a NATURAL or USING join, LATERAL, recursive CTEs, DuckDB's COLUMNS('...'), and functions masking can't see into (version()) - name the columns instead. A caller with rules also never sees the database's own error text, which can quote a value.

t: Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent
x: Every run records what was masked, in run history: {"key_name": "acme-partner", "masked": [{"column": "email", "action": "hash", "source": "customer.email"}], ...} So "was the email ever returned unmasked to this partner?" is a search in GET /api/v1/history?key=acme-partner.

t: Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent
h: Step 5: Files for the partner, masked too
x: An export carries its own rules, whoever runs it (deliver a daily file): curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/exports -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "acme-contacts", "query": "customer_contacts", "destination": "acme-drop", "format": "csv", "path": "contacts/{date}.csv", "mask": [{"column": "customer.email", "action": "hash"}, {"column": "customer.last_name", "action": "drop"}] }' customer_id,first_name,contact 1,Isla,eafbbd68098fdc3c 2,Ava,4b3ca6ce45e20366 The codes match the partner's API key's: one hash key per store, so a partner can join a file to an API response on them. Masking an export's incremental column is refused - the watermark is made of its values.

t: Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent
h: Step 6: Or mask a column for everyone, on the query
x: When a column should never leave a particular query unmasked - no matter who calls it, admins included - put the rule on the query rather than on each caller. In the Console it's the Column masking field on the save form (API Repository → New version, or the API Designer's Save as New API); the same field in the Designer's Settings pane masks a preview before you save. In a query definition it's a mask array, the same shape as a caller's: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/queries -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "customer_contacts", "connection_name": "examples", "sql": "SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name, email AS contact FROM customer", "mask": [{"column": "customer.email", "action": "hash"}] }' Now everyone who runs customer_contacts gets contact hashed, including demo-key. A caller that also carries a mask on its key gets both: per column, the stricter action wins (drop > null > mask > hash), so a query's hash and a key's drop on the same column drops it. Query-level masking traces SQL columns the same way, so it's not available on Mongo queries, and a query whose mask can't be traced is refused rather than served unmasked - exactly as for a caller's rules.

t: Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent
x: Asking about a value without selecting it. A caller that writes SQL can still filter and group on a masked column: # SELECT count(*) AS n FROM customer WHERE email LIKE 'a%' [{"n": 15}] Masking hides values in what comes back; it doesn't stop a question about them. When that matters - an AI agent near sensitive data - give the caller saved queries only (no connections grant), or allowed_tables on a view that leaves the column out. Hashes are keyed, so a likely value can't be hashed and compared - but equal values are visible as equal, which is the point of hash.

t: Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent
x: Views are traced only as far as the view. A rule on customer.email can't tell whether contact_view.email is that column, so a query reading it is refused until a rule names the view: *.email (which covers every table and view), contact_view.email with an action, or contact_view.email with keep to say it's fine. Window functions are masked when they order or partition by a masked column - RANK() OVER (ORDER BY email) comes back hashed. Over other columns they're fine. Administrators see data as it is - masking is for the callers you hand data to. Auditors see no data at all. The hash key is made once per store and shared by every instance; set QUERYAPIGATE_MASK_KEY to choose it. Changing it changes every code. Supported on MySQL, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, SQLite and DuckDB connections (it needs the sqlglot package - queryapigate[flow], in the Docker image). A caller with rules is refused on H2, JDBC and MongoDB connections, for now.

t: Let AI clients sign in through your identity provider
x: Time: 30 minutes. You'll end up with: an AI client - a connector in a hosted assistant, or your own agent - connecting to your MCP server by signing its user in through your identity provider, not with an API key you hand out: the user's role decides what the agent can reach, its masking rules apply, every run is recorded under the user's name, and a token issued for anything else is refused. Stable - OAuth for the MCP server is under the compatibility promise since 0.30 (what that means). Every command and response below was run against a real MCP server and a real Keycloak 26 (in Docker), with the example APIs loaded, and a real MCP client - the Python SDK's - going through the whole sign-in: discovery, the login page, the authorization code with PKCE, the token, the tool call.

t: Let AI clients sign in through your identity provider
x: AI client --(1) POST /mcp, no token--> MCP server --> 401 + where to sign in QueryAPIGate only checks tokens. Your identity provider issues them, signs the user in (with your MFA, your policies), and registers the client. QueryAPIGate never sees a password and issues no tokens of its own.

t: Let AI clients sign in through your identity provider
h: Step 1: At your provider - a scope whose tokens name the MCP server
x: A token is accepted only if its audience (aud) is the MCP server's own URL - so a token your provider issues for some other application can't be used here. Make that happen with a scope. In Keycloak, in your realm: Client scopes → Create client scope: name queryapigate.mcp, type Optional, Include in token scope on. In it, Mappers → By configuration → Audience: Included Custom Audience https://data.example.com/mcp (the MCP server's URL, exactly as clients reach it), Add to access token on. A token requested with scope=queryapigate.mcp now carries: {"iss": "http://localhost:58080/realms/qag-test", "aud": ["http://127.0.0.1:5001/mcp", "account"], "sub": "7222e50f-b640-4e00-ab30-da4c0c9c9261", "azp": "agent", "scope": "openid queryapigate.mcp profile email", "exp": 1791692237, ...} (In this run the MCP server's URL was http://127.0.0.1:5001/mcp; yours is its public https:// URL.) Other providers have the same idea under another name - an API, resource or application ID URI whose identifier becomes the token's audience, and a scope on it. Whatever yours calls it, check a real token: aud must be the MCP server's URL, scope (or scp) must hold queryapigate.mcp, and sub must be there.

t: Let AI clients sign in through your identity provider
h: Step 2: In QueryAPIGate - a role for agents
x: What a signed-in agent may do is a role's, as for any signed-in user: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/roles -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "agents", "connections": ["examples"], "mask": [{"column": "customer.email", "action": "hash"}] }' Give it as little as the agents need: saved queries only (a queries or collections grant, no connections) is the safest; a connection grant adds the ad-hoc execute_sql and list_tables tools, and masking hides what they shouldn't see.

t: Let AI clients sign in through your identity provider
x: QUERYAPIGATE_MCP_RESOURCE_URL=https://data.example.com/mcp \ QUERYAPIGATE_MCP_AUTH_SERVER=https://idp.example.com/realms/acme \ QUERYAPIGATE_MCP_ROLE=agents \ queryapigate mcp Here, against the local Keycloak: MCP sign-in through http://localhost:58080/realms/qag-test, for tokens issued to http://127.0.0.1:5001/mcp (scope queryapigate.mcp) INFO: Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:5001 (Press CTRL+C to quit) QUERYAPIGATE_MCP_AUTH_SERVER is the provider's issuer - for Keycloak, https:///realms/. Its keys are found from its published metadata; if that can't be fetched, the log says so at startup and every token is refused until it can. QUERYAPIGATE_MCP_ROLE_CLAIM instead (or as well) lets the token pick the role: a claim holding a role name, or a list - the first that exists wins. Both URLs must be https:// (only localhost may be plain HTTP), and a hosted client reaches the MCP server from the internet: put it behind a reverse proxy with real TLS.

t: Let AI clients sign in through your identity provider
h: Step 4: Check it the way a client will
x: The metadata a client reads first: curl https://data.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp {"resource": "http://127.0.0.1:5001/mcp", "authorization_servers": ["http://localhost:58080/realms/qag-test"], "scopes_supported": ["queryapigate.mcp"], "bearer_methods_supported": ["header"], "resource_name": "QueryAPIGate"} And the answer to a request with no token - the client's cue to sign the user in: curl -i -X POST https://data.example.com/mcp/ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}' HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized www-authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="http://127.0.0.1:5001/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp", scope="queryapigate.mcp" {"error": "Unauthorized: missing or invalid X-API-Key or bearer token", "code": "unauthorized", "request_id": "..."}

t: Let AI clients sign in through your identity provider
x: The client needs a client ID at your provider. There are three ways, and which one works is between the client and your provider - QueryAPIGate plays no part: Register it yourself (any provider): create a client - in Keycloak Clients → Create client, Client authentication off (a public client, using PKCE), Standard flow on, the client's redirect URL under Valid redirect URIs - then add queryapigate.mcp under its Client scopes as Optional, and give the client ID to whoever configures the AI client. Creating clients through Keycloak's admin API or a realm import? Create the client, then add the scope: a client created with its scopes listed gets none of Keycloak's default ones - basic, which puts sub in the token, among them - and its tokens are then refused (the access token names no user). Client ID Metadata Documents: the client's ID is an HTTPS URL describing it, which the provider fetches - nothing to register, if your provider supports it. Dynamic Client Registration: the client registers itself. Keycloak supports it, but two of its default policies refuse an anonymous registration, as this run found in turn: Allowed Client Scopes (a client asking for queryapigate.mcp, until the scope was made a realm-wide optional one), then Trusted Hosts (a request from a host not on its list). Opening that up lets anyone register a client in your realm: decide it deliberately, or registe

t: Let AI clients sign in through your identity provider
h: Step 6: Sign in, and call a tool
x: With the Python SDK's OAuth client - the same steps a hosted client takes, the login page in a browser: from mcp.client.auth import OAuthClientProvider from mcp.shared.auth import OAuthClientMetadata auth = OAuthClientProvider( "https://data.example.com/mcp", OAuthClientMetadata(client_name="My agent", redirect_uris=["http://127.0.0.1/callback"], grant_types=["authorization_code", "refresh_token"], response_types=["code"], token_endpoint_auth_method="none"), storage, redirect_handler=open_browser, callback_handler=wait_for_callback) async with streamablehttp_client("https://data.example.com/mcp", auth=auth) as (read, write, _): async with ClientSession(read, write) as session: await session.initialize() await session.call_tool("execute_sql", {"connection_name": "examples", "sql": "SELECT first_name, email FROM customer LIMIT 2"}) The client got the 401, read the metadata, found Keycloak's, and sent the user to sign in with scope=queryapigate.mcp, a PKCE challenge, and resource=http://127.0.0.1:5001/mcp. After signing in: Tools: 13 ['example_all_rentals', 'example_film_lookup', 'example_film_search'] ... Result: {'rows': [{'first_name': 'Isla', 'email': 'ae33faddd7f39b68'}, {'first_name': 'Ava', 'email': '3cdc177ae6b31f79'}], 'truncated': False} The role's masking rule hashed the email. The run is in history under the user: {"key_name": "jwt:7222e50f-b640-4e00-ab30-da4c0c9c9261"

t: Let AI clients sign in through your identity provider
x: Revoking access. A token can't be recalled before it expires - keep access tokens short-lived (minutes, as providers do by default; the client refreshes them). Disabling the user at your provider stops new tokens; disabling or narrowing the role here takes effect on the next request. The resource URL is an identity, not a location: clients compare it with the URL they connected to, and the provider puts it in aud. Set it to the public URL, https://data.example.com/mcp - not the internal address the server listens on. A scope named by URI (api://queryapigate/queryapigate.mcp, as some providers require): set QUERYAPIGATE_MCP_SCOPE to it; a token carrying its last part, queryapigate.mcp, is accepted. Which person was it? The sub claim - for Keycloak, a user's ID. from_claim parameters bind to the token's claims, so a saved query can return only the signed-in user's rows.

t: Tell AI agents what your data means, and see what they did
x: Time: 15 minutes. You'll end up with: an agent that is told what each table and column means - imported from your database's own comments, or written in the Console - and the joins and metric definitions to use, so it writes the right SQL; and, afterwards, a view of what every agent asked, read and was refused, with an alert when one suddenly reads far more than it usually does. Stable - descriptions and agent usage are under the compatibility promise since 0.30 (what that means). Every command and response below was run against a real server and its MCP server, with the example APIs loaded, a PostgreSQL 16 database as a second connection, and a real MCP client (the Python SDK) as the agent. demo-key is an admin; the agent is a scoped key, rentals-bot.

t: Tell AI agents what your data means, and see what they did
h: Step 1: Import what your database already says
x: Many databases already carry comments. In PostgreSQL: COMMENT ON TABLE orders IS 'One row per order, from checkout'; COMMENT ON COLUMN orders.amt IS 'Net revenue in EUR, refunds excluded'; COMMENT ON COLUMN orders.status IS 'open, paid or refunded'; Bring them in: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections/shop/descriptions/import -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' {"found": 3, "imported": 3, "kept": 0, "items": [ {"table": "orders", "column": null, "description": "One row per order, from checkout", "source": "database", ...}, {"table": "orders", "column": "amt", "description": "Net revenue in EUR, refunds excluded", "source": "database", ...}, {"table": "orders", "column": "status", "description": "open, paid or refunded", "source": "database", ...}]} PostgreSQL, MySQL, ClickHouse and DuckDB comments can be imported. Run it again after the comments change: a description someone wrote in QueryAPIGate ("source": "written") is kept, unless you send {"overwrite": true}. Read an import before relying on it. Whoever can COMMENT in the database writes what agents will be told.

t: Tell AI agents what your data means, and see what they did
h: Step 2: Write the rest - and the connection's notes
x: What the database doesn't say, write. The connection's own notes ("table": null) are where joins and metric definitions go: curl -X PATCH http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections/examples/descriptions -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"items": [ {"table": "rental", "column": null, "description": "One row per film rented: who, which film, when"}, {"table": "rental", "column": "return_date", "description": "When it came back; null while still out"}, {"table": "rental", "column": "amount", "description": "Rental fee in EUR, before late fees"}, {"table": "customer", "column": "email", "description": "Where receipts go"}, {"table": "customer", "column": "country", "description": "ISO 3166 two-letter code"}, {"table": null, "description": "Join rental to customer on customer_id, and to film on film_id. Late fees are in payment, not rental: revenue is SUM(payment.amount)."} ]}' A null or empty description removes one. In the Console: API Designer → Schema, ✎ beside a table for it and its columns, and ✎ Describe connection for the notes and Import comments. Owners and admins may write them; every change is in the audit log with what it said before.

t: Sign in to the Console through your identity provider
x: Time: 30 minutes. You'll end up with: administrators signing in to the Console through your identity provider (Keycloak, Entra ID, Okta, Google Workspace, ...) - with its MFA and policies - and their role coming from the groups they're in there; someone leaving, or moving team, changes their access at their next sign-in, without anyone touching QueryAPIGate. Administrators who had tokens keep their names and history. Stable - Console sign-in through SSO is under the compatibility promise since 0.30 (what that means). Every step below was run against a real Keycloak 26 (in Docker) and a real server, signing in through the Console in a real browser (Chromium) - the provider at http://localhost:58080/realms/qag-sso-test and the Console at http://localhost:5094, shown below as https://idp.example.com/realms/acme and https://data.example.com. Names you'll see: alice (in qag-admins), bob (in no group with a role) and carol (an existing administrator with a token, in qag-owners).

t: Sign in to the Console through your identity provider
x: Console --"Sign in with SSO"--> /auth/sso/login --> your provider's sign-in (MFA, policies) <------------------- /auth/sso/callback <-- a code, exchanged by the server for an ID token session cookie, role from the person's groups The server runs the sign-in (the authorization code flow with PKCE), as a confidential client with a secret; the browser never holds a token. It gets a session cookie - HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict - that only authenticates a request together with a CSRF token the Console sends; no other site can use it.

t: Sign in to the Console through your identity provider
h: Step 1: At your provider - a client, and groups in the ID token
x: In Keycloak, in your realm: Clients → Create client: OpenID Connect, client ID queryapigate-console. Client authentication on (a confidential client), Standard flow on, Direct access grants off. Valid redirect URIs: https://data.example.com/auth/sso/callback - exactly the address people reach the Console on. Valid post logout redirect URIs: https://data.example.com/*. Advanced → Proof Key for Code Exchange Code Challenge Method: S256. Credentials: copy the client secret. Client scopes → queryapigate-console-dedicated → Add mapper → By configuration → Group Membership: token claim name groups, Full group path off, Add to ID token on. Groups: one per role you'll use - qag-owners, qag-admins, ... - and put people in them. Other providers name these differently; what QueryAPIGate needs is the same everywhere: Microsoft Entra ID: an app registration with a client secret and the redirect URI (type Web). Group claims are object IDs unless you emit names; app roles are often simpler - assign people to app roles and set QUERYAPIGATE_SSO_GROUPS_CLAIM=roles. Okta: an OIDC Web Application with the redirect URI, and a groups claim on its authorization server, filtered to your qag- groups and included in the ID token. Google Workspace: ID tokens carry no groups. Use QUERYAPIGATE_SSO_DEFAULT_ROLE with QUERYAPIGATE_SSO_ALLOWED_DOMAINS (below) - a Google client accepts any Google account, so th

t: Sign in to the Console through your identity provider
x: QUERYAPIGATE_SSO_ISSUER=https://idp.example.com/realms/acme QUERYAPIGATE_SSO_CLIENT_ID=queryapigate-console QUERYAPIGATE_SSO_CLIENT_SECRET=... # from the provider QUERYAPIGATE_SSO_REDIRECT_URL=https://data.example.com/auth/sso/callback QUERYAPIGATE_SSO_ROLES=owner=qag-owners,admin=qag-admins queryapigate serve Experimental: Console sign-in through SSO (QUERYAPIGATE_SSO_CLIENT_ID, QUERYAPIGATE_SSO_CLIENT_SECRET, ...) - may change in any minor release, ... QUERYAPIGATE_SSO_ROLES maps groups to roles - owner, admin, developer, auditor; a role may be listed more than once (admin=qag-admins,admin=platform). Someone in several gets the most capable. Everything must be https:// (only localhost may be plain HTTP), and the Console must be reached over HTTPS: the session cookie is Secure. Put the server behind a reverse proxy with real TLS. Anything half-set stops startup, saying what's missing. Settings → Console sign-in (SSO) shows what's in use - the secret only as "configured".

t: Sign in to the Console through your identity provider
x: The Console's sign-in page now offers Sign in with SSO, above the token field. alice clicks it, signs in at Keycloak, and lands back on the page she was on, Signed in as alice · Admin via SSO. Her administrator was created at that sign-in; her session, as the Console sees it: {"sso": true, "signed_in": true, "sso_only": false, "admin": "alice", "role": "admin", "email": "alice@example.com", "csrf": "5sA4vM...", "expires_at": "2026-10-11 19:57:13"} The cookie alone is not enough - the same request without the CSRF token gets 401. In the audit log: {"actor": "alice", "via": "sso", "action": "create_admin", "target": "alice", "changes": {"role": "admin", "email": "alice@example.com", "issuer": "https://idp.example.com/realms/acme"}} {"actor": "alice", "via": "sso", "action": "sign_in", "target": "alice", "changes": {"role": "admin", ...}} and every change she makes says "via": "sso". Sign out ends the session here and at the provider.

t: Sign in to the Console through your identity provider
x: bob signs in at Keycloak too - but he's in no group mapped to a role. Nothing is created; the Console says: Sign-in through SSO didn't go ahead: You signed in, but you're in no group that's given a role here - ask an owner to add you to one (sso_no_role) {"actor": "-", "via": "sso", "action": "sign_in_refused", "target": "bob@example.com", "changes": {"code": "sso_no_role", "reason": "You signed in, but you're in no group that's given a role here - ..."}} The role is decided at every sign-in: move alice from qag-admins to qag-owners and she's an owner from her next one; take her out of every mapped group and her next sign-in is refused.

t: Sign in to the Console through your identity provider
x: carol has been a developer with a personal token since before SSO. To keep her name and history, an owner marks her - Administrators → Edit → Sign-in through SSO → Link at their next sign-in, or: curl -X PATCH https://data.example.com/api/v1/administrators/carol -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"sso": "pending"}' # ... "role": "developer", "sso": {"status": "pending"} Her next SSO sign-in, with a verified email matching hers, is bound to her account - once: {"name": "carol", "role": "owner", "email": "carol@example.com", "created_by": "cli", "sso": {"status": "linked", "issuer": "https://idp.example.com/realms/acme"}} She's an owner now: linked, her role is her groups' (she's in qag-owners), not what she had. Changing it in QueryAPIGate is refused - 409 sso_managed, their role comes from their groups at the identity provider - change it there. Her email and whether she's active can still change here. {"sso": null} unlinks her. Link people before they first sign in through SSO; someone who signs in first gets an administrator of their own (carol-2, if the name is taken), and the two have to be sorted out by hand.

t: Sign in to the Console through your identity provider
x: With every person linked, stop personal tokens routing around the provider's MFA and policies: QUERYAPIGATE_SSO_ONLY=yes carol's old token now gets 401, and issuing her one is refused - 409 sso_only. Accounts for automation (ci-deploy), linked to no one, keep their tokens. The break-glass key keeps working, audited and alerted: it's how owners get in if the provider is down.

t: Sign in to the Console through your identity provider
x: Sign-in through it stops; sessions already open keep working. The Alerts screen says so - sso_unreachable, critical: Console sign-in through SSO is down. Owners sign in with a token or the break-glass key until it's back.

t: Sign in to the Console through your identity provider
x: Someone leaving is removed at the provider: they can't sign in again, but a session already open lasts until it expires - QUERYAPIGATE_SSO_SESSION_HOURS, default 8. Switching them off in QueryAPIGate ends it at once. Who controls qag-owners controls QueryAPIGate. Keep that group small, and its membership managed like any other privileged group. A default role for providers without groups: QUERYAPIGATE_SSO_DEFAULT_ROLE=auditor with QUERYAPIGATE_SSO_ALLOWED_DOMAINS=example.com - for people with a verified email there. Never owner; startup refuses one without the other. Linking trusts email_verified: only link at a provider where people can't set and verify an email they don't own. Refused sign-ins carry a code: sso_no_role, sso_state (expired, used, or started in another browser - sign in again), sso_id_token (the provider's answer didn't verify - check the clock and the client ID), sso_inactive, sso_denied, sso_unreachable, sso_ambiguous (two administrators wait for the same email), sso_busy.

t: Let an AI agent write - with a person approving each write
x: Time: 20 minutes. You'll end up with: a support agent that opens tickets by itself, and closes one only when a person has approved that exact change - each write limited to the rows it may change, run once, and on record with who asked and who approved. Stable - write tools over MCP are under the compatibility promise since 0.30 (what that means). Every command and response below was run against a real server, its MCP server and a PostgreSQL 16 tickets table, with a real MCP client (the Python SDK) as the agent - the Console at http://localhost:5098 in this run.

t: Let an AI agent write - with a person approving each write
x: Agents read only, unless a saved query's author marks it for agents and the agent's key may write through it. Then it's a write tool, in one of two modes: insert - one INSERT, run at once. It can add rows, never change or remove one. approval - the first call writes nothing and answers with a link; a person approves that exact write; the agent's second call runs it, once. Either way the write runs in a transaction, rolled back if it changed more rows than the query allows.

t: Let an AI agent write - with a person approving each write
h: Step 1: Mark the queries agents may write through
x: On the server, writes must be on (QUERYAPIGATE_ALLOW_WRITES=1), and QUERYAPIGATE_CONSOLE_URL makes the approval links full addresses: curl -X POST http://localhost:5098/api/v1/queries -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "file_ticket", "connection_name": "helpdesk", "description": "Open a ticket for a customer", "publish": true, "sql": "INSERT INTO tickets (customer, title) VALUES (:customer, :title) RETURNING id, status", "parameters": {"customer": {"type": "string"}, "title": {"type": "string", "max_length": 200}}, "agent_writes": "insert" }' curl -X POST http://localhost:5098/api/v1/queries -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "close_ticket", "connection_name": "helpdesk", "description": "Close a ticket", "publish": true, "sql": "UPDATE tickets SET status = '\''closed'\'' WHERE id = :id", "parameters": {"id": {"type": "integer", "min": 1}}, "agent_writes": "approval" }' max_affected_rows is how many rows one write may change - 1 unless you say more. Only one INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE can be marked - never DDL. "sql": "TRUNCATE tickets" with agent_writes: An agent-writable query must be an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE - one statement that changes data and nothing else. PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and DuckDB.
