t: Let an AI agent write - with a person approving each write
h: Step 5: It runs - that write, once
x: close_ticket {"id": 2, "approval": "wr_4cfa357ce998"} -> {"status": "done", "request": "wr_4cfa357ce998", "rows_affected": 1} close_ticket {"id": 3, "approval": "wr_4cfa357ce998"} -> {"error": "These arguments are not the ones approved - an approval is for exactly one write. ...", "code": "approval_mismatch"} An approval is for exactly the arguments shown, by this caller, before it expires (15 minutes, QUERYAPIGATE_WRITE_APPROVAL_MINUTES - and once approved, the agent has that long again to run it). Calling again with the same approval returns the first result: a retry never writes twice.

t: Let an AI agent write - with a person approving each write
h: When a write would change more than it may
x: close_customer_tickets - UPDATE tickets SET status = 'closed' WHERE customer = :customer, max_affected_rows: 2 - asked for and approved for acme, who has four open tickets: -> {"error": "This write would have changed 4 rows, and this query may change at most 2 - nothing was changed", "code": "too_many_rows_affected"} It ran in a transaction, saw 4 rows, and rolled back: all four tickets are as they were. The limit is checked when it runs, so a write approved when it would change one row, and that would change hundreds by then, is still stopped.

t: Let an AI agent write - with a person approving each write
h: Step 6: Why the agent has its own key
x: If the agent were given maria's token, the write it asks for would be under her name - and approving it with that same token is refused: {"error": "This write was asked for under your own name - another approver must decide it", "code": "own_write"} So a client configured with an approver's credential can't approve whatever its model asks for. t: Rotate an API key without downtime
x: Time: 10 minutes. You'll end up with: a partner's key on a new secret, with the old one working until they've switched, then stopped. Same key name, same grants, the same history. Every command and response below was run against a real server on http://127.0.0.1:5098, with a PostgreSQL 16 orders table behind the saved query orders_by_customer (new in 0.22).

t: Rotate an API key without downtime
x: Before 0.22, "rotating" meant creating a second key, copying the grants across by hand, and revoking the first. The partner had an outage unless both of you switched at the same minute, the copied grants could differ, and run history and the audit log split across two names. Reissuing the secret avoids all three.

t: Rotate an API key without downtime
x: A key that may run one query (guide 14): curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5098/api/v1/api-keys -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"name": "partner-acme", "connections": [], "queries": ["orders_by_customer"]}' curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5098/q/orders_by_customer?customer=acme' -H "X-API-Key: $OLD_SECRET" # [{"id":1,"total":120.5},{"id":2,"total":80.0}]

t: Rotate an API key without downtime
h: Step 2: Rotate the secret, keeping the old one for a day
x: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5098/api/v1/api-keys/partner-acme/rotate -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"grace_minutes": 1440}' {"name": "partner-acme", "secret": "sk_quSL2_SHS6CWDGOQMyOW6XH8q0tbiA7mfRRILykmwRQ", "previous_expires_at": "2026-10-12 18:28:43", "previous_last_used_at": null, "queries": ["orders_by_customer"], ...} The new secret is in this response only, sent with Cache-Control: no-store, as when the key was created. Give it to the partner. Until previous_expires_at both secrets work: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5098/q/orders_by_customer?customer=acme' -H "X-API-Key: $OLD_SECRET" # [{"id":1,...}] curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5098/q/orders_by_customer?customer=acme' -H "X-API-Key: $NEW_SECRET" # [{"id":1,...}] grace_minutes is 60 if you leave it out, at most 10080 (a week). Both secrets are the same key: its active, expiry, allowed_ips and rate limit apply to each, and they share one rate-limit budget - the old secret is never a second allowance. Who may rotate: anyone who may change keys (access.write - owners and admins). In the Console: API keys → Edit (the pencil) → Secret: choose how long to keep the old secret working, then Rotate secret. The new secret is shown once, and the key gets a rotating tag in the list.

t: Rotate an API key without downtime
x: curl http://127.0.0.1:5098/api/v1/api-keys/partner-acme -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" # "last_used_at": "2026-10-11 18:28:43", "previous_expires_at": "2026-10-12 18:28:43", # "previous_last_used_at": "2026-10-11 18:28:43" previous_last_used_at is when the old secret was last used (to the minute). Once it stops moving, they've switched. The Console's Edit drawer shows the same: The old secret works until ... · last used ....

t: Rotate an API key without downtime
x: Once they have switched, end it rather than waiting for the grace period to run out: curl -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:5098/api/v1/api-keys/partner-acme/previous -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" # "previous_expires_at": null, "previous_last_used_at": null curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5098/q/orders_by_customer?customer=acme' -H "X-API-Key: $OLD_SECRET" # {"error":"Unauthorized","code":"unauthorized"} In the Console, End now. Left alone, the old secret stops by itself at previous_expires_at. One rotation at a time. Rotating again while an old secret still works is refused, so a second click can't cut off the secret the partner is still using: {"error": "The secret this key had before its last rotation works until 2026-10-12 18:28:43 - end that first (DELETE .../previous), or wait for it", "code": "key_rotation_pending", "previous_expires_at": "2026-10-12 18:28:43"}

t: Rotate an API key without downtime

h: Step 4: One trace, end to end
x: In Jaeger (http://localhost:16686), the app's trace - here 5d1b7946cc208d89e08d0758967125e2 - has QueryAPIGate's spans inside it: shop-backend: GET /customers/{id}/orders 39.4 ms queryapigate: GET /q/ 12.8 ms http.route=/q/ status 200 caller=shop-backend queryapigate: query orders_by_customer 11.7 ms queryapigate.rows=10 queryapigate: SELECT shop 10.1 ms db.system.name=postgresql db.namespace=postgres server.address=localhost db.response.returned_rows=10 queryapigate: serialize json 0.1 ms queryapigate.format=json queryapigate.bytes=226 So of 12.8 ms in QueryAPIGate, 10.1 went to PostgreSQL. Each span records only what the list says. The parameter (acme), the statement, the API key and the database password appear nowhere in the stored trace (checked by searching it), and that holds for every span: tests fail if one ever does. From the other side: the same trace_id is in the run's history entry (GET /api/v1/history), in an error's body beside request_id, and in each JSON log line (QUERYAPIGATE_JSON_LOGS=1) with its span_id - so a slow run, an error a caller reports, or a log line leads straight to its trace.

t: Give a partner a quota and a concurrency cap
x: A rate limit counts calls, not their cost. A partner under 60/minute can still run twenty two-second reports at once and hold every connection the pool has, while everyone else on that connection waits. And contracts are written in quotas - "1,000 calls a day" - which a per-minute rate only approximates.

t: Send the audit log to your SIEM, and prove nobody edited it
x: Time: 20 minutes. You'll end up with: every administrative change signed into a hash chain, streamed over mutual TLS to your SIEM as it happens - and a check, in one command, that what QueryAPIGate holds, and what your SIEM received, is what was written. Stable - the SIEM stream is under the compatibility promise since 0.32 (what that means), as the chain itself already was. Every command and output below was run against a real server, with rsyslog 8.2604 as the SIEM - RFC 5425 syslog over TLS, requiring a client certificate - and an OpenTelemetry Collector 0.160.0 taking OTLP logs beside it: the receivers .github/scripts/siem_receivers.sh starts, the same ones CI tests the stream against on every push.

t: Send the audit log to your SIEM, and prove nobody edited it
x: python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(32))" # the audit key QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_KEY= QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_LOG_EXPORT_FILE=/var/log/queryapigate/audit.jsonl # a copy on disk too Keep the key outside the store, as you keep QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY. Every audit entry is then signed with it (hmac-sha256:...), chained to the one before - someone who can write to the store but hasn't the key can't re-sign an edit. Setting it is the chain's first entry here: audit_key_set.

h: Step 4: Changes, as the SIEM sees them
x: A key created, its rate limit changed, its secret rotated - and later deleted. rsyslog's file, as rsyslog parsed each message - APP-NAME, MSGID, structured data, the message: queryapigate audit_key_set [meta sequenceId="1"] {"action": "audit_key_set", "actor": "startup", "changes": {"entries... queryapigate create_key [meta sequenceId="2"] {"action": "create_key", "actor": "admin", "changes": {"active": true, ... queryapigate update_key [meta sequenceId="3"] {"action": "update_key", "actor": "admin", "changes": {"rate_limit": {"... queryapigate rotate_api_key [meta sequenceId="4"] {"action": "rotate_api_key", "actor": "admin", "changes": {"grace_m... queryapigate delete_key [meta sequenceId="5"] {"action": "delete_key", "actor": "admin", "changes": {"active": true, ... RFC 5424, facility 13 (log audit): the action is the message ID, seq is [meta sequenceId], and the message is the entry with its seq, prev_hash and hash - what the SIEM indexes, and what it drops a repeat by. The Collector got each as a log record - service.name queryapigate, scope queryapigate.audit - with the entry as its body and these attributes, here for entry 3: {"queryapigate.audit.seq": "3", "queryapigate.audit.hash": "hmac-sha256:9278fc6bbe80696c8f0ad6590e4aab03c7d017b207110f707878ee09c23ca466", "queryapigate.audit.prev_hash": "hmac-sha256:b318f06633e30e89d3294f920aae2f3fa6aaeaaa47b3c1733dae76face28371d"

x: The key was deleted while rsyslog was stopped: {"output": "syslog", "delivered_seq": 4, "head_seq": 5, "behind": 1, "last_error": "ConnectionRefusedError: [Errno 111] Connection refused"} {"output": "otlp", "delivered_seq": 5, "head_seq": 5, "behind": 0, "last_error": null} Nothing is lost: each output's cursor is in the store, and entries it hasn't had are kept even past QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_LOG_LIMIT (up to ten times it). Each output is on its own - OTLP kept up throughout. 15 seconds after rsyslog started again, it had caught up: {"output": "syslog", "delivered_seq": 5, "head_seq": 5, "behind": 0, "last_error": null} More than five minutes behind raises audit_delivery_behind. Delivery is at least once, so a SIEM's copy may hold an entry twice, or out of order after a retry - an exact repeat (the same seq and hash) is dropped and counted, and entries are checked in seq order. A repeat that differs is reported (conflicting copies, naming both lines): one of the two isn't what was written. The SIEM's copy with one entry changed - the rate limit made 6000/minute: BROKEN at entry 3 (update_key, 2026-10-13 13:22:55): changed (exit 1). The store is held to the same: the server checks it every five minutes and raises audit_chain_broken at the first entry that doesn't verify - changed, removed, inserted, reordered, or re-written without the key. The SIEM's copy is what catches what the chain can't on its own - the newest entries deleted from the store, or a rewrite by someone holding both the store and the key: check the two against each other, and the SIEM's against itself, with the same command. Without the

x: Rotating the audit key: QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_KEY=, - the first signs, both verify; startup records audit_key_rotated. Keep the old key while entries signed with it are kept. Syslog over TCP has no acknowledgement. A SIEM that closes its end, or refuses the certificate, is noticed before anything is written into the connection - stopping rsyslog with a connection open is noticed, CI checks. Every command and output below was run against two real servers: dev and prod, each with its own store and its own SQLite database of sales, with prod started with QUERYAPIGATE_CONFIG_LOCKED=1. h: Step 4: A change, as a pull request
x: On a branch: the partner gets 120 calls a minute, and a new query. @@ roles: rate_limit: 60/minute rate_limit: 120/minute @@ queries: +- name: best_month collection: finance connection_name: sales description: The month with the most revenue sql: |- SELECT month, amount FROM revenue ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 1 CI posts what it would do to prod on the pull request - the review is of this, not only of the YAML: $ queryapigate config diff --server https://prod.example.com queryapigate.yaml queries[best_month] collection: "finance" connection_name: "sales" description: "The month with the most revenue" query_type: "sql" sql: SELECT month, amount FROM revenue ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 1 ~ roles[partner] rate_limit: "60/minute" -> "120/minute" ~ api_keys[partner-a] rate_limit: "60/minute" -> "120/minute" 1 to create, 2 to change. (exit 2: there are changes.) The key changes too: its grants are the role's. A file with a problem fails this step with every problem listed, and nothing reaches prod. Meanwhile, someone tries the shortcut - the same change straight on prod: PATCH /api/v1/roles/partner {"rate_limit": "120/minute"} 409 {"code": "config_managed", "error": "roles[partner] is managed by a configuration file - change it there; this server takes changes to it only from a file (QUERYAPIGATE_CONFIG_LOCKED)"}

Applied: the server matches the file (sha256 a30e8ac0451d). $ queryapigate config diff --server https://prod.example.com queryapigate.yaml No changes: the server matches the file. Prod's audit log says who applied which file, and each change it made: 2026-10-12 16:31:22 admin break-glass config_applied a30e8ac0451d 2026-10-12 16:31:22 admin config update_key partner-a 2026-10-12 16:31:22 admin config update_role partner 2026-10-12 16:31:22 admin config save_query best_month 2026-10-12 16:30:33 admin break-glass config_applied 7f25ab941ccd ... x: Delete best_month from the file and the diff, by default, leaves it alone - it only says so: On the server but not in the file - applying leaves them alone: queries[best_month] With --prune, it's deleted - because a file put it there: $ queryapigate config diff --prune --server https://prod.example.com queryapigate.yaml queries[best_month] 0 to create, 0 to change, 1 to delete. config apply --prune then deletes it. t: Manage your setup as code, and promote it from dev to prod through a pull request
x: A CI workflow is these two steps: config diff --server on every pull request (post its output as a comment; exit 1 fails the check), and config apply --server on merge. The diff is read-only, but posts the file to the server: give both the owner key only as a protected secret. On Kubernetes, skip the CI apply: the chart's configAsCode mounts the file and the first new pod applies it as it starts (Install on Kubernetes with Helm), so Argo CD or Flux syncing the chart is the deploy. Elsewhere, QUERYAPIGATE_CONFIG_FILE does the same. Without the lock, a change made on prod shows up as drift: config diff names it, and the next apply undoes it. Run the diff on a schedule to see it. Rotating the partner's key is a pull request too: a new secret_sha256 from config new-key. The old secret keeps working for 60 minutes, as a rotation does. Use config new-key for every key's secret. A hash is safe to keep in git only because the secret behind it is 32 random bytes; a secret someone chose could be guessed from its hash.

t: Use short-lived database credentials from Vault
x: Time: 20 minutes. You'll end up with: QueryAPIGate with no database password anywhere - Vault makes a database user for each lease, QueryAPIGate moves to the next one before the last expires, and not one call fails while it does; when Vault is down, it keeps serving while it safely can, then fails closed. Stable - secrets from Vault, and its short-lived database credentials, are under the compatibility promise since 0.34 (what that means). AWS's are still experimental. Every command and output below was run against Vault 1.21 (dev mode) and PostgreSQL 16, with QueryAPIGate signing in to Vault through AppRole. The leases last 60 seconds so that a few rotations fit in the guide; an hour is usual.

t: Use short-lived database credentials from Vault
h: Step 1: Vault makes the database's users
x: What Vault's administrator sets up - the database secrets engine, managing a role that may only read revenue: vault secrets enable database vault write database/config/warehouse plugin_name=postgresql-database-plugin \ connection_url="postgresql://{{username}}:{{password}}@warehouse.internal:5432/postgres" \ username=vault password=... allowed_roles=reporting-ro vault write database/roles/reporting-ro db_name=warehouse default_ttl=60s max_ttl=1h \ creation_statements="CREATE ROLE \"{{name}}\" WITH LOGIN PASSWORD '{{password}}' VALID UNTIL '{{expiration}}'; GRANT SELECT ON revenue TO \"{{name}}\";" And for QueryAPIGate, a policy that reaches exactly that - and revoking its own leases - with an AppRole for it to sign in with: path "database/creds/reporting-ro" { capabilities = ["read"] } path "sys/leases/revoke" { capabilities = ["update"] } vault auth enable approle vault write auth/approle/role/queryapigate token_policies=queryapigate token_ttl=1h vault read auth/approle/role/queryapigate/role-id # the role ID vault write -f auth/approle/role/queryapigate/secret-id # the secret ID - into a file only QueryAPIGate reads

x: QUERYAPIGATE_VAULT_ADDR=https://vault.example.com:8200 QUERYAPIGATE_VAULT_AUTH=approle QUERYAPIGATE_VAULT_ROLE_ID= QUERYAPIGATE_VAULT_SECRET_ID_FILE=/run/secrets/vault-secret-id QUERYAPIGATE_VAULT_DATABASE_ROLES=reporting-ro@warehouse.internal:5432 The last line says which roles a connection may ask for - and where their credentials may go: reporting-ro only to the warehouse. (On Kubernetes, QUERYAPIGATE_VAULT_AUTH=kubernetes with the chart's vaultToken.enabled, and no secret ID at all.)

h: Step 3: A connection with no password

Pointing the role anywhere else is refused - otherwise an administrator could have the server log in to a host of theirs with the warehouse's credentials: POST /api/v1/connections {"name": "elsewhere", "host": "db.attacker.example", ..., "credentials": {"source": "vault-database", "role": "reporting-ro"}} 400 {"code": "invalid_body", "error": "credentials vault-database is refused: 'reporting-ro' is bound to warehouse.internal:5432 by QUERYAPIGATE_VAULT_DATABASE_ROLES - not db.attacker.example:5432"}

t: Use short-lived database credentials from Vault
h: Step 4: Leases come and go; calls don't fail
x: GET /q/revenue every 200 ms for three minutes - three of those 60-second leases: answered 861, failed 0 from 18:57:24: v-approle-reportin-8zBMUctzHI5CG3EW6P4s-1791811633 (179 calls) from 18:58:01: v-approle-reportin-a4lOjbOTU2pSuW4ykWGG-1791811681 (229 calls) from 18:58:49: v-approle-reportin-WwAVdOPwmARxZO2aH8m4-1791811729 (231 calls) from 18:59:38: v-approle-reportin-1dRYtNa6w8ziCcjnsNmr-1791811778 (222 calls) Four database users, each taking over about 48 seconds after the last: QueryAPIGate asks Vault for the next pair at 80% of a lease, and stops using a pair - and retires every pooled connection opened with it - a tenth of the lease before it ends (at least 5 seconds, at most 5 minutes). Every connection opened in between shares one pair: one lease in Vault, not one per connection.

x: Vault paused right after QueryAPIGate took a fresh pair, calls once a second: 19:06:02 Vault paused 19:06:02 answered as v-approle-reportin-HCkAeIlkRnhgyui... 19:07:01 answered as v-approle-reportin-HCkAeIlkRnhgyui... (10.1s) 19:07:02 503 secret_unavailable 19:07:21 503 secret_unavailable (10.1s) 19:07:23 Vault back 19:07:34 answered as v-approle-reportin-qYgPOHrZaN6Bsso... For 48 seconds nothing changed: the pair it held was good. At the refresh point, one call waited on Vault - the 10-second timeout - and was still answered with the pair still within its time. The log says so, as a warning: The credential source vault-database failed (Vault at ... could not be reached: timed out) - using the credentials it gave before, good for ...s more. Then the pair was too close to its end, and QueryAPIGate failed closed: 503 secret_unavailable, at once - Vault is asked again only every 10 seconds, so calls don't each wait on it. With Vault back, the next call got a new pair. After five minutes of that, the secret_provider_failing alert says so, and Settings shows each provider's last answer: vault-database: ok at 19:01:55, or failing since ... with the error.

Pooled connections are retired before their pair's lease ends, however recently used - a query never runs on a user Vault is about to drop.

t: Answer a security questionnaire about data and cryptography
h: "What personal data does the system process, and why?"
x: From the page's personal data table: callers' names (an email address, for a person signed in with a token - jwt:alice@example.com), administrators' names and email addresses, IP addresses, an AI agent's write arguments - and whatever your databases hold, which passes through. Answer it for your deployment by what you've turned on: no SSO and no JWTs, and no person is named at all, only API keys.

t: Answer a security questionnaire about data and cryptography
x: A call that sends the email address in the URL: GET /q/orders?email=alice@example.com Authorization: Bearer [{"id": 1, "total": 42.5}, {"id": 3, "total": 7.25}] What the access log and the application log say about it: 21:25:26,945 INFO queryapigate [5c383d185428 key=jwt:alice@example.com]: Executing on shop (sqlite), limit=10 offset=0 timeout=30.0: SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE email = :email 21:25:26,946 INFO queryapigate [5c383d185428 key=jwt:alice@example.com]: GET /q/orders -> 200 in 2.8ms 127.0.0.1 - [12/Oct/2026:21:25:26 +0530] "GET /q/orders HTTP/1.1" 200 46 0.003582s rid=5c383d185428 "curl/8.5.0" The path, never the query string; no referrer; the statement with its placeholder, :email - the value is bound, not written into it. The caller is named: jwt:alice@example.com is personal data, in the log. Lines in the log with the email address that was in the URL: 0 The answer: Requests are logged by path, method, status, time, request id, client address and caller name - a signed-in person's caller name is their identifier; parameter values are not logged - unless you set QUERYAPIGATE_ACCESS_LOG_QUERY=1. Say what can still reach the log: an ad-hoc statement's text (QUERYAPIGATE_HISTORY_ADHOC_SQL=hash keeps it to a hash), and a database's own error message, which can quote a value.

t: Answer a security questionnaire about data and cryptography
x: A connection's password, as the store's file holds it: warehouse password, as stored: enc:gAAAAABqzQLfRV4CV5r8TOcz0G3Q0nJWxsBk_3tW... Fernet - AES-128 and HMAC-SHA256 - under QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY, kept outside the store; API keys and admin tokens are only ever stored as SHA-256 hashes. The answer: credentials at rest are encrypted or hashed; the store itself (configuration and run history, no query results) should sit on an encrypted volume or database, which is the platform's - QueryAPIGate doesn't encrypt the whole file. Or keep passwords out of the store entirely: references to Vault or AWS Secrets Manager (ADR 0015).

The page's store table gives every kind's retention and the setting that bounds it; copy the rows that apply. Logs, traces and SIEM copies are kept as your platforms keep them - say so, with their retention.

h: "Can you delete an individual's data on request?"
x: How much there is - queryapigate history forget ... --dry-run, or through the API: DELETE /api/v1/history?caller=jwt:alice@example.com&dry_run=true {"runs": 3, "usage_periods": 0} queryapigate history forget jwt:alice@example.com Deleted 3 run(s) and 0 usage period(s) of jwt:alice@example.com; recorded in the audit log by its hash, not its name. Alice's runs are gone; Bob's are not (0 runs and 1 run). The audit log records that it happened: {'actor': 'cli', 'action': 'forget_caller', 'target': 'history', 'changes': {'caller_sha256': '9e5bf797f99329d553c1ded1513172191bcaed59d54d26322c946aaf41b2e08d', 'runs': 3, ...}} sha256("jwt:alice@example.com") is 9e5bf797...e08d: anyone who knows the name can confirm the request was met; the log names no one to anyone who doesn't. What isn't erased, and why - the audit log's entries about administrators, write requests for their 30 days, your log platform - is on the page.

t: Answer a security questionnaire about data and cryptography
x: The precise answer: QueryAPIGate uses only FIPS-approved algorithms, and runs on a FIPS 140-validated module when the platform provides one. Validation belongs to the module (OpenSSL), not the application. The page lists every use - what it protects, the algorithm, the library - and a test fails if the code ever gains one that isn't approved. On Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 in FIPS mode, with Python and cryptography from the distribution - what CI runs the whole suite on: OpenSSL (ssl): OpenSSL 3.5.8 25 Aug 2026 cryptography 41.0.7 on OpenSSL 3.5.8 25 Aug 2026 - FIPS: True md5 refused: [digital envelope routines] unsupported Fernet round trip: True Say what is outside that boundary in your deployment: the PostgreSQL and MySQL drivers' binary wheels (build psycopg2 from source), DuckDB's TLS for remote files, and a JDBC or H2 connection's Java runtime.

t: Answer a security questionnaire about data and cryptography

Callers see only what their key or role grants, after column masking. The page's tables have a "Read by" column for each kind of data.

A record of processing (GDPR Article 30) can be built from the page's personal-data and store tables: the categories, the purposes, the retention, who reads it. QueryAPIGate isn't certified, and can't be: SOC 2 and ISO 27001 audit your organisation. The page and these checks are what your auditor reads about this part of it.

t: Keep the server's own secrets, and its metrics, in
x: Time: 15 minutes. You'll end up with: connections that can reference only the environment variables you list, never the server's own credentials, and /metrics readable by your Prometheus and your administrators and no one else - each checked on a running server. Two things a server can hand out without anyone meaning it to, both closed in 0.30: A connection's ${VAR} password is read from the server's environment - and the environment holds more than connection passwords: the cloud credentials the server runs with, tokens for other services. An administrator who may change connections could point one at a host of theirs and have the server send it one of those as a password. /metrics needs no API key - a scraper shouldn't hold one - so anyone who can reach the server reads it, and its labels name your API keys, saved queries and connections. Every command and output below was run against a real server (queryapigate serve), a PostgreSQL 16 database, and Prometheus 3.15. The server's environment held the warehouse password, an AWS secret key (standing in for the identity it runs with) and a credential for something else: QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY=ci-admin-key WAREHOUSE_PASSWORD=warehouse-pw-1 AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY DB_ADMIN_PW=root-pw-not-for-queryapigate

t: Keep the server's own secrets, and its metrics, in
h: The server's own credentials are never reachable
x: A connection whose password is a reference, and a query on it: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5077/api/v1/connections -H "X-API-Key: $ADMIN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"name": "warehouse", "db": "postgres", "host": "127.0.0.1", "port": 55443, "user": "postgres", "password": "${WAREHOUSE_PASSWORD}", "database": "postgres", "active": true}' GET /q/orders [{"id":1,"total":42.5},{"id":2,"total":19.0}] The same, with the server's AWS key, and a host that isn't yours - connections/test saves nothing, so it's the quickest way to try: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5077/api/v1/connections/test -H "X-API-Key: $ADMIN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"db": "postgres", "host": "collector.attacker.example", "user": "x", "password": "${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}", "database": "x"}' {"error":"${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY} is a cloud, Vault or Kubernetes credential the server itself may use and can't be referenced - use a variable of its own for the secret","code":"invalid_body"} Refused before any connection is tried. AWS_*, AZURE_*, ARM_*, GOOGLE_*, GCP_*, VAULT_* and KUBERNETES_* are always refused, like the server's own QUERYAPIGATE_* and OTEL_* settings.

t: Keep the server's own secrets, and its metrics, in
h: List the variables your connections use
x: What no rule knows about is still reachable: a connection referencing ${DB_ADMIN_PW} saved (201), and at the next start the server said so: WARNING queryapigate: Connections and destinations reference environment variables (DB_ADMIN_PW, WAREHOUSE_PASSWORD), and QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_ENV_VARS is unset: an administrator could reference any other variable too, and have the server send it to a host of theirs as a password. Set it to the ones in use. Set it - names, or prefixes ending in * (WAREHOUSE_*,QAG_*): QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_ENV_VARS=WAREHOUSE_PASSWORD The warning is gone, the warehouse query answers as before, and anything else is refused - when it's saved: {"error":"${DB_ADMIN_PW} isn't one of QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_ENV_VARS and can't be referenced - use a variable of its own for the secret","code":"invalid_body"} and when it's used, for a connection saved before the list was set: POST /execute_sql {"connection_name": "other", "sql": "SELECT 1"} {"error":"${DB_ADMIN_PW} isn't one of QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_ENV_VARS and can't be referenced by a connection or destination","code":"connection_misconfigured"} Settings in the Console shows the list as Environment secrets. A configuration file is held to it too: config export names a password the store held as a value ${QAG_...} - add QAG_* to the list before applying one.

x: QUERYAPIGATE_METRICS_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32) # at least 16 characters Then, with a partner's API key and an administrator, alice.smith, having made a call each: /metrics with no token: 401 /metrics with the partner's API key: 401 /metrics as alice (an administrator): 200 An administrator who may observe reads it without the token - that's the Console's Metrics screen. Everyone else needs Authorization: Bearer . What it shows: queryapigate_requests_total{method="GET",endpoint="api.run_named_query",status="200",key="partner-acme"} 1 queryapigate_requests_total{method="GET",endpoint="v1.list_connections",status="200",key="admin"} 1 queryapigate_queries_total{connection="warehouse",dialect="postgres",status="success",key="partner-acme"} 1 alice's call is key="admin": every administrator is counted under that one label, as signed-in users are under jwt, so no person's name is a label. t: Verify a release before you run it
x: Time: 20 minutes. You'll end up with: proof that the image and chart you run were built by this repository's release workflow, from the commit it names - and a cluster that refuses anything else. From 0.31, every image and the Helm chart is signed keyless with cosign, by digest, by .github/workflows/docker.yml on the release's tag, with SLSA provenance, an SBOM and a GitHub attestation (ADR 0018). Keyless means there's no key to trust: the signing certificate names the workflow and the tag it ran on, and the signature is recorded in Sigstore's public log. Every command and output below was run for real, against the release workflow's rehearsal - the same workflow, run by hand on main, publishing under -rehearsal names (ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate-rehearsal). So its identity ends @refs/heads/main. For a release, it ends @refs/tags/v, and the names have no -rehearsal: | | Rehearsal (below) | A release | | Image | ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate-rehearsal | ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate | | Chart | ghcr.io/anantharajuc/charts-rehearsal/queryapigate | ghcr.io/anantharajuc/charts/queryapigate | | Identity | https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/.github/workflows/docker.yml@refs/heads/main | ...docker.yml@refs/tags/v0.31.0 | The tools: cosign 3.1.3 and, for GitHub's attestation, the gh CLI (or cosign, as shown).

t: Verify a release before you run it
x: cosign verify ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate-rehearsal:rehearsal-d4b295f19b4f \ The following checks were performed on each of these signatures: The cosign claims were validated Existence of the claims in the transparency log was verified offline The code-signing certificate was verified using trusted certificate authority certificates The same for the -h2 image and the chart. What doesn't verify: # the same image, as the v0.31.0 release - it was signed on main, not that tag Error: no matching attestations: failed to verify certificate identity: no matching CertificateIdentity found ... # as another repository's workflow Error: no matching attestations: failed to verify certificate identity: no matching CertificateIdentity found ... # 0.30.0, released before signing Error: no signatures found Each release is signed in two forms: the Sigstore bundle (cosign verify, the default) and the classic .sig tag (cosign verify --new-bundle-format=false). Both verify; admission controllers below need the second.

t: Verify a release before you run it
h: Have a cluster refuse anything else › Kyverno
x: With Kyverno 1.19.1 (Helm chart kyverno/kyverno 3.9.1): apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1 kind: ClusterPolicy metadata: name: queryapigate-signed spec: validationFailureAction: Enforce webhookTimeoutSeconds: 30 rules: name: signed-by-its-release-workflow match: any: resources: kinds: [Pod] verifyImages: imageReferences: ["ghcr.io/anantharajuc/*"] mutateDigest: true verifyDigest: true attestors: entries: keyless: issuer: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com subjectRegExp: '^https://github\.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/\.github/workflows/docker\.yml@refs/tags/v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$' roots: | rekor: url: https://rekor.sigstore.dev Give it roots. Without them Kyverno 1.19.1 refused the signed image - cert verification failed: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority - because its built-in Sigstore root predates Fulcio's current intermediate. With the two certificates Fulcio publishes at /api/v2/trustBundle, it admitted the signed image and rewrote the pod to run it by digest (mutateDigest), and refused 0.30.0: no signatures found.

A maintainer account that's compromised can still tag a release - and Rekor's public log then records it. Pin by digest, not tag. A tag can be moved to other bytes; a digest can't, and it's what was signed. Releases before 0.31 aren't signed. A policy like the ones above refuses them.

t: Give each team its own workspace
x: Time: 15 minutes. You'll end up with: one QueryAPIGate serving several teams, each managing its own connections, saved queries and API keys in a workspace of its own - its owner running it without reaching anyone else's, its apps calling it as if it were the only one, and you, the platform team, seeing all of it. Experimental - workspaces are new in 0.38 and may change in a minor release, always noted in the changelog (what that means). A server that never creates one behaves exactly as before. Until 0.38 a server had one namespace: every administrator's role applied to every connection, key and query, so "the payments team runs its own APIs and can't touch the catalogue team's" took a server per team. A workspace (ADR 0023) is that boundary inside one server. Everything a server had is in the workspace default. It is delegated administration, not tenant isolation: every workspace runs in the same process, on the same store, and you - an owner of the server - see everything. It keeps teams out of each other's way and reach. Every command and response below was run against a real server, with the shared key demo-key.

t: Give each team its own workspace
x: As an owner of the server: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/workspaces -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"name": "payments", "description": "The payments team"}' # {"name":"payments","description":"The payments team","created_at":"2026-10-16 20:16:58","created_by":"admin","members":0} Or in the Console: Access → Workspaces → New workspace.

t: Give each team its own workspace
h: Step 2: Give the team's lead a role in it - and only there
x: Bea leads payments. She gets no role on the server itself ("role": null - say so: leaving role out is refused, so it is never by accident) and the role owner in her workspace: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/administrators -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"name": "bea", "role": null, "email": "bea@corp.com"}' curl -X PUT http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/workspaces/payments/members/bea -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"role": "owner"}' # {"admin":"bea","role":"owner","created_at":"2026-10-16 20:16:58","added_by":"admin"} Issue her a token as in guide 43 (POST /api/v1/administrators/bea/tokens). A role in a workspace is the same four roles, for that workspace only - an owner there manages its members, but not the server's administrators, settings or other workspaces.

Signed-in app users (JWT): set QUERYAPIGATE_JWT_WORKSPACE_CLAIM to a claim that names each user's workspace, so the token decides it - a user can't reach another team's by changing the /w// prefix. Unset, every signed-in user acts in default. No per-workspace limits yet (each key's own rate limits and quotas work as before), and no mapping of identity- provider groups to memberships. See Workspaces for the full reference.

t: Connect to Trino
x: Time: 10 minutes. You'll end up with: one connection that reaches every catalog behind a Trino endpoint - Hive, Iceberg, Delta, Kafka, object stores, other databases - each one a governed, saved REST and MCP query, with allowed_tables, masking and a real query time limit. Experimental (ADR 0026). What it covers, the catalog model and its limits: Trino connections. Before this, Trino was reachable only through generic JDBC - no time limit, no schema browser, no allowed_tables or masking. The native type fixes all of that. Trino is a federation engine: one endpoint, many catalogs, each a different underlying system. That one fact shapes everything below - most of all how allowed_tables works.

t: Connect to Trino
x: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "warehouse", "db": "trino", "host": "trino.internal", "port": 8080, "user": "queryapigate", "database": "tpch", "options": { "schema": "tiny", "http_scheme": "http" }, "active": true }' Needs pip install "queryapigate[trino]". The fields that are specific to Trino: database is the Trino catalog (here tpch, a catalog every Trino ships with). This is the one field that reads differently from the SQL dialects, where database is a database on the server. options.schema is the default schema within that catalog (here tiny), and options.http_scheme is http or https. A password, if given, is sent as HTTP basic auth and only over https. Test and browse it like any other connection - the schema browser reads the catalog's information_schema, scoped to the default schema: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections/test -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"db": "trino", "host": "trino.internal", "port": 8080, "user": "queryapigate", "database": "tpch", "options": {"schema": "tiny", "http_scheme": "http"}}' # {"elapsed_ms": 518.1} curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/connections/warehouse/schema -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' # {"tables": [{"name": "customer", ...}, {"name": "nation", ...}, {"name": "orders", ...}], "truncated": false}

t: Connect to Trino
h: Step 2: database is a catalog - switch between them
x: A Trino endpoint usually exposes several catalogs. In the Console, Connections → (the connection) → switch database lists them with SHOW CATALOGS and switches which one the connection queries: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections/databases' -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -X POST -d '{"db": "trino", "host": "trino.internal", "port": 8080, "user": "queryapigate", "database": "tpch", "options": {"http_scheme": "http"}}' # {"databases": ["jmx", "memory", "system", "tpcds", "tpch"]} Within a catalog, tables are addressed by schema.table, and across catalogs by catalog.schema.table - ordinary Trino SQL. Save a query exactly as for any SQL connection (guide 01): curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/queries -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "nations_by_region", "connection_name": "warehouse", "sql": "SELECT n.name FROM nation n JOIN region r ON n.regionkey = r.regionkey WHERE r.name = :region", "parameters": {"region": {"type": "str", "required": true, "description": "Region name, e.g. EUROPE"}}, "author": "you", "description": "Nations in a region", "publish": true }' curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/nations_by_region?region=EUROPE' -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' # [{"name": "FRANCE"}, {"name": "GERMANY"}, {"name": "ROMANIA"}, {"name": "RUSSIA"}, {"name": "UNITED KINGDOM"}]

t: Connect to Trino
h: Step 3: allowed_tables is fully qualified - the federation safety point
x: For every other dialect, allowed_tables matches a bare table name. For a federation engine that would be dangerous: a grant of orders would match orders in every catalog the connection can see. So on Trino the match is fully qualified - catalog.schema.table - with the catalog and schema a reference omits filled in from the connection's defaults. A grant of orders on the warehouse connection above (tpch / tiny) therefore means tpch.tiny.orders only: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/api-keys -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "reporting", "connections": ["warehouse"], "allowed_tables": ["orders"] }' # the default catalog + schema's orders: allowed curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/execute_sql -H 'X-API-Key: reporting-secret' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"sql": "SELECT count(*) FROM orders", "connection_name": "warehouse"}' # [{"_col0": 15000}] # the SAME table name in another schema or catalog: refused curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/execute_sql -H 'X-API-Key: reporting-secret' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"sql": "SELECT count(*) FROM sf1.orders", "connection_name": "warehouse"}' # {"error": "This API key may only query these tables: tpch.tiny.orders. Forbidden: tpch.sf1.orders.", # "code": "table_not_allowed"} To grant a table in another schema or catalog, qualify the grant: "allowed_tables": ["sf1.

t: Connect to Trino
h: What governance you get - and what you don't
x: Everything works through sqlglot's trino dialect, so it's the same as any SQL connection: Column masking (guide 45) and the tables-and-joins diagram both work. The query time limit cancels the running query on the Trino cluster, so a slow federated query can't run forever. Read-only rests on the SQL guard (Trino has no read-only session mode), the same as duckdb/h2/jdbc: a non-read statement is refused before it runs. Not there yet: Agent writes (guide 49) aren't supported on Trino. Primary/foreign keys and DDL in the schema browser (Trino has no enforced constraints).

t: Connect to Trino
h: The outer boundary: a scoped Trino user
x: A connection reaches whatever its Trino user can reach. allowed_tables narrows within that, but the strongest boundary is Trino's own access control: give each connection a read-only Trino user scoped to the catalogs and schemas it should see, and let QueryAPIGate's grants narrow from there. That way a mistake in a grant can't reach a catalog the user was never allowed to touch.

t: Connect to Trino
x: Restrict a key to specific tables - the full allowed_tables reference; Trino's qualified matching is the one dialect-specific twist. Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent - masking works on Trino like any SQL connection. Let an AI agent call your saved queries via MCP - a Trino-backed saved query is an MCP tool like any other.

t: See what's being used, from the Console
x: Time: 10 minutes. You'll end up with: a clear read on which keys, connections, queries and tools are actually in use - which ones are busy, which are granted but never touched - without wiring up any external monitoring. There are two kinds of usage view in the Console, and it helps to know which you're looking at: Activity over the last 30 days - drawn from the run log, so it survives restarts. This is the sparklines and the per-key usage history below. Live counts since this server process started - in-memory, reset on restart. This is the "Usage" column on each table, the Metrics screen, and /metrics.

t: See what's being used, from the Console
h: 1. Activity sparklines: who's busy, who's idle
x: Five Console tables now carry a small 30-day activity sparkline per row - a GitHub-style graph of runs per day: | Screen | One sparkline per… | Shows | | Access → API keys | key | how much each key is used (and links to its details) | | Access → Roles | role | the combined activity of the keys created from that role | | Data → Connections | connection | traffic to each database | | Data → Caching | cached query | which cache_ttl queries actually get hit | | MCP server | tool | a saved-query tool's MCP calls (built-in tools show "—") | A drawn line means traffic; a flat baseline means "granted but never used in 30 days" - often the most useful thing on the screen, because it points at access you can take away. Hover any sparkline for the totals (for example "example-reporting: 28 runs over 30 days · 3 failed · peak 3/day").

t: See what's being used, from the Console
h: 2. A key in full: the Details screen
x: On Access → API keys, each row has a Details link. It opens a page built entirely from that key's own activity: the saved queries (APIs) it can reach, and how each is granted; the connections and tables behind them, its limits and masking; last used, and its full run history - every call, with when, what, rows, duration and result; a per-API sparkline, scoped to this key, so you can see which of its granted APIs it actually calls. Clicking a query there opens its SQL. This is the fastest way to answer "what has this partner's key been doing?"

t: See what's being used, from the Console
h: 3. Who's using how much: usage quotas
x: Usage quotas (ADR 0011) count calls and rows per caller, per day and per month, in the store - so they're durable like the sparklines. GET /api/v1/usage/quotas is what the Console reads: curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/usage/quotas -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' {"items": [ {"caller": "example-dashboard", "per": "month", "period": "2026-10", "calls": 24, "rows": 8013, ...}, {"caller": "example-executive", "per": "month", "period": "2026-10", "calls": 19, "rows": 6937, ...}, ...]} These are the numbers a key's quota is measured against (Give a partner a quota and a concurrency cap).

t: See what's being used, from the Console
h: 4. Server-wide, right now: the Metrics screen
x: Observability → Metrics shows request volume, latency and error rate across the whole server. These come from in-memory counters, the same ones /metrics exposes in Prometheus format - so they count only since this process started, and a restart resets them. That's why a freshly restarted server shows low "Usage" numbers on the key and connection tables even when the 30-day sparklines are full: the sparklines read the durable run log, the Usage column reads these live counters. For dashboards and alerting over time, scrape /metrics - Wire up Prometheus and Grafana.

t: See what's being used, from the Console
h: 5. What agents did: the Agents screen
x: Observability → Agents is the usage view for AI clients: what each agent called over MCP, in the recent window. GET /api/v1/usage/agents backs it: curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/usage/agents -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' # {"since": "...", "until": "...", "sample_rate": 1.0, "truncated": false, "items": [...]} For the data dictionary agents see, and more on this screen, see Tell agents what your data means, and see what they did.

t: See what's being used, from the Console
h: 6. The run log behind all of it
x: Every view above the sparklines and histories is the run log, read different ways. Query it directly, filtered by key, query, status, kind or a time window: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/history?key=example-reporting&limit=3' -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' {"items": [ {"query": "example_top_films", "kind": "saved", "executed_at": "2026-10-19 05:51:56", "connection_name": "examples", "transport": "rest", "status": "success", "rows": 613, "duration_ms": 748}, ...], "next_cursor": null} For a live feed rather than history, the Home screen's requests panel updates in real time as queries run (over /events), and you can build your own - Build a client that watches queries run.

t: See what's being used, from the Console
x: Wire up Prometheus and Grafana - the live counters as dashboards and alerts. Read the audit log - not what ran, but who changed the configuration. Send the audit log to your SIEM - ship the record off the box.

t: Tune a deployment for throughput
x: Time: 20 minutes to read, plus a load test of your own. You'll end up with: threads, CPU, logging, cache and disk settings chosen for your queries and your database's distance, a number of containers to start from, and the figures each one rests on. Every figure here is measured on 0.43, in Performance, v4 (PostgreSQL) and Performance on MySQL, v2 - or, where those didn't rerun a block, in v3 and MySQL v1 - on one laptop with the gateway, the database and the load generator each on their own cores. Measure your own queries before you commit to a size.

t: Tune a deployment for throughput
h: 1. One worker per container, more containers for more
x: The image runs gunicorn with one worker and keeps it that way: each process has its own /metrics, its own response cache without Redis, and its own /events streams. Python runs one thread at a time per process, so a worker saturates about one core. More capacity means more containers, behind a load balancer, on a shared PostgreSQL store and Redis (Run several instances).

t: Tune a deployment for throughput
h: 2. Threads: by how long your calls wait
x: A worker's threads let it run Python for one call while others wait on the database. They help only while calls spend real time waiting. Measured, one worker, 32 callers: | Threads | PostgreSQL lookup, same host | MySQL lookup, same host | MySQL stock_level, same host | MySQL order_status, 0.5 ms away | | 1 | 904 req/s | 865 | 630 | 405 | | 2 | 1,012 | 823 | 772 | 648 | | 4 | 928 | 722 | 683 | 730 | | 8 (the default) | 896 | 676 | 642 | 685 | (PostgreSQL and the network column on 0.43; the MySQL same-host columns from v1, on code 0.43 didn't change for them.) Past what the waiting needs, threads cost: they compete for Python's interpreter lock. On fast queries next to their database, the best setting was 13-28% faster than the default eight; with the database 0.5 ms away, four threads were best. So: | Your calls | QUERYAPIGATE_THREADS | | Fast lookups (well under 1 ms) on a database on the same host or rack | 2 | | Queries of a few ms, or a database a network hop away | 4-8 | | Slow reports (tens of ms and up), or a warehouse or Trino across a network | 8-16, while CPU allows | The waiting limit of one worker is threads ÷ (query time + round trips × network round-trip time) calls a second. From 0.43 a PostgreSQL call makes 1 round trip to its database and a MySQL call 2, plus 3 to a PostgreSQL store, none with the metadata cache (section 4). A 20 ms report query at 0.5 ms away,

t: Tune a deployment for throughput
x: At full load one worker used 1.1-1.3 cores: one for Python, the rest for its threads' I/O (PostgreSQL 1.2, MySQL 1.1-1.3). A CPU limit below that throttles it, and the throttling shows up as latency, not as an error. | | Request | Limit | | A small or shared cluster (the Helm chart's default) | 250m | none | | Serving at capacity | 1 | 1.5, or none | # Helm resources: requests: {cpu: "1", memory: 256Mi} limits: {cpu: 1500m, memory: 1Gi} On one host, give each container its own physical core. Measured: four workers on one hyperthread of each of four cores served 2,250 calls a second; on both hyperthreads of two cores, 1,807 - a core's second hyperthread is worth about 0.6 of a core. Four workers allowed all eight hyperthreads of four cores did worse than on four (1,756), because the scheduler sometimes put two on one core.

t: Tune a deployment for throughput
h: 4. The metadata cache: +10-22%, and most of the network's cost
x: QUERYAPIGATE_METADATA_CACHE_TTL=5 keeps the key, saved query and connection a call reads from the store for 5 seconds instead of reading them on every call. Measured on 0.43: +15-19% on PostgreSQL, +10-18% on MySQL, +15-22% on a PostgreSQL store with 1-8 workers, and the store's load cut to a third. Across a network it matters most: with PostgreSQL and the store 0.5 ms away, one call took 4.39 ms without it and 1.60 ms with it - one round trip instead of four. The cost: a change made on another instance (or with the CLI) takes up to the TTL to arrive there - a revoked key keeps working on the other instances for that long. A change made through the same instance is seen at once. With one instance, turn it on; with several, decide whether a 5-second revocation delay is acceptable (the metadata cache).

t: Tune a deployment for throughput
h: 5. Logs: off where something else already logs
x: | Setting | What it writes | Cost measured | Turn off when | | QUERYAPIGATE_ACCESS_LOG=off | gunicorn's access line per request, on stdout | 6-7% of throughput | the proxy or load balancer logs requests | | QUERYAPIGATE_LOG_REQUESTS=off | QueryAPIGate's own request and query lines (INFO) | another 14% | the same - errors, warnings, slow queries and agent writes are still logged | Both off: +21% on one worker (MySQL v2). With the metadata cache on, logging is the largest single cost left in a call: a quarter of the CPU samples on PostgreSQL. Turn the access log off with the setting, not by sending it to /dev/null: that still formats and writes every line. At these rates the logs grow by gigabytes an hour - 6.6 GB in a five-hour MySQL run.

t: Tune a deployment for throughput
x: Every call is recorded in the store's event log (ADR 0020), kept for 24 hours by default: about 570 bytes a call on a SQLite store, more on PostgreSQL. | Sustained calls a second | Event log after 24 hours | | 50 | about 2.5 GB | | 500 | about 25 GB | | 2,000 | about 100 GB | QUERYAPIGATE_EVENTS_RETENTION_HOURS shortens it, and the disk with it. It is also how far back a queryapigate events client can resume after a disconnect, so keep it above the longest outage a client must ride out.

t: Tune a deployment for throughput
x: Per worker, at 75% of measured capacity, where p99 stays at about 4-5 ms: | | Plain | With the metadata cache | Cache, both request logs off | | PostgreSQL, fast OLTP calls | 670 calls a second | 780 | - | | MySQL, order_status-class calls | 500 | 545 | 650 | (0.42's were 550 / 650 and 440 / 490.) For a sense of the ceiling: one laptop with six performance cores, twelve workers of two threads and both logs off, served about 3,500 multi-database MySQL joins a second, sustained. Containers = the larger of (your calls a second ÷ that figure) and (your calls a second ÷ the waiting limit from section 2), plus one to lose without falling over. Every millisecond of Python a call costs beyond these simple lookups lowers the CPU figure; masked keys and large pages cost more. Then load-test your own queries at 75% of what you plan to serve, and watch p99, not the average: it holds flat to about 75% and triples by 90%.

t: Tune a deployment for throughput
x: Containers on separate hosts. The scale-out figures are workers sharing one laptop's cores; separate hosts should scale better, by an amount not yet measured. The light-load p99.9. At a quarter of capacity, a few calls in a thousand take about 30 ms, in bursts every few seconds; p99 is 3.4 ms. The history writer and, mostly, the garbage collector are ruled out; the cause isn't found yet (MySQL v2).

t: Try the Rust data plane in front of /q/
x: Time: 10 minutes. You'll end up with: the data plane on your public port, serving your saved-query reads itself, Python behind it doing everything else, and a way to see which calls it served. The data plane is a second process, queryapigate-dataplane, in the Docker image beside Python. For the calls it serves, it measured 3 to 9 times the calls a second per core of Python on its own, with p99 2 to 20 times lower (Performance, v5). It is experimental (ADR 0028, ADR 0030): what it serves, its settings and its headers may change in a minor release. It isn't in the PyPI package, and it isn't for a deployment that needs FIPS 140 - its cryptography isn't a validated module.

t: Try the Rust data plane in front of /q/
h: What it serves, and what it leaves to Python
x: On a server with QUERYAPIGATE_RATE_LIMIT or OpenTelemetry tracing (OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT) set, it serves nothing: it forwards every call, since those need state it doesn't share yet. Otherwise it serves a call itself when all of these hold, and forwards it to Python, unchanged, when any doesn't: a GET or POST to /q/, answered as JSON (no ?format=, no streaming); with a scoped API key in the default workspace, with no rate limit, quota, concurrency, time or row limit of its own. Administrators, signed-in users, MCP and other workspaces always go to Python; on a PostgreSQL or MySQL connection, for a read-only saved query with bound parameters (no {name} text placeholders, no embed parameters, no response cache of its own); behind trusted proxies (QUERYAPIGATE_TRUST_PROXY), with X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto it reads exactly as Python does: one line each, no quotes or empty items, http or https. A proxy's ordinary headers are; and Python has answered the same call with the same key once already. That first call gives the data plane its plan: the SQL to send, the masking to apply, and digests of the key, query and connection rows it was made from. Every later call reads those rows again and is served only while they're unchanged. Everything else - the Console, the Management API, writes, MCP, /events, /metrics - passes through to Python as if the data plane weren't th

t: Try the Rust data plane in front of /q/
x: One value: each API server pod gets a second container from the same image, which takes the pod's port, and Python moves to the pod's loopback. The chart makes the secret the two share, and keeps it across upgrades. dataplane: enabled: true resources: requests: {cpu: 500m, memory: 64Mi} limits: {cpu: "2", memory: 256Mi} # about 2 CPUs a pod without a run store - see "What to watch for" helm upgrade --install qag oci://ghcr.io/anantharajuc/charts/queryapigate -f values.yaml kubectl logs deploy/qag-queryapigate -c dataplane # queryapigate-dataplane 0.47.0: listening on 0.0.0.0:5000, ... Behind the chart's ingress it serves as above: the chart sets QUERYAPIGATE_TRUST_PROXY=1, and the data plane reads the controller's X-Forwarded-For as Python does. With helm template or Argo CD, which can't see a Secret already in the cluster, give your own: dataplane.existingSecret, with the secret (at least 16 characters) under dataplane.key.

t: Try the Rust data plane in front of /q/
x: Two containers from the same image, the second sharing the first one's network: Python on 127.0.0.1:5001, the data plane on port 5000. Both need the same secret, settings and store. export QUERYAPIGATE_DATAPLANE_SECRET="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" # at least 16 characters; the same for both IMAGE=ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate:0.47.0 docker run -d --name qag -p 5000:5000 -v qag-data:/data --env-file qag.env \ -e QUERYAPIGATE_DATAPLANE_SECRET -e QUERYAPIGATE_BIND=127.0.0.1:5001 "$IMAGE" docker run -d --name qag-dataplane --network container:qag -v qag-data:/data --env-file qag.env \ -e QUERYAPIGATE_DATAPLANE_SECRET -e QUERYAPIGATE_DATAPLANE_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:5000 "$IMAGE" queryapigate-dataplane qag.env holds your other settings, as before. The port is published on the first container, and the image's health check reaches both: in the shared network, port 5000 is the data plane, which passes /health to Python. In Compose, the second service takes network_mode: service:; for the scale-out example, add deploy/scale-out/docker-compose.dataplane.yml: docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dataplane.yml up -d

t: Try the Rust data plane in front of /q/
x: Call the same saved query a few times with a scoped key: for id in 7 8 9; do curl -s -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" "http://localhost:5000/q/customer?id=$id"; sleep 1; done The answers are byte for byte what Python would send. Python answers the first, which gives the data plane its plan, and calls go on reaching Python until it has recorded the key's use, within one flush interval (QUERYAPIGATE_HISTORY_FLUSH_INTERVAL, 1 s). After that they show up in the data plane's log, not Python's: an Executing on ... line and the request line, in Python's format. Their runs appear in run history and the Console's live feed within a flush interval, and /metrics counts them as Python would. If a call you expect to be served keeps going to Python, check it against the list above: an administrator's key, a key with a rate limit, ?format=csv or a text placeholder are the usual reasons. A data plane from another release than Python's serves nothing, and Python logs why once: in the image, both come from one build.

t: Try the Rust data plane in front of /q/
x: | Setting | Default | What it does | | QUERYAPIGATE_DATAPLANE_SECRET | none: required | Shared with Python. Without it, Python gives no plans and the data plane can't start | | QUERYAPIGATE_DATAPLANE_LISTEN | 127.0.0.1:5000 | Where clients connect | | QUERYAPIGATE_DATAPLANE_UPSTREAM | http://127.0.0.1:5001 | The Python server | | QUERYAPIGATE_DATAPLANE_THREADS | the CPUs it may use | Tokio worker threads; a container's CPU limit counts | | QUERYAPIGATE_DATAPLANE_POOL_SIZE | 16 | Connections per database it serves from, on top of Python's pool | | QUERYAPIGATE_BIND | 0.0.0.0:5000 in the image | Where the image's gunicorn listens: 127.0.0.1:5001 behind the data plane | It also reads Python's own settings that change an answer or a log line, and applies them as Python does: QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY, QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY, QUERYAPIGATE_MASK_KEY, QUERYAPIGATE_QUERY_TIMEOUT, QUERYAPIGATE_MAX_PAGE_SIZE, QUERYAPIGATE_METADATA_CACHE_TTL, QUERYAPIGATE_HISTORY_FLUSH_INTERVAL, QUERYAPIGATE_LOG_REQUESTS, QUERYAPIGATE_ACCESS_LOG, QUERYAPIGATE_JSON_LOGS, QUERYAPIGATE_SLOW_QUERY_THRESHOLD, QUERYAPIGATE_HISTORY_ADHOC_SQL, QUERYAPIGATE_TRUST_PROXY and QUERYAPIGATE_HSTS_MAX_AGE. The metadata cache is where much of its speed comes from: with QUERYAPIGATE_METADATA_CACHE_TTL=5, a call reuses the key, query and connection rows it read in the last 5 seconds instead of reading the store, and a revoked ke

t: Try the Rust data plane in front of /q/
x: Without the image: you need Rust (dataplane/rust-toolchain.toml names the version, and rustup installs it), and the same environment, user and store for both processes. git clone https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate && cd QueryAPIGate cargo build --release --manifest-path dataplane/Cargo.toml QUERYAPIGATE_BIND=127.0.0.1:5001 gunicorn --workers 1 --worker-class gthread \ -c python:queryapigate.gunicorn_conf 'queryapigate.app:create_app()' & QUERYAPIGATE_DATAPLANE_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:5000 dataplane/target/release/queryapigate-dataplane Build it from the same commit as the Python you run: Python serves plans only to a data plane of its own release. Keep 127.0.0.1:5001 unreachable from outside the host: a request that reaches Python directly skips the data plane, which is harmless, but the data plane should be the only way in.

t: Try the Rust data plane in front of /q/
x: In the chart, dataplane.enabled: false. With Docker, stop the second container and start the first without QUERYAPIGATE_BIND. Nothing is stored on the data plane's side: plans live in its memory only.

t: Try the Rust data plane in front of /q/
x: Runs it can't record are dropped and counted in queryapigate_history_runs_total{outcome="dropped"}. One Python worker records about 17,000 runs a second, and a data plane serves about 9,000 calls a second per CPU. Without a run store, keep a pod's data plane near 2 CPUs and add pods past that - held to 2, it recorded every one of 9.8 million runs at 16,400 calls a second (measured); with one (guide 65), the data plane writes its runs there itself and there's no such limit. More workers per pod would lift it too, but /metrics is kept per worker, so a scrape would see one of them. The run history and event log grow with its rate. The event log keeps every run for QUERYAPIGATE_EVENTS_RETENTION_HOURS; at tens of thousands of calls a second, that is more than a SQLite store should hold. Shorten it, or keep runs in ClickHouse. More database connections: each data plane opens up to QUERYAPIGATE_DATAPLANE_POOL_SIZE to each database it serves from, beside Python's pool. Count them per pod against the database's limit. Writes and other forwarded calls pay one extra hop: about 0.35 ms at p50 on the benchmark laptop.

t: Keep run history and the event log in ClickHouse
x: Time: 20 minutes, with a ClickHouse server. You'll end up with: every run recorded in ClickHouse instead of the metadata store - history, the event log and usage rollups - written in batches by the Python server and by the Rust data plane, if you run one. The metadata store (SQLite or PostgreSQL) records two rows per run: one in history and one in the event log. At a few hundred calls a second that's fine. At the data plane's rates, 20,000 or more a second, it's 1.7 billion events a day. A ClickHouse run store keeps them in about 13 bytes a run, expires them by partition, and counts usage from all of them. It is a prototype (ADR 0029, measured and decided go): its tables, its event ids and how it's switched on may change before it graduates. Try it on a test deployment first. Keys, queries, connections and the audit log stay in the metadata store. /metrics doesn't change.

t: Keep run history and the event log in ClickHouse
x: ClickHouse 24.8 or later. On it, a database and a user for QueryAPIGate, which creates its tables at startup: CREATE DATABASE queryapigate; CREATE USER queryapigate IDENTIFIED BY '...'; GRANT SELECT, INSERT, CREATE TABLE, CREATE VIEW, ALTER TABLE, ALTER VIEW, ALTER DELETE ON queryapigate.* TO queryapigate; With a data plane, give it a user of its own that can only insert runs. It can't read anything, and the views QueryAPIGate made still fill history and the rollups from what it inserts: CREATE USER queryapigate_dataplane IDENTIFIED BY '...'; GRANT INSERT ON queryapigate.events TO queryapigate_dataplane;

t: Keep run history and the event log in ClickHouse
x: Set the same URL on every instance - the server, queryapigate events, MCP, exports and the CLI - and restart them all together. Use https:// (port 8443 on ClickHouse Cloud); plain http:// is refused except to this machine. export QUERYAPIGATE_RUN_STORE_URL=https://queryapigate:...@clickhouse.internal:8443/queryapigate # or QUERYAPIGATE_RUN_STORE_URL_FILE=/run/secrets/run-store-url The first instance to start logs: Run store: runs, events and usage are kept in ClickHouse at clickhouse.internal:8443/queryapigate from now on (1234 events copied) It copied the event log's last 24 hours with their ids, so a client that was connected to /events resumes as if nothing had happened. The metadata store now records where runs are kept: an instance started without the URL, or with a different one, refuses to start and says so, rather than recording runs somewhere else. History from before the switch is still in the metadata store. To bring it across, once: queryapigate runs copy-to-clickhouse

t: Keep run history and the event log in ClickHouse

It then writes the runs it serves straight to ClickHouse, with event ids from a block Python leases it, and Python only counts them for /metrics. The lease names where Python keeps runs: a data plane whose URL names another server or database writes none of them, and logs Python keeps runs in ClickHouse at ..., not ... until it's corrected. One gunicorn worker behind it is enough again: Python no longer queues every run.

t: Keep run history and the event log in ClickHouse
x: History is kept by time, not by a count per version: QUERYAPIGATE_HISTORY_RETENTION_DAYS, 30 days unless set. QUERYAPIGATE_HISTORY_LIMIT still sets how many runs per version the Console shows. Live events arrive about a second later. An event is delivered once it's a second old, so a client resuming from any id it was given misses nothing. queryapigate_events_late_total in /metrics counts the rare insert acknowledged later than that; a client resuming from a newer id could miss one. Above zero, ClickHouse is too slow for its inserts. Usage reports are exact for any window within the event log's retention, 24 hours by default: every run counts, whatever QUERYAPIGATE_HISTORY_SAMPLE_RATE keeps in history, and nothing is truncated. With these rates, the sample rate can be set low: history becomes examples to look at, not the record. Backups: a backup of the metadata store doesn't hold the runs any more. Back up ClickHouse with its own tools, if you need history kept. queryapigate history forget erases a person from all five tables in ClickHouse too. Ad-hoc statements are kept as text, by minute, only as long as the event log; the hourly rollup keeps a year of their SHA-256 hashes instead.

t: Keep run history and the event log in ClickHouse
x: queryapigate runs leave-clickhouse # with QUERYAPIGATE_RUN_STORE_URL still set Then unset QUERYAPIGATE_RUN_STORE_URL on every instance and restart them. The metadata store's event ids continue above ClickHouse's, so clients still resume. The runs already in ClickHouse stay there; nothing is copied back.

t: Every run, recorded
x: QueryAPIGate is a governed gateway: a saved query becomes /q/, and every call is checked, run, masked where it has to be, and recorded. Who called, which query, when, how many rows, what was refused. That record is run history, the event log behind /events, and the usage reports. For a gateway that sits in front of production data, it's not a nice-to-have. It's half the point. In 0.44 we put a Rust data plane in front of the Python server: Python decides, Rust serves. It served about 8 times the calls a second per core. And it found the next limit straight away. The data plane reported every run back to Python, and Python wrote each one twice to the metadata store, SQLite or PostgreSQL: one row in history, one in the event log. At the 64-caller peak, the data plane served 34,240 calls a second and 52% of the runs were recorded. The rest were counted as dropped. The gateway kept up. Its audit trail didn't.

t: Every run, recorded
x: At 20,000 calls a second, every run recorded is 1.7 billion events a day. That's more than SQLite or the PostgreSQL store should hold, and the metadata store has other work to do: keys, queries, connections, the audit log. What runs need is different. They're written once and never changed, read mostly by time, counted in aggregates, and dropped when they age out. That's what ClickHouse is built for. It compresses columns of similar values very well, takes large batched inserts cheaply, and can drop a whole partition when its time is up instead of deleting rows. So 0.45 adds an optional run store: set QUERYAPIGATE_RUN_STORE_URL, and run history, the event log and usage rollups are kept in ClickHouse. Everything that decides who may do what stays in the metadata store.

t: Every run, recorded
x: One insert per batch. A batch of runs is one insert into a table called events: up to 100,000 runs from the data plane. ClickHouse fills history, per-query run counts and per-minute and per-hour usage rollups from that one insert, through materialized views. Each table's retention is a TTL on its partitions. The data plane writes its own runs. It gets its own ClickHouse user that can only insert into events. It can't read anything. The views that fill the other tables run as the user who created them. Python is told only how many runs there were, for /metrics. Event ids that clients can trust. /events clients resume with Last-Event-ID, so ids must keep increasing and must never be handed out twice. Two kinds of writer now mint them, Python and the data plane, with no shared counter. So an id is the millisecond since 2026-01-01, times 4,096, plus a number from a block of each millisecond that the writer leases in the metadata store. Two writers never hold the same block. Ids stay below 2^53, so a JavaScript client holds them exactly. Delivered once settled. An insert that's acknowledged later than another can still carry the lower id. So the events server delivers an event only once it's a second old, and a client resuming from any id it was given misses nothing. A rare insert later than that is counted in /metrics.

t: Every run, recorded
x: We measured it the way we measured the data plane: on a fixed laptop, against the store it replaces, with the go or no-go criteria written down first (ADR 0029, section 9). It didn't pass at first. The data plane's batches were too small. At 500 runs an insert, ClickHouse spent 1.6 cores merging parts. At up to 100,000, it spent 0.20. The usage report took 4,991 ms. It parsed every run's JSON entry to find its error code, masking and statement. Those became columns written with the run, then whole minutes came from the per-minute rollup: 16 ms, and still exact. The Console's version list took 723 ms. It scanned a query's whole history for its run counts. A small table, kept up by a view, now holds them: 6 ms. A filtered replay of the log took 41 seconds. It read the large entry column for nearly every block to find 1 match in 2,400. It now finds a page's ids first, then reads only those rows. Each one came from ClickHouse's own query log, not from guessing.

t: Every run, recorded
h: A security review, then 250 million runs
x: A new store that holds every run's record needed a review before it could graduate. It found six things. The three that mattered: A forged row could split an event stream. The events server copied a stored event into its frame as it was. A line break in a row, written by anyone with an insert credential, could start frames of the writer's own, with an id that moved every client's resume point. Frames are one line now, and the table refuses ids above 2^53. A data plane pointed at another ClickHouse would have written its runs there, out of history and out of reach of an erasure. Python's instances already refused to start in that case; the data plane didn't check. Now Python tells it where runs belong, and it writes nothing until they agree. Ad-hoc SQL text lived longer than the retention settings said, in the hourly rollups, for 400 days. They keep a hash of each statement now.
