h: Where it doesn't help, and what's left
x: It's experimental. It shipped in 0.45.0. The review's fixes and the faster replay are in the next release, and it graduates once a release goes out unchanged. The data plane writing its own runs needs the data plane, which is still built from the repository, not shipped in the image. One laptop, one ClickHouse server. On a replicated cluster, a read from a replica behind the one that took the insert could miss the settle window. That's an open question. The events server is the next ceiling. One queryapigate events process delivers about 6,500 to 10,000 events a second per stream. Run several behind a load balancer, each reads the store on its own. Live events arrive about a second later, by design, and history is kept by time, 30 days unless you set it. If you run the data plane, or record enough runs that the metadata store struggles, guide 65 switches it on. Try it on a test deployment first. All the figures are in the first measurement and the 250-million-run one, with the harness to run them yourself.

t: Python decides, Rust serves
x: QueryAPIGate puts governed REST endpoints in front of SQL databases: a saved query becomes /q/, and every call is checked, run, masked where it has to be, and recorded. Our last two benchmarks (PostgreSQL, MySQL) gave the same answer: the database isn't the limit, the gateway is. MySQL answers a per-user lookup in 0.03 ms, and the gateway adds 1.0-1.3 ms of Python around it. One worker serves 650-1,000 calls a second. Eight workers on eight cores serve about 3,000-3,500, because Python's workers don't scale well on shared cores. The time is spread out. Logging, gunicorn and HTTP, Flask, the store reads and the driver each take 8-23% of a call. No single hot function would pay off rewriting. So we tried a different thing: a small Rust process in front of Python that serves the hot path itself, without taking any decisions away from Python.

t: Python decides, Rust serves
h: The rule: Python decides, Rust applies
x: Rewriting the governance in Rust would have meant two implementations of the most security-sensitive code we have: the SQL guard, table allow-lists, column masking. Two parsers that must agree, kept in agreement by a fuzz that can only sample. We didn't want that, so the data plane doesn't decide anything. It sits on the public port. The first time a scoped key calls a saved query, the data plane forwards the call to Python, which answers as it always does and adds a plan to a successful response: the statement to send, which columns to mask and how, and digests of the three rows the verdict was computed from (the key, the saved query and the connection). The data plane keeps the plan in memory and strips it from the response. On every later call it reads those three rows again, with the same SELECTs Python uses, and serves only if they still digest the same. A key that's revoked, expired or re-scoped, or a query that's edited, changes a digest, and the call goes to Python. So does anything the prototype doesn't handle: writes, CSV, streaming, administrators, signed-in users, rate-limited keys. The data plane never answers 401 or 403 on its own, so it can never disagree with Python about one. Python still records everything. The data plane reports each run it served in batches, and Python writes it into run history, the event log and /metrics, as if it had served it.

t: Python decides, Rust serves
h: The gate: answer exactly as Python does
x: "Exactly" means byte for byte: the JSON body (Python's float formatting, its dates and decimals, its escaping), the headers, the error bodies, and the history row each call leaves. The parameters go into SQL as literals, the way psycopg2 and mysql-connector do it, so the quoting is the injection boundary and gets its own care. The test that decided whether any of this counted is a differential test. Random calls from every kind of key (plain, masked, table-restricted, IP-restricted, rotated, expired), with valid, invalid and hostile parameters, are sent to Python directly and through the data plane, and the answers are compared whole. Partway through, grants change, a key is revoked and a query gets a new version. Any difference fails it, a refusal included. Over 22,500 calls on PostgreSQL and MySQL, it found none.

t: Python decides, Rust serves
x: The first full run went wrong twice before it measured anything useful, and both failures were worth having. It filled the disk. At tens of thousands of calls a second, the request logs grow by about a gigabyte a cell, and the event log keeps every run for 24 hours: more than a million rows each cell. Each cell now starts with both empty, and the benchmark refuses to start one with less than 3 GB free. Most of the runs went unrecorded. The data plane served 16,000-39,000 calls a second, and Python recorded about 3,000 runs a second of them. For each run reported, it parsed the entry, encoded it again, built the event and its JSON, and worked out every metric label one at a time: about 27 µs a run, under one interpreter lock. The rest were dropped from a full queue, and nothing counted them. The fix moved work to where it's cheap. The data plane now sends each run already serialized, exactly as Python's json.dumps writes it, with its labels and timings. Python queues a whole batch at once, writes only the history rows it will keep, and inserts a batch's events in one statement: about 7 µs a run. Any run the data plane can't queue is counted in /metrics. With two Python workers behind it, every run is recorded up to about 24,000 calls a second on this laptop. The lesson for the benchmark: a cell counts only if it recorded what it served. Every data-plane cell now reports the shar

x: Measured on one laptop, each part on its own CPUs: the gateway on 8 hardware threads, the database on 4, the load generator on 8. Each figure is the median of 5 rounds, with the builds taking turns. The multiples compare the data plane with the Python build behind it, metadata cache with cache, and count Python's cores in the data plane's figure. The full report is Performance, v5. Each side at its best on the same 8 cores (MySQL, a customer lookup, 64 callers, every run recorded): | | Python, 8 workers + cache | Data plane + cache, 2 Python workers behind it | | Calls a second | 2,976 | 23,619 | | Gateway cores used | 7.34 | 7.34 | | p99 | 93 ms | 3.8 ms | That's 7.9 times the calls a second per core. PostgreSQL, at a fixed 20,000 calls a second, every run recorded: the data plane + cache used 2.97 of its 8 cores, with p99 at 1.8 ms. That's 6,734 calls a second per core, against 925 for Python + cache: 7.3 times. One caller at a time, a PostgreSQL lookup: 1.01 ms at p50 through Python + cache, and 0.11 ms through the data plane. Without the metadata cache, the data plane gets 3.2-4.4× per core on lookups. Each call then reads its three store rows from the database, and that read costs the data plane what it costs Python. The cache, which both processes honour the same way, is where much of the speed comes from.

t: Python decides, Rust serves
x: Writes are forwarded to Python, so they pay a hop: 0.35 ms more at p50, and 0.8× the calls a second per core. Serving them was never the data plane's job. A 100-row page on PostgreSQL without the cache gets 2.8× per core, because PostgreSQL itself is the limit there. The first call for each query and key goes through Python, as does every call using something the prototype forwards. These are steady-state figures: the same queries, called again and again.

t: Python decides, Rust serves
h: What the differential test couldn't see
x: Before the pull request, a code review of the whole branch found real bugs the differential test missed, because it varies parameters and keys, not SQL text, sockets or failures. Two examples: MySQL's time-limit hint went in at the wrong place. Python gave its position in characters, and Rust read it in bytes, so non-ASCII text in a comment before SELECT could move the hint into the comment. IP allow-lists could disagree on a dual-stack socket. Rust judged ::ffff:203.0.113.9, while Python judged 203.0.113.9. Both are fixed and tested, along with seven more. The differential test is necessary, not sufficient.

t: Python decides, Rust serves
x: It's a prototype. It's built from the repository, isn't in the Docker image or the Helm chart, and is marked experimental. The decision it was built to reach was go: it cleared the 3× bar we set in advance on every lookup, with p99 lower everywhere. Two things come before it ships: Shipping it: the image, the chart, and which of what it forwards to serve next. A store for runs at its rate. Every run recorded at 20,000 calls a second is 1.7 billion rows a day, more than SQLite or the PostgreSQL store should hold. That's the next design question. To try it now: Try the Rust data plane. The design and the decision are in ADR 0028.

t: One MySQL server, six services, one gateway
x: A common shape for a growing system is one MySQL server, with a database per microservice: crm for customers, orders, billing, inventory, and so on. Sooner or later, something needs to read across them: a support tool, a partner API, an AI agent. "Show me this user's latest order, with the items and their payments" is three services' data in one query. MySQL can join across databases on the same server, so the question is what putting a governed gateway in front of that costs. We measured it. We loaded TPC-C's data into MySQL 8.4 (600,000 customers, 6 million order lines) and split its tables into six databases, one per service. Then we ran six per-user queries through QueryAPIGate and straight into MySQL, side by side. The full write-up, with every table and its ranges, is Performance on MySQL.

t: One MySQL server, six services, one gateway
x: | Query | MySQL directly | Through the gateway | Added | | One customer by id | 0.03 ms | 1.16 ms | 1.1 ms | | TPC-C Order-Status (customer, last order, its lines) | 0.08 ms | 1.40 ms | 1.3 ms | | TPC-C Stock-Level (a range and a COUNT(DISTINCT)) | 0.42 ms | 1.64 ms | 1.2 ms | These are single calls at p50, with the metadata cache on. The gateway adds about the same 1.1-1.3 ms to every query, so the cost is fixed, not a percentage. For a query MySQL answers in microseconds, that cost is most of the call. For one that takes 20 ms, it's noise. The cost is the gateway's work: identity, the grant check, the SQL guard, the record of the run, and the HTTP response. All of it is Python. One worker serves 580-780 of these calls a second, while MySQL, on two cores, could answer 8 to 110 times more. So you scale with workers. At eight workers, the heaviest query kept MySQL busy on 2.5 of its 4 hardware threads, and the lighter ones on less than one.

t: One MySQL server, six services, one gateway
h: Three round trips, one of them a ping
x: We counted every statement MySQL received: two per call, the query and a ROLLBACK when the pooled connection goes back to the pool. That's half what PostgreSQL gets, because the MySQL driver sets read-only mode and the time limit once per connection, not once per query. Then we timed calls at 0, 0.5, 1 and 2 ms of simulated network delay. The slope of latency against delay counts the round trips a call actually waits for, and it said three. The third turned out to be in the MySQL client library. Every time code asks mysql-connector for a cursor, the library pings the server first, and our driver asked for a new cursor on every query. A ping isn't a statement, so the log never showed it. Across a 0.5 ms network, that's 0.6 ms a call we can take back by reusing a cursor. It's on the list for the next release.

t: One MySQL server, six services, one gateway
x: | Threads per worker | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | | One customer by id (0.03 ms) | 865/s | 823 | 722 | 676 | | Stock-Level (0.42 ms) | 630 | 772 | 683 | 642 | The Docker image runs eight threads per worker. For a 0.03 ms lookup, one thread was 28% faster than eight: extra threads only compete for Python's interpreter lock. The 0.42 ms query wanted two, because with one thread a worker sits idle while MySQL works. The rule is simple: the faster the query, the fewer threads it needs. Slow reports and exports are the opposite, and that's what the eight threads are for.

t: One MySQL server, six services, one gateway
h: Busy users make a response cache pay
x: Real traffic isn't uniform. A few accounts call far more than the rest. We drew users from a Zipf distribution and gave the Order-Status query a 30-second response cache (cache_ttl: 30): 59% of calls were answered from the cache, throughput rose 23%, and MySQL got 58% fewer statements. With uniform users, the same cache cost 8%. Only 5% of 600,000 equally likely users came back within 30 seconds, and storing the rest bought nothing. So put cache_ttl on queries whose callers repeat themselves, such as dashboards and popular accounts, and not on lookups every user makes once.

t: One MySQL server, six services, one gateway
x: QueryAPIGate reads three rows of its own on every call: the API key, the saved query and the connection. On one instance with its store on local SQLite, those reads are cheap in time but not in CPU: a fifth of the worker's. Several instances share a PostgreSQL store instead, and then the reads cross the network too: | QueryAPIGate's store | One call | | SQLite, local | 3.5 ms | | PostgreSQL, 0.5 ms away | 6.1 ms | | PostgreSQL, 0.5 ms away, with the metadata cache | 3.4 ms | The metadata cache (QUERYAPIGATE_METADATA_CACHE_TTL) keeps those three rows in memory. It caches rows, never decisions: whether a key is active, expired or used from an allowed address is checked on every call. For a multi-instance deployment, it's the difference between the second row and the third. On a single instance, it still adds 12-15% throughput.

t: One MySQL server, six services, one gateway

t: One MySQL server, six services, one gateway
x: Six services in one server raise a question the performance numbers don't answer: can a key for one service be kept out of another's tables? We checked. A key allowed to read customer could read crm.customer, as intended, and could also read a billing.customer table in another service's database. On MySQL, QueryAPIGate's table allow-list matches bare table names; only Trino connections match the full catalog.schema.table. Until that changes, keep services apart with MySQL's own grants. Give each service a MySQL user that can only see its own databases, add it as its own QueryAPIGate connection, and grant keys that connection only. Matching schema.table on MySQL is planned for the next release. Saved queries aren't affected: a key granted named queries can only run their SQL, which the publisher wrote.

For 0.42 we measured it on PostgreSQL, had the method reviewed twice, fixed what the reviews found, and published the harness so you can check our numbers. This post is the whole of it.

What a governed call costs

A laptop isn't a server, so most of the method is about keeping it from changing under us: AC power, and the performance power profile and CPU energy preference. Turbo stays on, since turning it off needs root; its effect is measured below. Every part on its own cores, so none takes CPU from another: | Part | CPUs | How | | QueryAPIGate (gunicorn) | 0-7: four performance cores, both threads of each | taskset -c 0-7 | | PostgreSQL | 8-11: two performance cores | docker run --cpuset-cpus 8-11 | | Load generator (oha) and pgbench | 12-19: the efficiency cores | docker run --cpuset-cpus 12-19 | No proxy in the path. Both sessions sagged about 10% in their last hour, after 90 minutes of load. That's why every table compares builds only within its own block, where they take turns. The load generator was never the bottleneck. It used at most 0.79 of its 8 cores, at 2,700 calls a second

t: What a governed call costs
x: The busiest gateway core's clock was sampled every two seconds of every run: Overall, 2.4 to 4.4 GHz. That range is between blocks: with eight busy workers, the cores run at a lower all-core turbo. Within a cell - the same build, call and setting - only ±1%. The rare fast outlier rounds are clock spikes. One 0.41 round ran at 4.09 GHz against its cell's usual 3.65, and served 11% more. So one turbo burst can make one round look good. That's why there are 5 rounds, and why the rule looks at ranges: an outlier widens a range instead of moving a median.

t: What a governed call costs
h: How we measured › When a difference counts
x: Builds take turns in an order that rotates each round - A B C, then B C A, then C A B - so none always runs first, warmest or coolest. A difference counts only when the two ranges don't overlap. How often would that rule call a difference real when there isn't one? If two builds were really the same, every ordering of their 2n results would be equally likely, and the ranges would come out clear in 2 of the C(2n, n) orderings. For 5 rounds, that's 2 in 252, under 1%. For 3 rounds it's 2 in 20, which is 10% - too likely, which is why our second attempt's 3-round blocks were all rerun with 5. Across the roughly 40 comparisons here, perhaps one of the narrow ones is luck. The big ones aren't.

t: What a governed call costs
x: Closed loop, for throughput. oha -c N keeps N callers busy, each sending its next request when the last one answers: 30 seconds per run, after a 5-second warm-up that fills the pool and the governance caches. Open loop, for latency under load. oha -q R --latency-correction sends R requests a second whatever happens, and times each from when it should have gone out. A closed loop under-reports latency at saturation, because a slow answer delays the next request; this avoids that, which is called coordinated omission. The rates run from 25% to 110% of capacity, 20 seconds each, and capacity is measured first in the same block.

x: One worker, the lookup, 32 callers: | Threads | Calls/s | p99 | | 1 | 788 (782-792) | 51.7 ms | | 2 | 843 (842-851) | 47.5 ms | | 4 | 777 (772-778) | 51.0 ms | | 8 | 735 (734-737) | 54.5 ms | An earlier post on this blog said queries spend most of their time waiting on the database, so threads do well. That's true for slow queries, and wrong for fast ones: Two threads were the fastest. One runs Python while the other waits on the database. Eight threads were 13% slower than two, and even slower than one. That's the Docker image's setting, and the extra threads compete for Python's interpreter lock and the logging module's lock. Threads are for calls that wait: slow queries, ?stream=true exports, and /events connections that stay open. Match them to your queries; the sizing rule below shows how.

t: What a governed call costs
x: A worker runs out of one of two things first: CPU. Plan on about 550 fast calls a second per worker, or 650 with the metadata cache. That's 75% of measured capacity, where p99 stays around 4 ms. Every millisecond of Python a call costs beyond this lookup lowers it. Waiting. A worker holds at most as many calls at once as it has threads, and each call waits for its query plus its round trips: 7 in 0.42, or 4 cached, at the network's round-trip time each. So a worker serves at most threads ÷ (query time + round trips × round-trip time) calls a second. Workers needed = the larger of (calls a second ÷ the CPU figure) and (calls a second ÷ the waiting figure), plus one you can afford to lose. Two examples, with a 0.5 ms network round trip and 8 threads: | Calls | CPU figure | Waiting figure | What limits a worker | | A 0.03 ms lookup, like ours | 550 a second | 8 ÷ (0.03 + 7 × 0.5 ms) ≈ 2,270 a second | CPU - so fewer threads would do | | A 20 ms report query | 550 a second, or fewer | 8 ÷ (20 + 3.5 ms) ≈ 340 a second | Waiting - so more threads would help | These are planning figures from one machine and one query shape. Before you commit to a number, measure your own queries at 75% of what you plan to serve.

t: What a governed call costs
x: Size with the rule above, then measure your own queries, which will usually cost more than ours. Turn on QUERYAPIGATE_METADATA_CACHE_TTL if you can accept a few seconds' delay for a change made on another instance to reach this one. It caches the rows, never a decision: whether a key is active, expired or used from an allowed address is still checked on every call, and a change made through the same server clears the cache at once. In return, a worker serves 16-23% more, PostgreSQL does half the work, and across a network a single call takes 41% less time. Match threads to your queries: 2 for fast lookups, which beats the default 8 by 15% here. Keep 8 or more for slow queries, exports and /events. Turn off gunicorn's access log if a proxy in front of it already logs requests: +7%. Scale with processes on their own cores. A hyperthread gave about half a core here.

t: What a governed call costs
x: The profile and the round-trip count turned the benchmark into a to-do list: Fewer round trips per query. Set the read-only mode and the time limit once per pooled connection instead of in every transaction, which takes a query from 4 round trips to 1. At a 0.5 ms round trip, that's about 1.7 ms off every call: from 6.2 to about 4.5 ms, and from 3.7 to about 2 ms cached. Skip the file-path safety check for server databases. Only SQLite, DuckDB and H2 open a file, so this saves 7-10% of CPU on every PostgreSQL, MySQL, ClickHouse and Trino call. Cache the masking hash key, which is read on every governed call and almost never changes. Cheaper logging: a setting to skip the per-request lines, and no single lock for every thread to wait on. Refresh the schema and masking trace in the background, so no governed call pays the 75 ms each minute.

x: This is our third write-up of these numbers. The first two had problems that reviewers caught. The first had two errors: It compared single runs on a laptop that, it turned out, was on battery and a power-saving profile, with nothing pinned. It reported about half the throughput this post does - 368 lookups a second where we now measure 743, with the same code. Three things changed at once since: power, core pinning, and taking Docker's proxy out of the path. We didn't test them one at a time, so we can't say which was worth how much. Power is likely most of it, because /health, which never touches PostgreSQL, doubled as well. It miscounted the store reads. It said a call's store transactions went from about 5.5 to 2.6. They actually went from 7 statements to 3. PostgreSQL can hold back an idle session's statistics for up to 10 seconds, and we read them 2 seconds after each run. The second fixed the method - pinning, interleaving, ranges, open-loop load - and a review rated it 4.1 out of 5. It still had problems, each fixed here: Some 3-round comparisons, which, as above, are wrong 10% of the time. Every one was rerun with 5. A threads result that cleared by 3 calls a second. With 5 rounds, it's clear by 50. Two overstatements. "Halved single-call latency" is now "−41%". "60-140 ms spikes every minute" is now "about 75 ms every minute, more on the first call". t: What a governed call costs
x: One machine. The gateway, the database and the load generator share one memory bus and one cooling system, on separate cores. Four physical cores for the gateway limit what scale-out can show. No TLS, load balancer or Redis in the path. Each would add to the cost of a call. A simulated network: one-way delay, without jitter or loss. Uniform random keys. Real traffic is skewed. A profiler that counts threads waiting for Python's lock as busy. So the shares say where time goes, not exactly how much a fix would save. No soak or failure tests: hours at 75% load, or losing PostgreSQL or a worker mid-run.

t: Agents can write now. A person approves each write.
x: QueryAPIGate 0.21 lets an AI agent write through a saved query, under rules its author set and with a person in the loop. It is experimental, and labelled as such in the product and the changelog.

t: Agents can write now. A person approves each write.
x: Until 0.21 the MCP server only ever read. Saved queries that write were not listed as tools, and since 0.20.1 a call naming one is refused before it runs. That rule still holds for every query not explicitly opened to agents. A saved query's author can now mark it agent_writes. It must be a single INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE; DDL is never allowed. Marked that way, it becomes a write tool for callers whose grant allows the write. Two modes: "approval" – the agent's first call does not run anything. It creates a write request with the exact SQL and the exact arguments. An administrator with the writes.approve capability sees it on the Console's new Approvals screen (or at /api/v1/write-requests), approves or rejects it, and the agent's second call runs it once, with exactly the approved arguments. Change an argument and the approval no longer matches. "insert" – an INSERT runs at once, with an idempotency key, for the cases where opening a ticket by itself is the point.

t: Agents can write now. A person approves each write.
x: Every agent write runs in a transaction and is rolled back if it touches more rows than the query's max_affected_rows. The credential that asked can never approve its own request (own_write). An agent cannot pile up more than 100 waiting writes. The audit log records the argument names and a hash, never the values. Whatever a write returns through RETURNING is masked like any read. A writes_awaiting_approval alert and the Agents screen's write counts keep the queue visible.

t: Agents can write now. A person approves each write.
h: Why a person, not a policy
x: A policy can say which rows an agent may change. It cannot say whether this particular change, right now, is the one you meant. For writes that matter, the approval step gives you that, with the SQL and arguments in front of you, and leaves both decisions in the audit log. Supported on PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and DuckDB. Guide 49 walks through it end to end.

t: Why every front door runs the same eight steps
x: QueryAPIGate has five ways in: REST endpoints, the MCP server, server-sent events, the export CLI and the Management API. Behind all of them is one engine, and one fixed sequence.

t: Why every front door runs the same eight steps
x: Identify the caller. API key, admin token, JWT or OAuth token, resolved to a named principal. Apply its limits. Rate limit, IP allow-list, expiry. Check the grant. This query, on this connection, in this mode. Validate parameters. Types, ranges, lengths. Values are bound, never spliced. Guard the SQL. Single statement, tables inside the allow-list, writes only where permitted. Run it. A pooled connection, a time limit, a row limit, a transaction for writes. Mask and format. Masking traced to source columns, then the format asked for. Record it. Run history, metrics, an event; the audit log for configuration changes. A step that fails stops the call with a typed error code, the same code whichever door the call came through.

t: Why every front door runs the same eight steps
x: The temptation with a new transport is to bolt on what it needs and move on. The MCP server, when it arrived, could have had its own authentication and its own idea of limits. Backlog item 61 moved rate limits, metrics and authentication out of REST's Flask hooks and into the core precisely so that could not happen. The consequence is simple to state: an AI agent cannot be governed less than an application because it arrived through a different protocol. The same grant, the same limits, the same masking rules, the same log.

t: Why every front door runs the same eight steps
x: A security fix lands once. 0.20.1 and 0.22.1 each closed a gap in one place. The access map is truthful. "Who can reach what" has one answer, not one per transport. New front doors are cheap. Exports to object storage and incremental deliveries reused everything from step 1 to step 8. The architecture diagram on the home page is this sequence drawn out, with the front doors on the left and the databases on the right.

t: One worker, many threads, and what Redis is actually for
x: Two deployment questions come up more than any others: why does the recommended gunicorn command run a single worker, and do I need Redis?

t: One worker, many threads, and what Redis is actually for
x: /metrics is per process. Prometheus scrapes one process and sees that process's counters. With four gunicorn workers behind one port, each scrape lands on a random one and the numbers jump around. So the recommended shape is one worker with several threads: gunicorn --workers 1 --worker-class gthread --threads 8 --timeout 120 "queryapigate.app:create_app()" Queries spend most of their time waiting on the database, so threads do well here. When one process is not enough, run more instances, each with its own port and its own /metrics, behind a reverse proxy. Prometheus scrapes them all and the bundled Grafana dashboard sums across instances.

t: One worker, many threads, and what Redis is actually for
x: Nothing, until you have more than one instance. Then it does three things: One response cache. A saved query with cache_ttl is warmed by whichever instance answered first and served from cache by all of them. Without Redis each process has its own cache. One rate-limit budget. A key limited to 60 requests a minute gets 60 across the fleet, counted as an atomic token bucket on Redis's clock, not 60 per instance. One event stream. queryapigate events reads every instance's runs.
